questions.fun_fact: In Japan, manga are read from right to left, starting from what would be the last page of a Western book.

questions.question: What kind of tree is the tallest in the world?
hints: It grows in forests near the coast of California, in the United States.
The tallest one is taller than a 30-story building.
Its name tells you the color of its bark and wood.
questions.description: A question you'll need to tilt your head way, way back for.
questions.fun_fact: The tallest known redwood is called Hyperion, it is about 116 m (381 ft) tall, and its exact location is kept secret to protect it.

questions.question: Look at this close-up: what is it?
hints: It grows on a tree, not in a vegetable garden.
Inside, it keeps seeds between its woody scales.
It comes from a tree that many people use as a real Christmas tree.
questions.description: It looks like a suit of armor made of scales, but nobody's inside.
questions.fun_fact: Pine cones open when the air is dry and close when it's damp, as if they could check the weather forecast.

questions.question: What were the names of the brothers who made the first flight in a powered airplane, in 1903?
hints: They were American, and their first names were Orville and Wilbur.
Before building airplanes, they had a shop where they fixed and sold bicycles.
Their last name sounds just like a word that means “correct”.
questions.description: Two brothers who, instead of fighting over the TV remote, started inventing things that fly.
questions.fun_fact: The Wright brothers’ first flight lasted only 12 seconds and covered about 37 m (120 ft), shorter than a modern passenger jet!

questions.question: In the NBA, a game is split into four quarters. How many minutes long is each quarter?
hints: It's longer than a quarter at the Olympics.
All four quarters together add up to almost an hour: 48 minutes.
It's the same number as the months in a year.
questions.description: The basketball clock is so stingy it stops every few seconds so it never gives away a single one.
questions.fun_fact: Because the clock stops for every foul and every time the ball goes out, an NBA game can really last more than two hours.

questions.question: In basketball, what do you call the play where a player jumps and pushes the ball down through the hoop from above?
hints: There are whole contests just for this play, full of amazing jumps.
Sometimes the player hangs from the rim for a moment afterward.
It's also what you do when you dip a cookie into a glass of milk.
questions.description: A play that leaves the hoop shaking and the other team looking up.
questions.fun_fact: Some dunks have been so hard that they shattered the glass backboard in the middle of a game.

questions.question: Which country does the sports car brand Lamborghini come from?
hints: It's a country in Europe.
Pizza was invented there too.
The country is shaped like a boot.
questions.description: A car so low that you almost have to lie down to get in.
questions.fun_fact: Before he made sports cars, Ferruccio Lamborghini built tractors for farms.

questions.question: The black sheet wrapped around many sushi rolls is called nori. What is it made of?
hints: It comes from a place full of water.
Before it was dried, it grew stuck to rocks.
If you see it at the beach, it sways with the waves.
questions.description: It looks like black paper and crunches like paper, but don't even think about writing on it.
questions.fun_fact: Nori sheets are made almost like paper: the seaweed is chopped, spread in thin layers and left to dry.

questions.question: Tempura came to Japan about 450 years ago from a European country. Which one?
hints: It is a country on the Iberian Peninsula.
It is the same country that colonized Brazil.
Its capital is Lisbon.
questions.description: A dish so Japanese that, surprise, it came over on a ship from Europe.
questions.fun_fact: The word “tempura” is thought to come from the Latin “tempora”, the fasting days when the Portuguese ate no meat and fried fish and vegetables instead.

questions.question: What is the largest hot desert in the world?
hints: It's in Africa.
It covers a large part of the north of that continent.
Its name comes from an Arabic word that simply means “desert.”
questions.description: A sandbox so big that all the cats in the world couldn't fill it.
questions.fun_fact: The Sahara is almost as big as the whole United States, and if you count cold deserts too, the largest desert of all is Antarctica.

questions.question: What did the ancient Egyptians do to a pharaoh's body after death, to preserve it for thousands of years?
hints: They used salts, oils and resins to dry it out.
At the end, they wrapped it in lots and lots of cloth bandages.
In horror movies, this bandaged body climbs out of its stone coffin.
questions.description: Pharaohs wanted to look good for thousands of years, and anti-wrinkle cream hadn't been invented yet.
questions.fun_fact: Preparing a pharaoh's body could take about 70 days.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this ring of light that sometimes appears around the Sun called?
hints: It shows up on days with very high, thin clouds.
It is made by millions of tiny ice crystals that bend the sunlight.
It has the same name as the ring drawn above angels' heads.
questions.description: Looks like the Sun put on a giant hoop to go out partying.
questions.fun_fact: The ice crystals that make a halo have six sides, like a tiny pencil, which is why the ring is almost always the same size.

questions.question: In a right triangle, what is the longest side called, the one opposite the right angle?
hints: The other two sides, the ones that form the right angle, have a different name.
It appears in the famous Pythagorean theorem.
Its long name starts with a sound like “hippo”.
questions.description: The longest side in the family, and it loves to show off about it.
questions.fun_fact: By the Pythagorean theorem, if a right triangle has legs of 3 and 4 centimeters, its hypotenuse is exactly 5.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this ancient board game called?
hints: It is one of the oldest board games in the world, and it is very popular in Africa.
You play it by moving seeds or small stones from hole to hole, with no dice.
Its name comes from an Arabic word that means “to move,” and it starts with “Man...”.
questions.description: A game where sowing seeds has nothing to do with gardening.
questions.fun_fact: Mancala boards carved into stone have been found that are more than a thousand years old.

questions.question: In chess, which piece moves in an “L” shape and can jump over other pieces?
hints: It's the only piece that can jump over others.
On the board, it's shaped like an animal's head.
It's the animal that neighs.
questions.description: One piece can't walk in a straight line, and it jumps over everyone too.
questions.fun_fact: A chess knight can visit all 64 squares of the board without landing on any square twice, a puzzle called the “knight's tour”.

questions.question: In the story of Pinocchio, what happens to him every time he tells a lie?
hints: It happens on his face.
You can see it from far away, and it gets longer.
It's the part of the body we smell with.
questions.description: A wooden puppet with a lie detector built right into his face.
questions.fun_fact: Pinocchio was written by the Italian author Carlo Collodi and first came out in chapters in a children's newspaper in 1881.

questions.question: What is the highest mountain in the Americas?
hints: It is in the Andes mountains.
It is in Argentina, close to the border with Chile.
Its name starts with “Acon…” and it is almost 7,000 m (23,000 ft) high.
questions.description: From Alaska down to the tip of Chile, only one peak gets to wear the crown.
questions.fun_fact: Aconcagua is the highest, but the top of Chimborazo in Ecuador is the point on Earth farthest from the planet's center, because Earth bulges out a little at the equator.

questions.question: The Bronze Age is named after bronze, which is made by mixing copper with another metal. Which one?
hints: It's not a precious metal: nobody made expensive jewelry from it.
It can't be iron, because iron got its own age later.
It's a soft, gray metal used to solder electronic wires.
questions.description: The secret recipe of prehistory: take one metal, add another, and name a whole era after it.
questions.fun_fact: The Iron Age came next, because working iron needed much hotter furnaces than bronze did.

questions.question: What does the Japanese word “kawaii” mean?
hints: It became famous around the world thanks to Japanese fashion and cartoons.
It's what people say when they see a baby kitten.
Hello Kitty is the perfect example of this word.
questions.description: Japan sent us cars, video games and words that stick like chewing gum.
questions.fun_fact: Hello Kitty is drawn without a mouth, and she is still one of the most famous characters in the world.

questions.question: When basketball was invented in 1891, what was hung on the gym walls for players to throw the ball into?
hints: They were containers used on farms and at markets.
They were used to carry fruit.
That fruit is round, fuzzy on the outside, and has a big pit inside.
questions.description: Before modern hoops, basketball had to make do with whatever was lying around in the storeroom.
questions.fun_fact: The first baskets still had their bottoms, so every time someone scored, the ball had to be fetched out with a ladder or a stick.

previous.feedback: The translation replaced the source's wrong answers (apple crates, milk buckets, fishing nets) with laundry, bread and egg baskets, even though the notes say the source options were kept. Because Peach baskets is now the only fruit container among the options, hint 2 ("They were used to carry fruit") gives the answer away. Make one wrong answer another fruit container, e.g. "Apple baskets", or keep the source's "Apple crates". Alternatively, rewrite hint 2 so it doesn't single out fruit.

questions.question: What is it called when your body jumps by itself again and again, and people say a scare or a drink of water makes it stop?
hints: Sometimes it starts after eating too fast or laughing a lot.
It comes in little jumps, one after another.
Its name sounds almost like the noise it makes.
questions.description: A little noise that shows up uninvited and won't leave no matter how nicely you ask.
questions.fun_fact: An American man named Charles Osborne had the hiccups for about 68 years in a row.

questions.question: What is the writing system of the ancient Egyptians called?
hints: They carved it into temples and tombs, and also painted it on papyrus.
For centuries nobody could read it, until the Rosetta Stone was found.
When someone's handwriting is impossible to read, people say it looks like… this.
questions.description: Long before emojis, the Egyptians were already sending messages full of little faces, birds and eyes.
questions.fun_fact: In 1822, the Frenchman Jean-François Champollion cracked the code of hieroglyphs with the help of the Rosetta Stone.

questions.question: Look at the photo: which Winter Olympic sport are they playing?
hints: This sport was born in Scotland centuries ago.
Players slide a heavy stone across the ice toward a target made of circles.
Teammates scrub the ice with brooms in front of the stone to guide it.
questions.description: A sport so calm your grandpa could play it in his slippers, and they still hand out Olympic medals for it.
questions.fun_fact: Almost all Olympic curling stones are made of granite from one small Scottish island called Ailsa Craig.

questions.question: At a store, you buy 3 empanadas at 2,500 pesos each and a soft drink for 3,000 pesos. You pay with a 20,000-peso bill. How much change do you get?
hints: First work out how much the three empanadas cost.
The three empanadas cost 7,500 pesos; now add the drink.
You spend 10,500 pesos in total: subtract that from 20,000.
questions.description: A question to find out if you can afford your snack or need to borrow money from your brother.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia's old 20,000-peso bill showed Julio Garavito, an astronomer from Bogotá who has a crater on the Moon named after him.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is the name of this famous mountain?
hints: It stands on the border between Switzerland and Italy.
Its shape, like a crooked pyramid, makes it one of the most photographed mountains in the world.
For years it was drawn on the box of a famous Swiss chocolate made of triangles.
questions.description: A mountain so pointy it looks like a first grader drew it.
questions.fun_fact: The Matterhorn, called Cervino in Italian, was on the Toblerone chocolate logo until 2023, and that logo had a bear hidden in it!

questions.question: How many mountains in the world are taller than 8,000 m (26,247 ft)?
hints: There are so few that mountain climbers know the list by heart.
All of them are in Asia, in the Himalayas and the Karakoram.
There are more than 10 but fewer than 20.
questions.description: A club so exclusive that you need your head above the clouds to get in.
questions.fun_fact: These peaks are called “eight-thousanders,” and the first climber to reach the top of all 14 was Reinhold Messner from Italy, in 1986.

questions.question: Look at this museum skeleton: which prehistoric animal is it?
hints: It lived during the Ice Age, and early humans hunted it.
Look at those huge, curved tusks.
Manny from the movie “Ice Age” is one of them.
questions.description: This museum gentleman doesn't have an ounce of meat left, but he still poses for photos.
questions.fun_fact: The last mammoths lived on Wrangel Island in the Arctic until about 4,000 years ago, when the pyramids of Egypt had already been built.

questions.question: Many modern soccer jerseys are made from thread spun out of recycled trash. What trash is recycled to make that fabric?
hints: Almost every home throws this kind of trash out every week.
They are shredded, melted and stretched into thin threads.
Before becoming a jersey, it may have held water or juice.
questions.description: Your favorite jersey may have a secret past it would rather not talk about.
questions.fun_fact: At the 2010 World Cup, several national teams played in jerseys made from up to eight recycled plastic bottles each.

questions.question: The Flash, Aquaman and Cyborg: what do they have in common?
hints: All three fight together in a famous superhero team.
Batman, Superman and Wonder Woman are on that team too.
The team's name sounds like a group that stands up for what is fair.
questions.description: One runs, one swims and one is half robot: the strangest group chat in the universe.
questions.fun_fact: A movie about this team came out in 2017, and in 2021 the same director released another version that ran about 4 hours!

previous.feedback: The question asks “what do they have in common?” about three given characters, and that question style is retired (reason 7). The translation itself is faithful and reads naturally, but the format can't stay.

questions.question: He's a millionaire with no superpowers, goes out at night to watch over his city and has a secret hideout in a cave. Which superhero is he?
hints: All his power comes from his brains, his training and his gadgets.
He has a butler named Alfred and a very famous car.
His costume is black and his symbol is an animal that flies at night.
questions.description: He has more money than a bank, and still he'd rather spend his nights chasing robbers.
questions.fun_fact: Batman first appeared in a comic book in 1939, more than 85 years ago!

questions.question: What planet does Superman come from?
hints: It's a made-up planet that exploded when Superman was a baby.
His parents sent him to Earth in a small spaceship.
The green rock that takes away his strength comes from this planet.
questions.description: An alien who works at a newspaper, and nobody recognizes him because he puts on glasses.
questions.fun_fact: There is a real gas called krypton, discovered in 1898; its name comes from a Greek word meaning “hidden.”

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this piece of a knight’s armor called?
hints: It protected the knight’s most important part: the one that does the thinking.
Many had only a tiny slit to look through.
It’s a short word that starts with H.
questions.description: The closest thing to a motorcycle helmet in the year 1200, just without the plastic visor.
questions.fun_fact: Some medieval helms weighed about 3 or 4 kg (7 to 9 lb). That’s like carrying several bags of rice on your head!

review.feedback: Fact check: wrong. The answer (Helm) and the wrong answers (breastplate, gauntlet, greave) are right, and the hints are fine. The fun fact overstates the weight. Surviving 13th-century great helms weigh about 1.5–3 kg: examples are 2.26 kg, 2.7 kg and a Templar-style helm at 3.0 kg. 4 kg (9 lb) is above that range.

questions.question: Which Italian coffee dessert has a name that means “pick me up” or “cheer me up”?
hints: It is served cold, with cocoa powder dusted on top.
It is built in layers in a dish, using long sponge cookies called ladyfingers.
Its name starts with “tira”...
questions.description: A dessert with caffeine: finally, something parents and kids both want to share.
questions.fun_fact: Two Italian regions, Veneto and Friuli, have been arguing for years over which one invented tiramisu.

questions.question: Which language has the most native speakers (people who learn it as babies) in the world?
hints: It is spoken mostly in one country in Asia.
That country has more than a billion people and a very, very long wall.
It is written with thousands of characters instead of letters, and it is the language of Beijing.
questions.description: If this language had a group chat, the phone would never stop buzzing.
questions.fun_fact: Spanish has the second most native speakers in the world, even more than English!

questions.question: Many English words that start with “al-”, like “algebra”, “alcohol” and “alchemy”, come from the same language. Which one?
hints: Many of these words came to Europe through scholars in medieval Spain, ruled for centuries by people from North Africa.
In this language, “al” means “the”.
Today it's spoken in Morocco, Egypt and Saudi Arabia.
questions.description: Words that went on a very long trip and decided to stay for centuries.
questions.fun_fact: The word “algorithm” comes from the name of al-Khwarizmi, a Persian mathematician who wrote his books in Arabic about 1,200 years ago.

questions.question: What do you call a program that chats with you in writing as if it were a person?
hints: Its name is made of two short words stuck together.
Many customer service websites use one to answer questions at any hour.
Its name joins “chat” with a short piece of the word “robot”.
questions.description: It's the friend who always answers right away, never gets tired, and doesn't even have a face.
questions.fun_fact: One of the first chatbots, ELIZA, was made in the 1960s and pretended to be a therapist who answered with more questions.

questions.question: Which inflatable Disney robot takes care of people's health and is Hiro's best friend?
hints: The movie is set in a city that mixes San Francisco with Tokyo.
In the end, he becomes a superhero with red armor in “Big Hero 6”.
His name starts with “Bay” and ends like the start of “maximum”.
questions.description: It's white, soft, puffs up like a balloon, and asks you to rate your pain from 1 to 10.
questions.fun_fact: The filmmakers got the idea from a real inflatable robot arm they saw at a university in the United States.

questions.question: What do the letters “www” stand for at the start of many website addresses?
hints: It's three English words, and the first one means the whole planet.
It's a huge network linking pages from all over the planet.
The last word is what a spider spins.
questions.description: Three letters you type without thinking, like saying “hello” without knowing where the word comes from.
questions.fun_fact: British scientist Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web in 1989 while working at CERN, a lab in Switzerland.

questions.question: What was the name of the Roman god of fire and blacksmiths, who made weapons in a forge hidden under a mountain?
hints: He was married to Venus, the goddess of love.
The Greeks called him Hephaestus.
His name sounds a lot like the mountains that spit out lava.
questions.description: The only god on Mount Olympus who went to work in overalls and smelled of coal.
questions.fun_fact: The word “volcano” comes from Vulcan, because the Romans believed the smoke from volcanoes came from his forge.

questions.question: Which Roman god gave his name to the month of March?
hints: He was the god of war.
A red planet is named after him.
His name sounds almost the same as the month's, just a few letters shorter.
questions.description: A calendar month that, deep down, is itching for a fight.
questions.fun_fact: For the ancient Romans, the year began in March; that's why “September” (from the Latin for seven) was the seventh month.

questions.question: What is the name of the big stone box that held a mummy's coffin?
hints: The word comes from ancient Greek.
Archaeologists find it inside tombs, sometimes with the dead person's face carved on the lid.
It starts with “sar-” and ends with “-ophagus”.
questions.description: A box so fancy that nobody is in a hurry to try it out.
questions.fun_fact: The word “sarcophagus” comes from Greek and means something like “flesh-eater”.

questions.question: What number comes next in this series: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25...?
hints: Look at how much it grows each time: 3, 5, 7, 9...
Each number is another number multiplied by itself.
questions.description: A series that grows like the pile of homework you leave for Sunday.
questions.fun_fact: They're called “square numbers” because 36 tiles can make a perfect 6-by-6 square.

questions.question: In Roman numerals, what number does the letter D stand for?
hints: It's a three-digit number.
It's bigger than C, which stands for 100.
It's exactly half of M, which stands for 1,000.
questions.description: The Romans conquered half the world without a calculator, and this is how they wrote their sums.
questions.fun_fact: The Romans had no symbol at all for zero.

questions.question: What is the white sap of the rubber tree, the one used to make rubber, called?
hints: It comes out white like milk and gets sticky in the air.
Balloons and doctors' gloves are made from it.
A common type of wall paint is named after it.
questions.description: Trees cry too, but their tears end up as car tires.
questions.fun_fact: Long before Europeans arrived, Indigenous peoples of the Americas were already making bouncing balls from this tree's sap.

questions.question: What is meringue, the base of Bogotá's merengón dessert, made of?
hints: It's whipped and whipped until it's white and stiff, then baked.
It comes from something that hens lay.
It's the clear part of the egg, not the yellow part.
questions.description: A dessert so fluffy it looks like a cloud that let itself get caught.
questions.fun_fact: If the whites are whipped well enough, you can turn the bowl upside down over your head and they won't fall out.

questions.question: What is the long, hollow tube that some Amazon peoples use to shoot small darts when hunting?
hints: It needs no string and no rubber band, only air.
It's used to hunt birds and monkeys high up in the trees, without making a sound.
Its name starts with what you do to the candles on a birthday cake.
questions.description: A hunting tool for people who like to keep things very quiet in the treetops.
questions.fun_fact: Some Amazon hunters coat their dart tips with curare, a plant poison that paralyzes the prey.

questions.question: What is the largest single flower in the world?
hints: It grows in the rainforests of Indonesia and Malaysia.
It has no leaves, no stem and no roots: it lives as a parasite on a vine.
It can be nearly a meter (about 3 ft) across and smells like rotting meat to attract flies.
questions.description: A flower so big it fits in no vase, and it smells awful too.
questions.fun_fact: Rafflesia smells like rotting meat on purpose: that's how it attracts the flies that help pollinate it.

questions.question: Robert Wadlow is the tallest man in history. About how tall was he?
hints: He was much taller than any basketball player.
A normal door is about 2 meters (6.5 ft) tall, and he had to duck low to get through.
He was almost three meters tall, but not quite.
questions.description: This man never had to ask for help reaching the top shelf.
questions.fun_fact: Robert Wadlow kept growing his whole life because his body made too much growth hormone.

questions.question: The company that created TikTok is from which country?
hints: It's a country in Asia.
Paper and gunpowder were invented there.
The Great Wall is there.
questions.description: An app that turns five quick minutes into three hours, and nobody knows how.
questions.fun_fact: TikTok isn't used inside that country, which has its own version called Douyin.

questions.question: You're watching a downpour in the distance while the sun warms the back of your neck. Looking toward the rain, what are you most likely to see in the sky?
hints: It always appears on the side opposite the sun.
Each tiny raindrop works like a prism that splits the light.
It is shaped like an arch and has seven colors, from red to violet.
questions.description: The weather can't decide between rain and sunshine, so the sky solves the problem in style.
questions.fun_fact: From an airplane you can sometimes see a complete rainbow shaped like a circle, because there is no ground to cut it off.

questions.question: If someone in Germany says “Danke” to you, what are they saying?
hints: Your parents taught you to say it when you were little.
It's one of the “magic words” of good manners.
It sounds a lot like its English meaning.
questions.description: Germany has some super long words, but this one is so tiny it fits on a stick of gum.
questions.fun_fact: “Danke” in German and “thank” in English sound alike because the two languages are cousins that grew from the same old language.

questions.question: The guinea pig is a popular pet. Which continent does it originally come from?
hints: Indigenous peoples tamed it thousands of years ago.
It comes from the same continent as the potato.
In Peru and Ecuador it's a traditional dish.
questions.description: Its name says pig, but it never oinks or rolls around in the mud.
questions.fun_fact: When a guinea pig is very happy, it jumps into the air; this is called “popcorning,” like a kernel of popping corn.

questions.question: Look at the photo: which famous museum in Paris has this glass pyramid at its entrance?
hints: Before it was a museum, this building was a palace of the kings of France.
The most famous painting in the world is kept here: the Mona Lisa.
Its name starts with the letter L.
questions.description: A royal palace that now gets more visitors than any king ever did in a lifetime.
questions.fun_fact: The Louvre is the most visited museum in the world, and it has so many works that seeing them all, one minute each, would take weeks.

questions.question: How many meters long is an Olympic swimming pool?
hints: A very fast Olympic swimmer gets from one end to the other in about 21 seconds.
It's roughly half as long as a soccer field.
In the 100-meter race, swimmers go to the far end and come back just once.
questions.description: A pool so big that your mom yells “Don't go too far!” and you're already halfway across.
questions.fun_fact: An Olympic pool holds at least 2.5 million liters (about 660,000 gallons) of water, enough to fill more than 10,000 bathtubs!

questions.question: Where does açaí, the purple fruit eaten in bowls with banana and granola, come from?
questions.answer: From a palm in the Amazon rainforest
wrong_answers: From a shrub in the high Andes grasslands
From a palm on Caribbean beaches
From a tree on Colombian coffee farms
hints: It grows somewhere very hot and humid, where it rains almost every day.
People there have eaten it for a very long time, long before it became trendy in cities.
It comes from the same rainforest as the river that carries the most water in the world.
questions.description: It's purple, comes with granola and costs more than a full lunch.
questions.fun_fact: In the Brazilian Amazon, many people eat açaí without sugar as part of lunch, with fish and cassava flour.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this typical sweet from the Colombian coast called?
hints: They're sold all over the beaches of Cartagena and Santa Marta, on trays carried on the head.
They're sticky and sweet, with little white shreds inside.
Their main ingredient is the hairy fruit that falls from palm trees.
questions.description: A sweet so sticky it keeps your teeth glued together until the next day.
questions.fun_fact: In Cartagena, the palenqueras, women street sellers in colorful dresses, sell cocadas in many flavors, like guava, pineapple and even milk.

questions.question: Look at this close-up: which dessert is it?
hints: It's a creamy dessert that lots of grandmas make in a pot.
It often gets cinnamon sprinkled on top.
Look at the little grains: they're the same ones often served with dinner.
questions.description: The dessert grandmas stir so patiently that they deserve an Olympic medal.
questions.fun_fact: Rice pudding is made in almost every Spanish-speaking country, and there's even a children's song about it: “Arroz con leche, me quiero casar” (“Rice pudding, I want to get married”).

questions.question: In tennis, what do you call a serve so good that the other player can't even touch the ball?
hints: Every player dreams of hitting one when stepping up to serve.
Big servers can hit dozens of them in a single tournament.
It shares its name with a playing card: the one with a single symbol in the middle.
questions.description: A serve so fast that the other player is still looking for the ball in the parking lot.
questions.fun_fact: The world's best servers hit over 220 km/h (137 mph), and the official record is around 250 km/h (155 mph).

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this type of tennis court surface called?
hints: It's Rafael Nadal's favorite surface.
At the French Open (Roland Garros) in Paris, players slide on it and kick up red dust.
It's made by crushing the same red bricks used to build houses.
questions.description: A court where players go home with socks of a whole new color.
questions.fun_fact: Rafael Nadal won the French Open, which is played on this surface, 14 times.

questions.question: What is a “vlog”?
questions.answer: A diary-style video where someone shows their everyday life
wrong_answers: A video where someone plays video games live
A short video where someone dances to a trending song
A video where someone teaches how to cook a recipe
hints: The word mixes “video” with another internet word.
That other word is “blog”, a website where someone keeps posting entries.
It's like writing a diary, but with a camera in your hand.
questions.description: A word that sounds like a swamp creature, but actually lives on YouTube.
questions.fun_fact: “Vlog” comes from joining “video” and “blog”, and “blog” itself comes from “web log”, something like a logbook of the web.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this object, once used to store computer files, called?
hints: You pushed it into a slot in the computer, and it made little noises while being read.
It's square and plastic, with a small metal cover that slides open.
Its picture is still the “Save” button in many programs.
questions.description: Your parents saved their school homework on this and prayed it wouldn't break.
questions.fun_fact: A floppy disk held just 1.44 MB: less than a single photo taken with a modern phone.

questions.question: What do you call the physical parts of a computer, the ones you can touch, like the keyboard, the screen and the mouse?
hints: Like the other options, it ends in “-ware”.
The opposite is programs and apps, which you can't touch.
Its first half is the opposite of “soft”.
questions.description: The thing you might want to kick when the computer freezes (please don't).
questions.fun_fact: There's an old joke among computer people: hardware is the part you can hit, and software is the part you can only yell at.

questions.question: At the Wimbledon tennis tournament in London, what color must almost all of the players' clothing be?
hints: It's a very old and very strict rule: they even check socks and caps.
People say it was once meant to hide sweat stains.
It's the color of milk and snow.
questions.description: A tournament so fancy it has a dress code, like your rich aunt's wedding.
questions.fun_fact: About 2 million strawberries with cream are eaten at Wimbledon during the tournament.

questions.question: An earthquake starts at a point deep underground. What is the point on the surface right above it called?
hints: This word comes up a lot in the news every time the ground shakes.
It starts with a Greek prefix that means “on” or “above.”
It literally means “the center on top.”
questions.description: When the Earth starts dancing without asking, this is where the party begins… at least when you look from above.
questions.fun_fact: The underground point where an earthquake really starts is called the hypocenter, and it can be more than 600 km (370 miles) deep.

questions.question: Think of a number. Multiply it by 2, add 10, divide the result by 2, and subtract the number you first thought of. What do you get?
hints: Try it with an easy number, like 1.
When you divide by 2, your number goes back to what it was… and the 10 gets cut in half too.
You end up with half of the number you added at the start.
questions.description: A magic trick where the magician is secretly a calculator in disguise.
questions.fun_fact: The trick works with any number: with 7, with 1,000, and even with your phone number.

questions.question: Look at this close-up of a vegetable cut in half: which vegetable is it?
hints: The wavy white lines are really leaves packed tightly against each other.
Whole, it's a heavy round ball, and people eat a lot of it in salads.
It's a purple cousin of the green leafy ball used to make sauerkraut.
questions.description: A purple maze that someone sliced in half with a knife.
questions.fun_fact: Red cabbage juice changes color: it turns pink with lemon and green or blue with baking soda.

questions.question: Which company bought YouTube in 2006, just one year after it started?
hints: This company's name comes from a math word for a gigantic number.
This company also makes Android, the system on lots and lots of phones.
When you don't know something, you look it up on its famous search engine.
questions.description: YouTube has a dad too, and it's a very, very rich dad.
questions.fun_fact: The first YouTube video, uploaded in 2005, is only 19 seconds long and shows one of its creators in front of some elephants at a zoo.

questions.question: Listen: which farm animal makes this sound?
hints: It's a working animal that carries loads on many farms.
It has very long ears.
Its sound is called braying: “hee-haw, hee-haw”.
questions.description: This farm neighbor sings at five in the morning, and nobody asked for a serenade.
questions.fun_fact: A donkey's bray can be heard more than 3 km (about 2 miles) away.

questions.question: Who holds the world record in the 100 meters?
hints: He's from a Caribbean country famous for its sprinters.
He's Jamaican and celebrated his wins by pointing at the sky as if throwing lightning.
His last name is also a word for a flash of lightning.
questions.description: If this man is late for school, it's because he never even left the house.
questions.fun_fact: Usain Bolt ran the 100 meters in 9.58 seconds in 2009, reaching almost 45 km/h (28 mph) at his fastest.

questions.question: On a painter's color wheel, red sits directly opposite green. By the same rule, what color sits directly opposite blue?
hints: Look closely: green is made by mixing the two primary colors that aren't red.
The color opposite a primary color is made by mixing the other two primary colors.
Mix red with yellow and you get the color of a fruit that has the same name.
questions.description: Some colors get along so badly that they stand face to face, just glaring at each other.
questions.fun_fact: Opposite colors are called complementary colors, and side by side they look brighter, which is why so many movie posters use blue and orange.

questions.question: A long-lasting light bulb, the phonograph and one of the first movie cameras: which inventor developed them?
hints: He was from the United States and worked with a big team in his lab.
This inventor was called “the Wizard of Menlo Park” and held more than a thousand patents.
His last name starts with E.
questions.description: Three inventions, one proud dad, and not one of them ever helped him with his homework.
questions.fun_fact: Edison registered more than 1,000 patents, and as a boy he went to school for only a few months: his mom taught him the rest.

questions.question: What invention did the Italian scientist Alessandro Volta present in 1800?
hints: His last name is hidden in a word used to measure electricity.
He stacked metal discs separated by cardboard soaked in salt water.
Today you put one in the TV remote when it stops working.
questions.description: An Italian with so much energy that they even named a unit of measurement after him.
questions.fun_fact: The unit “volt”, which you see printed on chargers and batteries, is named in honor of Volta.

questions.question: Papyrus, the sheet the ancient Egyptians wrote on, was made from a plant that grew along a river. Which river?
hints: It is a river in Africa.
It is one of the longest rivers in the world.
It flows very close to the pyramids and into the Mediterranean Sea.
questions.description: Long before notebooks, the Egyptians had their own stationery store… right by the water.
questions.fun_fact: The word “paper” comes from “papyrus”, even though today's paper is made from wood, not from that plant.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is the name of this famous site with its Maya pyramid?
hints: It is one of the New Seven Wonders of the World.
It is on the Yucatán Peninsula, in Mexico.
Its name has two words, and the second one starts with “I”.
questions.description: A pyramid with stairs on all four sides, in case the god couldn't be bothered to walk around.
questions.fun_fact: At the equinoxes, the shadows on the stairs form a serpent of light that seems to slide down the pyramid.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this bird that many farmers raise?
hints: It loves eating bugs and ticks in the grass.
It is dark gray, covered in little white dots, and has a bald head.
Its name joins an African country and an old word for farm birds like chickens.
questions.description: It wore a polka-dot dress to the party and forgot to comb its hair.
questions.fun_fact: Many farms keep them as an “alarm”: they screech loudly when a stranger arrives or they spot a snake.

questions.question: How many toes does a horse have on each leg?
hints: Fewer than the fingers on one of your hands.
A horse's hoof is made of the same stuff as your fingernails.
A cow's hoof is split in two, but a horse's hoof is one single piece.
questions.description: This animal has spent its whole life walking on tiptoe, like a ballet dancer.
questions.fun_fact: Millions of years ago, the horse's ancestors were the size of a dog and had several toes on each foot.

questions.question: What is a baby sheep called?
hints: It's not the baby of a cow or a horse.
Its mom's wool is used to make scarves.
Nativity scenes often have a small, white, woolly one next to the shepherds.
questions.description: So fluffy you'd love to use it as a pillow, but it would rather you didn't.
questions.fun_fact: A sheep can recognize the faces of about 50 other sheep and remember them for years.

questions.question: In the shot put, roughly how much does the shot thrown by men weigh?
hints: It is thrown with one hand, pushed off from the neck.
It weighs about as much as a well-fed six-month-old baby.
It weighs more than 5 kg, but less than 10 kg.
questions.description: It's not a bowling ball, but you still don't want to drop it on your foot.
questions.fun_fact: The men's shot weighs exactly 7.26 kg (16 lb), and the women's weighs 4 kg (about 8.8 lb).

questions.question: Look at this picture, taken very, very close up: what is it?
hints: These little tiles are so tiny that, all together, they look like dust.
Its owner flies, but it isn't a bird.
If you touch it with your fingers, you're left with a colorful powder.
questions.description: Colorful tiles for a roof the size of a fingernail.
questions.fun_fact: The “dust” left on your fingers after touching a butterfly is thousands of tiny scales from its wings.

questions.question: Crimson, scarlet and vermilion: what do they have in common?
hints: Painters use these names for colors.
Their color is one of the three primary colors in painting.
It's the color of a ripe strawberry.
questions.description: Three fancy names for something the rest of us call with just one word.
questions.fun_fact: Centuries ago, carmine, a very fine red, was made from tiny insects called cochineal that live on cactus plants in the Americas.

previous.feedback: The question asks what three given things have in common (“what do they have in common?”). That format is retired (reason 7), in the translation just as in the source, so this question should be dropped or recast as a new question.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this old invention called?
hints: Over 100 years ago, families had one at home for entertainment.
Many worked without electricity: you wound them up with a crank.
You set a black disc spinning and the music came out of that big horn.
questions.description: Your great-grandparents kept it in the living room and treated it better than the cat.
questions.fun_fact: For decades, gramophone records weren't made of vinyl but of shellac, a material that comes from an insect.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this meat-eating plant called?
hints: In the wild, it grows only in a few swamps in the United States.
Its leaves look like a mouth with teeth and snap shut when an insect touches them.
Its name includes a planet and tells you what it catches.
questions.description: A plant that ordered food delivery, and lunch flew right in.
questions.fun_fact: So it doesn't waste energy on false alarms, the trap only closes if an insect touches its tiny trigger hairs twice within a few seconds.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is the name of the river that flows under this famous bridge?
hints: This river ends in the North Sea.
It's the river of London, the capital of England.
Its name starts with “Th…”.
questions.description: A bridge that throws its arms in the air like someone just scored a goal.
questions.fun_fact: Tower Bridge opens in the middle to let tall ships through, and it still does so hundreds of times a year.

questions.question: In which present-day country was Tetris, the game where you fit falling blocks together, invented in 1984?
hints: It wasn't invented at a video game company, but at a computer research center.
The first Tetris ran on a computer so simple it had no graphics: the blocks were drawn with letters and symbols.
The inventor worked in Moscow, in what was then the Soviet Union.
questions.description: The one game where tidying up is fun, something your mom never managed with your bedroom.
questions.fun_fact: The famous Tetris tune on the Game Boy is an old Russian folk song called “Korobeiniki.”

questions.question: Which video game character is this? A round pink ball from Nintendo that sucks in enemies, swallows them and copies their powers.
hints: Its first game came out in 1992 on the Game Boy.
Besides swallowing enemies, it can puff up like a balloon to fly.
Its name starts with K.
questions.description: A piece of pink bubble gum with endless hunger and zero table manners.
questions.fun_fact: On the box of Kirby's first game in the United States, he was drawn white, because the Game Boy couldn't show colors.

questions.question: What is the longest river in Africa?
hints: It crosses a huge desert before it reaches the Mediterranean Sea.
The ancient Egyptians lived along its banks.
The pyramids and the pharaohs depended on it for water and crops.
questions.description: A river so long that if you paddle it in a canoe, you'll grow a beard on the way, even if you can't grow one.
questions.fun_fact: The Nile runs about 6,650 km (4,130 miles) through 11 countries, and for thousands of years its floods made Egypt's fields fertile.

questions.question: Which Marvel character is this? He's a scientist who turns into a super-strong green giant when he gets angry.
hints: He's one of the Avengers.
When he changes, his shirt rips to pieces, but his pants almost always survive.
When he's calm, his name is Bruce Banner.
questions.description: This guy has a serious temper problem, and it costs him a fortune in clothes.
questions.fun_fact: In his first comic, in 1962, Hulk was gray, but he was made green because the printer had trouble printing that color well.

questions.question: In the Marvel movies, what metal is Captain America's round shield made of?
hints: It's a made-up metal that doesn't exist in real life.
It can soak up hits and vibrations with almost no damage.
Black Panther's suit is made of this same metal.
questions.description: If this shield were made of cardboard, Captain America's career would have been very short.
questions.fun_fact: In his first comic, from 1941, Captain America's shield wasn't round: it was shaped like a knight's shield, pointed at the bottom.

questions.question: Which video game character is this? A blue robot boy built by the kind Dr. Light, with a cannon arm that copies each defeated boss's weapon.
hints: His first game came out in 1987 for the Nintendo NES console.
He was created by the Japanese company Capcom, and his great enemy is the evil Dr. Wily.
His name puts a word for “huge” in front of a word for “guy”.
questions.description: A robot with a simple shopping plan: beat the villain, then take his weapon home for free.
questions.fun_fact: In Japan he is called Rockman, and his robot sister is called Roll: together they make “Rock and Roll”.

questions.question: In the Super Mario games, which princess does Bowser kidnap again and again for Mario to rescue?
hints: She is the princess of the Mushroom Kingdom.
She wears a pink dress and a golden crown.
She shares her name with a soft, fuzzy fruit.
questions.description: The princess with the worst security system in the whole kingdom.
questions.fun_fact: In the game “Super Princess Peach,” the roles are reversed: she is the hero and has to rescue Mario.

questions.question: In the rainforests of Colombia, this animal is called a saíno. It looks like a wild pig, but it isn't one. What group does it really belong to?
hints: This group lives only in the Americas, from the southern United States down to Argentina.
They look like pigs, but their family split off from pigs millions of years ago.
Scientists also call this group tayassuids.
questions.description: It has the face of a pig, the smell of cheap perfume and zero interest in being mistaken for one.
questions.fun_fact: The saíno has a gland on its back that gives off a strong smell, and the herd uses it to recognize each other.

questions.question: They built the great pyramid of Chichén Itzá, and their languages are still spoken in Mexico and Guatemala. Who are they?
hints: They wrote with glyphs, little pictures that stood for words and sounds.
They used zero long before the Europeans did.
Their name is also the name of a famous cartoon bee.
questions.description: Neighbors who kept track of the days better than the calendar on your fridge.
questions.fun_fact: The Maya were using zero in their math more than 1,500 years ago, long before it was known in Europe.

questions.question: Scandinavia, in northern Europe, is the land of Vikings, fjords and northern lights. Which three countries make it up?
hints: All three are kingdoms that still have kings and queens.
Their languages are so alike that people there can almost understand each other.
One inspired the landscapes of “Frozen”, and another is the home of LEGO.
questions.description: A region so serious about the cold that even the furniture comes flat-packed in a box.
questions.fun_fact: Norwegians, Swedes and Danes can understand each other quite well while each speaks their own language.

questions.question: In which decade did George Eastman launch the first Kodak camera, with the slogan “You press the button, we do the rest”?
hints: It was in the same century that photography was invented.
Around those years, the telephone and Edison's light bulb also appeared.
The 20th century was only a little more than ten years away.
questions.description: Before phone cameras, taking a photo was an act of faith: you waited days to find out if your eyes were closed.
questions.fun_fact: The 1888 Kodak camera came loaded with film for 100 photos, and you had to mail the whole camera back to the factory to get them developed.

questions.question: In Monopoly, you run out of cash and mortgage a property that cost you $200. Under the classic rules, how much does the bank give you?
hints: The bank doesn't give back everything you paid.
The mortgage value is printed on the back of the title deed card.
It's exactly half the price.
questions.description: For when you run out of cash and pawn your streets to the bank like an old phone.
questions.fun_fact: While a property is mortgaged you can't collect rent on it, and to get it back you must pay the bank the mortgage plus 10% interest.

questions.question: In ancient Greece, one athlete ran, jumped, threw the discus and javelin, and wrestled. What was this contest called?
hints: Count on your fingers how many events the athlete had to do.
The Greek prefix in the name means the same number as the sides of a pentagon.
Penta- = five.
questions.description: When one sport wasn't enough to show off, the Greeks invented the full combo.
questions.fun_fact: In the long jump of the ancient pentathlon, athletes jumped holding stone or metal weights in their hands to push themselves farther.

questions.question: “Half man, half horse” is to centaur as “half woman, half fish” is to…
hints: She lives in the sea, but she is a creature from legends.
In the stories, she sings beautifully to lure sailors.
Ariel, from the Disney movie, is one of them.
questions.description: A singer who never goes on tour because she has no feet.
questions.fun_fact: When Christopher Columbus saw manatees in the Caribbean, he wrote that he had seen mermaids, but that they were not as pretty as people painted them!

questions.question: During a “red tide”, the sea looks reddish. Where does that color come from?
hints: The color comes from something alive.
They are too small to see with the naked eye, but millions of them together paint the water.
It's a kind of microscopic sea plant that multiplies like crazy.
questions.description: The sea blushes too, but not because it's embarrassed.
questions.fun_fact: Some of these microscopic algae make toxic substances, so during a red tide eating shellfish from the area is sometimes banned.

questions.question: If you tie a polystyrene foam cup to an underwater robot and send it down more than 6,000 m (19,700 ft), what happens to it?
questions.answer: It shrinks into a tiny cup
wrong_answers: It bursts into a thousand bits
It puffs up like a balloon
hints: Think about all the weight of the water above the cup.
The pressure down there is hundreds of times greater than at the surface.
Polystyrene foam is full of tiny air bubbles, and the pressure squashes them.
questions.description: Down there, the water squeezes harder than a hug from Grandma.
questions.fun_fact: Scientists on deep-sea trips often decorate foam cups and send them to the bottom, and they come back as souvenirs the size of a thimble.

questions.question: In the morning you build a sandcastle at low tide, when the water is farthest out. About how many hours until the next low tide?
hints: The tide goes up and down more than once in the same day.
Most beaches have two low tides a day.
It's roughly half a day.
questions.description: The sea keeps office hours: it leaves, comes back, and leaves again.
questions.fun_fact: Tides come about 50 minutes later each day because they follow the rhythm of the Moon, not the Sun.

questions.question: Which country has this long, narrow shape, stretching more than 4,000 km (2,500 miles) from north to south?
hints: It is in South America, along the Pacific Ocean.
The Andes mountains separate it from its neighbor to the east.
Its capital is Santiago.
questions.description: If this country were a spaghetti noodle, it would be the longest one on the plate.
questions.fun_fact: Chile has one of the driest deserts in the world, the Atacama, and also glaciers in the south.

questions.question: In which century did the Roman general Pompey clear the pirates out of the Mediterranean Sea?
hints: It was during the Roman Republic, before Rome had emperors.
Pompey was a rival of Julius Caesar.
It was just a few decades before the birth of Christ.
questions.description: Before streaming, Romans kept busy chasing pirates all over the Mediterranean.
questions.fun_fact: A few years earlier, a young Julius Caesar was kidnapped by pirates and, offended, told them to ask for a bigger ransom for him.

questions.question: Near Lake Maracaibo, the Catatumbo lightning flashes almost every night in the same spot. What did sailors use it for?
questions.answer: As a lighthouse to find their way
wrong_answers: As a clock to tell the time
As a warning of a hurricane
As a sign that pirates were near
hints: Think about what a ship needs when everything is dark.
What makes it useful is that the flashes always appear in the same spot and can be seen from very far away.
Sailors named it after the towers with lights that stand on coasts.
questions.description: A storm that works overtime almost every night of the year and never asks for a vacation.
questions.fun_fact: The Catatumbo lightning can produce thousands of flashes in a single night, and from far away you can hardly hear the thunder.

questions.question: I'm a saying grandmas repeat when troubles are finally over. I start like this: “After the storm comes the…”. What word do I end with?
hints: Think about how everything feels when the storm finally goes away.
It also describes a sea with no waves and no wind.
It rhymes with “palm” and means peace and quiet.
questions.description: A saying for days when everything goes wrong… until it stops going wrong.
questions.fun_fact: Many languages share this saying, and Spanish has an equally famous version: “After the storm, the sun comes out.”

questions.question: What is the outermost layer of the atmosphere called, where the air fades into space and some atoms escape?
hints: It is much higher up than where airplanes fly.
It begins above the height where the International Space Station circles Earth.
Its name starts with a Greek prefix that means “outside.”
questions.description: The top floor of Earth's air: no railings, but a great view of space.
questions.fun_fact: By some definitions, the exosphere reaches up to about 10,000 km (6,200 mi), only about 3% of the way to the Moon.

questions.question: What do you call a river mouth that splits into many branches and forms a triangle, like the Nile's?
hints: The same word is also used in math and physics.
It is named after a Greek letter shaped like a triangle.
It is the fourth letter of the Greek alphabet: alpha, beta, gamma…
questions.description: A river so long that by the end it gets tired and spreads out like a fan.
questions.fun_fact: The Greek historian Herodotus called the mouth of the Nile a “delta” because it looked like the Greek letter Δ.

questions.question: I'm shaped like a tower with a metal ring on top, and Nikola Tesla invented me. What am I for?
wrong_answers: Cooling the air in a room
hints: My inventor worked with electricity his whole life.
When I'm switched on, I give off sparks that look like lightning.
My bolts jump through the air because the electricity I make pushes with enormous force.
questions.description: An invention that makes even the most bored parents at a museum pull out their phones to film it.
questions.fun_fact: Some Tesla coils can “sing”: by changing the rhythm of their sparks, they play tunes you can hear in the air.

questions.question: At the ancient Greek Olympic Games, winners got a crown of branches instead of medals. Which tree were the branches from?
hints: It was a tree sacred to the goddess Athena.
It's a typical Mediterranean tree with silvery leaves.
Its fruit gives an oil that is very famous in cooking.
questions.description: A prize you couldn't keep in a display case, because it dried up in a few weeks.
questions.fun_fact: At the Athens 2004 Olympics, winners also received olive crowns, as a tribute to the ancient Games.

questions.question: Every year, more than a million wildebeest, zebras and gazelles travel in a big loop through the Serengeti and the Maasai Mara. Why?
questions.answer: To follow the rains and fresh grass
wrong_answers: To escape fires on the savanna
To look for salt in the mountains
To find shade in the rainforest
hints: The African savanna has dry seasons and rainy seasons.
Wildebeest are plant-eaters and eat a huge amount every day.
Where it rains, the food they need starts to grow.
questions.description: More than a million travelers with no suitcases, no GPS and no stops for gas.
questions.fun_fact: During the migration, hundreds of thousands of wildebeest calves are born within a few weeks, and they can walk just minutes after birth.

questions.question: Its name comes from a Russian word meaning “white.” What is this Arctic whale called?
hints: It lives in icy waters near the North Pole.
Sailors called it the “canary of the sea” because of its whistles and squeaks.
Its name starts with “Be…” and has three syllables.
questions.description: A Russian name for an animal that has never set foot in Moscow.
questions.fun_fact: Belugas are born gray and slowly turn white as they grow up.

questions.question: In which city was Antonio Vivaldi, the composer of “The Four Seasons”, born?
hints: It is in northern Italy, on the Adriatic Sea.
It is famous for its carnival of masks.
Instead of streets it has canals, and people get around by gondola.
questions.description: Spring, summer, fall and winter: a musician who never had to go shopping for inspiration.
questions.fun_fact: Vivaldi was called “il Prete Rosso”, the Red Priest, because he was a priest with red hair.

questions.question: What is the name of the camera that shows how hot everything is, with cold things in blue and hot things in yellow?
hints: Firefighters also use it to see through smoke.
It can also find animals hiding in the middle of the night.
Its name shares a root with “thermometer” and with the “thermos” that keeps your coffee hot.
questions.description: A photo where nobody shows up in their real colors, not even the volcano.
questions.fun_fact: With thermal cameras, volcanologists can notice a crater heating up before the volcano erupts.

questions.question: I'm Ryan, from the channel “Ryan's World”. I started on YouTube at age 3 and became the world's top-earning YouTuber. What kind of videos made me famous?
hints: What he did is what any kid does on Christmas morning.
Companies sent him boxes and boxes of stuff to show off.
He opened boxes, took out what was inside, played with it and said if he liked it.
questions.description: A kid who made more money before learning to tie his shoes than your dad will in his whole life.
questions.fun_fact: Forbes magazine named Ryan the world's highest-paid YouTuber in 2018 and 2019, when he was only about 7 or 8 years old.

questions.question: This volcano is Anak Krakatau, the “child of Krakatoa.” In which country is it?
hints: It is in Asia, in a country made up of thousands of islands.
It lies between the islands of Java and Sumatra.
The country's capital is Jakarta.
questions.description: Like father, like son: just as explosive.
questions.fun_fact: The 1883 eruption of Krakatoa was heard almost 4,800 km (3,000 miles) away, on islands in the Indian Ocean.

questions.question: In 1816, it snowed in June in Europe because of ash from Tambora, a volcano in Indonesia. Roughly how far is it from Europe?
hints: Indonesia is on the other side of the world, in Asia.
No two places on Earth are more than about 20,000 km (12,400 miles) apart.
It's roughly the distance of a flight from New York to Tokyo.
questions.description: You asked for a summer vacation and got a winter, gift-wrapped with a bow.
questions.fun_fact: People called 1816 “the year without a summer”, and the bad weather kept Mary Shelley indoors, where she wrote “Frankenstein”.

questions.question: It's the tiny picture you see before you open a video. YouTubers design it with wild faces and big letters so you click. What is it called?
hints: It's not the channel's profile picture.
Its name is about how small it is.
Its name says it's about as small as a fingernail on your hand.
questions.description: The reason every YouTuber poses with their mouth wide open, as if they'd just seen a ghost.
questions.fun_fact: Long before the internet, artists made quick little drawings called “thumbnail sketches”, because they were barely bigger than a thumbnail.

questions.question: Riddle: I'm a huge frog from North America. I was raised on farms in other countries, escaped, and now I eat the frogs there. What kind of species am I?
hints: It's a problem for the wildlife of the place where it arrived.
It's the opposite of a species native to that place.
It's like someone who walks into a stranger's house and takes over everything.
questions.description: A frog with the appetite of a bull and the manners of a guest nobody invited.
questions.fun_fact: A bullfrog will eat almost anything that fits in its mouth: insects, fish, other frogs, and even small birds!

questions.question: Which animal's name completes both? “___man” (a military diver) and “___ kick” (the leg kick of breaststroke).
hints: It swims by pushing with its back legs.
It lives between water and land.
It croaks in puddles.
questions.description: A question best answered with fins on and a mask pushed up on your forehead.
questions.fun_fact: Modern diving fins were inspired by the webbed feet of frogs and other swimming animals.

questions.question: Look at the photo: in the wild, this black salamander with yellow spots lives in the damp forests of which continent?
hints: It lives on a continent with oak and beech forests.
You can see it in Spain, France and Germany.
It's the continent of medieval castles.

questions.question: A harmless butterfly copies the colors of a bad-tasting one, so birds don't eat it. The trick is named after an English naturalist. What is it called?

questions.question: In a documentary, a mother pipa toad from the Amazon has dozens of eggs sunk into the skin of her back. What comes out of those holes months later?
wrong_answers: Eggs that drop into the water

They come out ready to live like tiny adults.

questions.question: Roughly how wide is a great egret from wingtip to wingtip with its wings spread?
hints: It's a big bird, but it's no condor.

A little less than the length of a bed.

questions.question: Ana checks every comma in her report but forgets the conclusion; Luis compares 30 paint colors and misses the leaking roof. Which saying fits them?
questions.answer: Can't see the forest for the trees
wrong_answers: As the twig is bent, so grows the tree
The apple doesn't fall far from the tree
Great oaks from little acorns grow

They need to step back and look at the whole picture.
The saying talks about lots of trees together.

questions.question: This headless Greek statue with huge wings stands at the top of a staircase in the Louvre. Which goddess does it show?
hints: She was a goddess who showed up whenever someone won a battle.
The statue was set on the front of a ship made of stone.
A famous sports shoe brand is named after her.

questions.question: It's round, it arranges colors like a rainbow biting its own tail, and the colors facing each other on it are called complementary. What is it?
hints: Painters and designers use it to match colors.
