questions.fun_fact: Isaac Newton was one of the first people to draw the colors in a circle, in 1704.

questions.question: Which style do the Paris metro entrances with iron stems, Alfons Mucha's posters and Victor Horta's curvy houses share?
hints: It was in fashion around the year 1900.
It loves curvy lines inspired by nature.
Its French name means “new art”.
questions.description: A style that loved plants but never watered a single one.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain this style was called modernismo, and Gaudí is its most famous architect.

questions.question: What do the flags of Mali, Ghana and Ethiopia have in common?
questions.answer: They use green, yellow and red
wrong_answers: They use red, white and blue
They use black, red and gold
They use green, white and orange
hints: All three countries are in Africa.
These colors are known as “Pan-African” colors.
The same three colors appear on a traffic light.
questions.description: Three flags that showed up in matching outfits without sending each other a single text.
questions.fun_fact: The Pan-African colors were inspired by the flag of Ethiopia, one of the few African countries that was never a colony.

questions.question: The outline of this island appears on its country's flag. Which country is it?
hints: It lies in the Mediterranean Sea, near Turkey.
In Greek mythology, Aphrodite was born there.
The Latin word for “copper” comes from this island's name.
questions.description: A country so proud of its figure that it put a self-portrait on its flag.
questions.fun_fact: Cyprus and Kosovo are the only countries with a map of their land drawn on their flag.

questions.question: This curved tool with a handle was used to cut wheat and grass. It appears crossed with a hammer on the red flag of the Soviet Union. What tool is it?
hints: My blade is shaped like a half moon.
I stand for the farmers, and the hammer stands for the factory workers.
My name has six letters and rhymes with “pickle”.
questions.description: A farm tool that ended up with a place of honor on a flag.
questions.fun_fact: The Soviet flag was used until 1991, when the country split into 15 republics.

questions.question: In what year did the Endurance, Ernest Shackleton's ship, set sail for Antarctica?
hints: It was early in the 20th century.
It was the same year a great war broke out in Europe.
The First World War was just beginning.
questions.description: A ship named after the very thing it would need most.
questions.fun_fact: The wreck of the Endurance was found in 2022, almost 3,000 m (nearly 10,000 ft) down, so well preserved that you could still read its name on the stern.

questions.question: My name reads the same forwards and backwards, and from high on the ship I spot other ships in thick fog. What do I “see” them with?
hints: I work even at night or in fog.
I send out invisible waves and listen for the echo.
My name starts with the same two letters as a device that plays music.
questions.description: A gadget with a name that reads both ways and eyes that aren't really eyes.
questions.fun_fact: “Radar” is short for “RAdio Detection And Ranging”: finding things and measuring their distance by radio.

questions.question: I'm a ship, and the captain shouts: “We've run aground!” What happened to me?
questions.answer: I got stuck on sand or rocks
wrong_answers: My sails ran out of wind
I got tied up at the dock
hints: It happens where the water is shallow.
My hull touched the bottom.
I can't move anymore because I'm stuck down below.
questions.description: When a ship decides to settle down somewhere it really shouldn't.
questions.fun_fact: In 2021 the giant ship Ever Given ran aground in the Suez Canal and blocked it for about six days.

questions.question: Bushido, “the way of the warrior”, was a code of honor that also valued the tea ceremony. Which country does it come from?
hints: It’s an island country in Asia.
The warriors who followed it carried katanas.
It’s the land of the samurai.
questions.description: A book of good manners for people who walked around with very sharp swords.
questions.fun_fact: The word “bushido” became famous around the world thanks to an English-language book from 1900 by Inazō Nitobe.

questions.question: Which of these cities is the capital of its country?
hints: It is a planned city, built almost from scratch.
It replaced Lagos as the capital in 1991.
It is in Nigeria.
questions.description: This influencer's GPS badly needs an update.
questions.fun_fact: Nigeria moved its capital to Abuja partly because it is closer to the center of the country than Lagos.

questions.question: What do Asunción, Vienna and Kabul have in common?
questions.answer: They are capitals of landlocked countries
wrong_answers: They are capitals on the Danube River
They are capitals in the Southern Hemisphere
They are capitals over 3,000 m (9,800 ft) high
hints: Look at the map, not at history.
Think of Paraguay, Austria and Afghanistan.
From none of these countries can you reach a beach without crossing a border.
questions.description: Three cities that have nothing in common… or almost nothing.
questions.fun_fact: Paraguay and Bolivia are the only countries in South America with no coastline.

questions.question: What is the final step of 3D animation, where the computer works out light, shadows and textures to make the finished image?
hints: It happens at the very end, after the characters are built and moved.
Pixar films need whole farms of computers to do it.
Architects use the same word for a realistic finished picture of a building that isn't built yet.
questions.description: The computer thinks about this one so long you have time to make yourself a coffee.
questions.fun_fact: In Pixar's early films, some frames took hours to render, and a single film has more than 100,000 frames.

questions.question: What do the zoetrope, the thaumatrope and the praxinoscope, all 19th-century inventions, have in common?
questions.answer: They create an illusion of motion
hints: They were popular toys long before television existed.
They use drawings that change just a tiny bit from one to the next.
Spin them fast enough and the drawings seem to come to life.
questions.description: The great-grandparents of the movies, from back when cinema couldn't even crawl yet.
questions.fun_fact: The word “zoetrope” comes from Greek and means something like “wheel of life.”

questions.question: I hang up at birthday parties, and blindfolded kids hit me with a stick. When I break, what falls out of me?
hints: Every kid loves what falls out.
Everyone dives to the floor to grab it fast.
Think lollipops, gummies and chocolates.
questions.description: The only party guest everyone wants to hit, and it's thrilled about it.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, the traditional piñata is shaped like a star with seven points.

questions.question: The Golden Bear is the top prize of the Berlin film festival. Which of these is NOT a film festival prize?
hints: Three of them are handed out in Venice, Cannes and San Sebastián.
The impostor is won with goals, not with films.
It goes to the top goal scorer in Europe's national leagues.
questions.description: A red carpet full of golden trophies, and one of them sneaked in without an invitation.
questions.fun_fact: The prize is a bear because the bear is the symbol of Berlin and appears on the city's coat of arms.

questions.question: With spaghetti and just three more things, garlic, olive oil and chili pepper, you make a famous Italian pasta. What is it called?
hints: It's a very cheap dish that Italians cook at midnight.
Its full Italian name lists its ingredients.
Its name is Italian for “garlic and oil.”
questions.description: The perfect recipe for when the fridge is empty and the pantry almost is too.
questions.fun_fact: In the movie “Chef” (2014), the main character cooks this dish for Scarlett Johansson in a famous scene.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this Japanese sweet is the favorite food of a famous cartoon character. Whose?
hints: This character comes from the future.
It has a magic pocket full of gadgets.
It's a blue robot cat with no ears.
questions.description: Two pancakes in a tight hug, with something sweet squeezed in between.
questions.fun_fact: The filling of a dorayaki is a sweet red bean paste called “anko.”

questions.question: This Mexican state on the Gulf coast gave the world the song “La Bamba” and a famous fish dish with tomatoes, olives and capers. Which state is it?
hints: It has one of Mexico's most important ports.
The red snapper dish is called “huachinango a la…”
Its name means “true cross” in Spanish.
questions.description: A place with so much rhythm that even its fish can dance.
questions.fun_fact: Many European spices and ingredients, like olives and capers, first reached Mexico through its port.

questions.question: On a cold morning in Mexico, you're served a hot, thick drink of corn dough, chocolate and piloncillo. What is it called?
hints: It's a type of atole, a traditional hot corn drink.
It's often served with tamales on the Day of the Dead and at Christmas.
Its name comes from the Spanish verb “champurrar”, to mix.
questions.description: A drink so thick you could almost eat it with a spoon.
questions.fun_fact: It's frothed with a wooden whisk called a molinillo, spun between the palms of the hands.

questions.question: It protects places like Machu Picchu and Cartagena, and living traditions too. In 2010 it added traditional Mexican cuisine to its list. Which organization is it?
hints: It is part of the United Nations.
It deals with education, science and culture.
It decides what becomes a “World Heritage Site.”
questions.description: An organization that collects treasures… but never locks them in a chest.
questions.fun_fact: In 2010, Mexican cuisine became the first national cuisine on the Intangible Cultural Heritage list, together with the French gastronomic meal.

questions.question: It has a main dish, fries and a drink, you order it by number, and it costs less than buying each item separately. What is it called?
hints: It's the most ordered thing at fast food restaurants.
Its name is short for “combination”.
It starts with “com…”.
questions.description: The math of hunger: burger plus fries plus soda equals… happiness.
questions.fun_fact: At many fast food places, you can “supersize” the fries and drink of your combo by paying just a little more.

questions.question: The sausage dog, long with short legs, comes from which country?
hints: It is a European country famous for its sausages.
The breed's usual name, “dachshund,” means “badger dog” in that country's language.
Its capital is Berlin.
questions.description: A dog shaped like a hot dog bun, or the other way around.
questions.fun_fact: In the United States, hot dogs were first called “dachshund sausages” because they looked like this breed.

questions.question: Complete: “Fries are to potatoes as coleslaw, the shredded salad with mayonnaise, is to…”
hints: It's a vegetable with tightly packed leaves in the shape of a ball.
The “cole” part comes from a Dutch word for this vegetable.
It's a relative of broccoli, and sauerkraut is made from it.
questions.description: A salad whose name sounds like a wizard's spell gone slightly wrong.
questions.fun_fact: “Coleslaw” comes from the Dutch “koolsla”, which means something like “cabbage salad”.

questions.question: A princess is playing by a well when her ball falls into the water, and a frog offers to fetch it if she'll be his friend. What is the ball made of?
hints: It's a toy fit for a princess.
It shines brightly, like a crown.
It's the same material as first-place medals.
questions.description: A princess plays next to a well, and then acts surprised when things go wrong.
questions.fun_fact: In the original Brothers Grimm version, the spell isn't broken by a kiss: the furious princess throws the frog against the wall.

questions.question: “Bicycle” is to “cyclist” as “skateboard” is to…
hints: Think about what you call the person who uses each thing.
The word sounds a lot like the name of the board with wheels.
You'll find lots of them doing tricks on ramps at the skatepark.
questions.description: Four wheels, zero engines and plenty of scraped knees.
questions.fun_fact: Skateboarding made its Olympic debut at the Tokyo 2020 Games.

questions.question: You’re watching a MotoGP race on TV, the fastest motorcycle championship in the world. What do the letters “GP” stand for?
hints: Each race in the championship has this name plus the name of the country.
Formula 1 also uses these words for its races.
The words come from French and mean “big prize”.
questions.description: Two wheels, one engine and a name with mysterious initials.
questions.fun_fact: MotoGP bikes go faster than 350 km/h (about 220 mph) on the longest straights.

questions.question: Tenzing Norgay, who climbed Everest with Hillary, belonged to a people whose name now means Himalayan guide. Which people?
hints: They live in the mountains of Nepal.
Today almost every Everest expedition hires them.
Their name is also used for a jacket with a fluffy lining.
questions.description: A job where the office is on the roof of the world.
questions.fun_fact: On the summit of Everest, Tenzing Norgay left some candy and cookies as an offering, following his Buddhist tradition.

questions.question: Look at the photo: Mongolian nomads in the Gobi Desert live in this round home they can take apart and carry along. What is it called?
hints: It has a wooden frame covered with wool felt.
It isn't the cone-shaped tent of the North American plains peoples.
In Mongolian, it's called a “ger.”
questions.description: A house you can put up, take down and load onto a camel: perfect for escaping unwanted visitors.
questions.fun_fact: A Mongolian family can take down its yurt in one or two hours and load it onto just a few animals.

questions.question: Many African countries are planting a long green wall of trees along the southern edge of the Sahara. What is it for?
questions.answer: To stop the desert from spreading
hints: Its enemy has no weapons: it's the sand.
Plant roots hold the soil so the wind can't blow it away.
Without it, the fertile land would slowly turn into sand.
questions.description: A wall built not with bricks, but with seeds and patience.
questions.fun_fact: The plan for the Great Green Wall is to cross Africa from side to side, from Senegal to Djibouti.

questions.question: It's a natural freshwater pool that forms when the roof of a cave falls in, and Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula has thousands. What is it called?
hints: The Maya used them to get water.
Many people travel to Mexico to swim in them.
The word comes from the Maya word “ts'ono'ot”.
questions.description: A natural swimming pool that made itself when the ground got tired of holding up.
questions.fun_fact: The Maya believed cenotes were doorways to Xibalba, the underworld.

questions.question: Complete: “Argentina is to the 2022 men's World Cup as Spain is to the…”
hints: It's a championship that Spain's women's team won.
It was the biggest title in women's national-team play.
It was played in Australia and New Zealand.
questions.description: An analogy question, so even your English teacher gets to cheer at a match.
questions.fun_fact: The first FIFA Women's World Cup was played in China in 1991, and the United States won it.

questions.question: What do Barcelona's Xavi, Iniesta and Busquets have in common?
hints: All three played in the middle of the field.

The style's name sounds like the ball going from foot to foot.
questions.description: Three men more in sync than a family group chat planning a birthday surprise.
questions.fun_fact: Spanish TV commentator Andrés Montes made the word “tiki-taka” popular during the 2006 World Cup.

questions.question: Look at this plant: it makes many cats wild with joy. Which plant family does it belong to?
hints: Look at the shape of its leaves, with edges like a saw.

If you crush it, it smells a bit like a plant used in chewing gum and mojitos.

questions.question: Kittens are born with their eyes closed. About how long does it take them to open them?

questions.description: Babies who arrive in the world without reading the instructions on how to open their eyes.
questions.fun_fact: All kittens are born with blue eyes; their final eye color shows up weeks later.

questions.question: People born in this city are nicknamed “gatos” (cats). Look at this detail from one of its most famous statues: which city is it?
hints: It's the capital of a country.
The statue appears on the city's coat of arms.

questions.description: A city where calling someone a “cat” is almost like checking their ID.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says they're called “cats” after a soldier who climbed Madrid's city wall like a cat in the Middle Ages.

questions.question: My name is Muezza. The story goes that I fell asleep on my owner's sleeve, and he cut it off rather than wake me. Who was my owner?

review.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. The question says "The story goes", so the answer Muhammad matches the popular legend, and the wrong answers are wrong. But the story is not in any verified hadith. Scholars say it probably comes from a tale about the saint Ahmad al-Rifa'i (d. 578 AH), and the cat is not named Muezza there. The fun fact about cats being loved and allowed in mosques is broadly true. The hint "He is a very important religious figure" is vague but fine.

questions.question: Who led the roughly fifty Greek heroes who sailed on the ship Argo in search of the Golden Fleece?

questions.question: Look at the photo: this Greek hero, dressed in a lion's skin, had to complete twelve almost impossible labors. Who is he?

questions.question: Listen: this insect sings by stridulation, rubbing one wing against the other. Which insect is it?

questions.description: A night-time concert with no tickets, no stage and no permission from the neighbors.
questions.fun_fact: Crickets chirp faster when it's warmer: by counting their chirps, you can estimate the temperature.

questions.question: Wasps build gray nests like this one. What are they made of?

hints: They get the material by scraping things in the yard.

questions.description: Builders with no license, no bricks and no cement, and still nobody dares to knock their house down.

questions.question: In 1947, fruit flies like this one became the first animals sent into space. Which country launched them?

questions.question: I'm two letters you see when you write an email, and my name comes from the carbon paper of typewriters. If you put someone in me, what do you do?
questions.answer: Send them a copy everyone can see
hints: My letters are “CC.”

questions.question: I'm the “s” added to the end of “http” in some web addresses. What am I for?
questions.answer: To encrypt data between your browser and the website

questions.question: This word comes from a made-up island in “Gulliver's Travels” whose people are about 15 cm (6 in) tall. Today it means “tiny”. What is it?
hints: When Gulliver reaches the island, he wakes up tied to the ground by a crowd of little people.

questions.question: Look at the photo: how many pieces does this cube-shaped puzzle have?
hints: Count slowly, one at a time.

questions.description: A cube that fell to pieces and is waiting for you to put it back together without glue.
questions.fun_fact: Danish inventor Piet Hein created the Soma cube in 1933, and its seven pieces can be put together into a cube in 240 different ways.

questions.question: What is the name of the shape with 20 faces, all of them triangles?
hints: It's a special die, very popular in role-playing games.
Its name comes from Greek and means “twenty faces.”
It starts with “ico.”
questions.description: A shape with so many faces that even the most two-faced person can't compete.
questions.fun_fact: Many viruses, like the adenovirus, have an outer shell shaped like an icosahedron.

questions.question: A hen raises chicks. In “The Wild Robot”, the robot Roz is shipwrecked on an island and raises a baby…
hints: It's a bird that swims in lakes.

questions.question: In Harry Potter, what does the spell “Wingardium Leviosa!” do?

questions.question: In Harry Potter, what are the Elder Wand, the Resurrection Stone and the Cloak of Invisibility called together?

questions.question: Like corals, some sea animals can bleach because they carry tiny algae inside them. Which of these can NOT bleach?

questions.question: A giant worm with a red plume has no mouth or stomach and lives off the bacteria inside it. Where does it live?
questions.answer: At hydrothermal vents on the seafloor
hints: It lives where sunlight never reaches.

questions.description: A worm with no mouth and no stomach that still never orders takeout.

questions.question: I was born in Pisa around 1170. My book “Liber Abaci” helped Europe adopt Arabic numerals and posed a famous puzzle about pairs of rabbits. Who am I?

questions.question: Riddle me this: I live inside remote controls and toys and give them power, and when I run out, you shouldn't throw me in the regular trash. What am I?
