questions.fun_fact: Batteries contain metals like zinc, manganese, and lithium, which can be recovered if you take them to a collection point.

questions.question: Riddle: I spin and spin when water from a dam, steam or wind pushes me, and that turns the generator that makes electricity. What am I?
hints: I don't store energy: I turn it into motion.
I have blades, like a giant fan working in reverse.
Passenger jets carry some on their wings too.
questions.description: Turn this question around a few times and the answer starts to come to you.
questions.fun_fact: The word “turbine” comes from the Latin “turbo”, meaning a whirlwind or something that spins.

questions.question: Look at the photo: why are factory chimneys built so tall?
questions.answer: So the smoke spreads out high above the ground
wrong_answers: So airplanes can see them from far away
So they can store more coal inside
So it rains less on the factory
hints: It has to do with what comes out of the top.
Up there, the wind blows harder than down below.
That way, people living nearby breathe in less smoke directly.
questions.description: Even a factory has to stretch its neck to get a breath of air.
questions.fun_fact: The world's tallest chimney stands at a power plant in Ekibastuz, Kazakhstan, and is about 420 m (1,380 ft) tall.

questions.question: Riddle: I'm a black Night Fury dragon who lost part of my tail. A young Viking built me a new one, and now we fly together. Who is he?
hints: He's the hero of “How to Train Your Dragon”.
He's skinny, loves inventing things, and his dad is the village chief.
His name is what you might get after drinking water too fast.
questions.description: A friendship that started with a direct hit, and not from Cupid's arrow.
questions.fun_fact: Toothless got his name because he can pull his teeth back into his gums, so at first he looks like he has none.

questions.question: This comic strip was created in 1973 by Dik Browne. Its hero is a big-bellied Viking with a horned helmet, and his wife is Helga. What is the strip called?
hints: It ran in the comics section of newspapers.
The hero has a dog named Snert.
The title is the hero's name plus a nickname meaning “terrible”.
questions.description: A Viking who raids castles but is more afraid of his wife.
questions.fun_fact: Real Vikings almost certainly didn't wear horned helmets in battle: that image became popular in the 19th century through operas and paintings.

questions.question: Grauballe Man is a body that the mud of a Danish bog preserved for centuries. What period is he from?
hints: He is much older than he looks, because he is so well preserved.
He lived about 300 years before Christ.
This period is named after a metal that replaced bronze.
questions.description: A man who took a nap in the mud and woke up as a museum piece.
questions.fun_fact: The acidic, oxygen-free water of the bog preserved Grauballe Man so well that you can still see his fingerprints.

questions.question: My pyramid is the second largest at Giza, but it looks the tallest because it stands on higher ground. The Great Sphinx is thought to have my face. Who am I?
hints: My tomb is at Giza, not in the Valley of the Kings.
I was the son of Khufu.
My pyramid still keeps part of its smooth outer casing at the top.
questions.description: A pharaoh who cheated in the tallest-pyramid contest: he built his on a hill.
questions.fun_fact: The Sphinx is about 73 m (240 ft) long and was carved straight out of the bedrock.

questions.question: Look at the stars above the crest on this jersey. What do they count?
questions.answer: The World Cups that team has won
wrong_answers: The famous players on the team
The Copa América titles it won
The times it played in a final
hints: They have nothing to do with the sky.
Brazil has five and Argentina has three.
You earn one by lifting the biggest trophy in soccer.
questions.description: Stars you never see at night, but you see them every time the team walks onto the field.
questions.fun_fact: Argentina added its third star after winning the 2022 World Cup in Qatar.

questions.question: I'm a Spanish midfielder: in 2023 I won the World Cup with my national team, was named its best player, then won the Ballon d'Or. Who am I?
hints: I play for Barcelona.
That World Cup was played in Australia and New Zealand.
My first name starts with A, but I'm not Alexia.
questions.description: A player who collects trophies the way other people collect stickers.
questions.fun_fact: With the 2023 title, Spain became the second country, after Germany, to win both the men's and the women's World Cup.

questions.question: An artist taped a fruit to a wall with gray duct tape and called it “Comedian.” Someone paid millions for it… and ate it! What fruit was it?
hints: It's yellow on the outside.
It grows in bunches in tropical places.
You peel it, and it's shaped like a crescent moon.
questions.description: The most expensive work of art that ever ended up as a snack.
questions.fun_fact: In 2024 the artwork sold at auction for more than 6 million dollars, and the banana itself had cost about 35 cents.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is inside these armbands that helps you float?
hints: Before you use them, you have to blow into them.
Birthday balloons have the same thing inside.
If they get a hole, they go flat.
questions.description: The little helpers that hug your arms so you don't sink.
questions.fun_fact: Air weighs much, much less than water, so something full of air pushes upward and helps you float.

questions.question: In what year were the Sydney Olympic Games, where swimmer Eric Moussambani became famous?
hints: They were the last Olympic Games of the 20th century.
Many people remember them as the Games at the turn of the millennium.
The year is a very round number.
questions.description: A swimmer so slow that he became more famous than many champions.
questions.fun_fact: Moussambani swam his heat alone because both of his rivals were disqualified, and the crowd cheered him all the way until he touched the wall.

questions.question: A special family dinner, hugs at midnight and presents under the tree on the night of December 24. What is this night called?
hints: It's the night just before Christmas Day.
It's not the night of December 31.
It's the night when children wait for Santa Claus to bring presents.
questions.description: The only night of the year when the whole family is awake at midnight and nobody gets scolded.
questions.fun_fact: In Spanish it's called “Nochebuena”, which means “the good night”.

questions.question: An old atlas says “Macedonia”; a new one says “North Macedonia”. In what year did the official name change?
hints: It happened only a few years ago, not in the last century.
The change came after a deal with Greece, which has a region called Macedonia.
It was just one year before the pandemic began.
questions.description: A country that added a compass direction to its name just to make peace with the neighbors.
questions.fun_fact: The fight with Greece over the name “Macedonia” lasted almost 30 years.

questions.question: I'm a country in Africa, and my name is Ivory Coast. What is the ivory in my name?
hints: It's a creamy white color.
It comes from a very big animal.
That animal has a trunk.
questions.description: A country that sounds like a very fancy beach.
questions.fun_fact: Ivory Coast's national soccer team is nicknamed “The Elephants.”

questions.question: At an arcade machine, you can pick Ryu, Chun-Li or Blanka to fight. What do these three characters have in common?
hints: All three are characters from a very famous fighting game.
That game started out in Capcom's arcade machines.
Its name says the fights happen out on the road, not in a ring.
questions.description: A tournament where nobody showed up to play checkers.
questions.fun_fact: In the game's story, Blanka, the green fighter who shoots out electricity, comes from Brazil.

previous.feedback: The question uses the retired "What do these three characters have in common?" style, which the source also uses. Apart from that, the translation is faithful and natural. The rewritten hint 3 works, and the kept image of a Mazinger Z arcade cabinet fits the question without giving the answer away.

questions.question: My name is course. Pirates set me before they sail, the helmsman keeps me all voyage, and the captain shouts to change me. What do I show?
questions.answer: Which way the ship is sailing
wrong_answers: How fast the ship is going
How much cargo the ship has
How deep the sea is below
hints: A compass helps keep me from getting lost.
Get me wrong and you'll never reach Treasure Island.
North, south, east, west...
questions.description: Without this, a pirate ship is just a floating party with nowhere to go.
questions.fun_fact: When people say their life has gone “off course”, they're using words that were born at sea.

review.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. The answer and wrong answers are fine: a ship's course is its heading, not speed, cargo or depth. The fun fact is shaky. "Course" comes from Latin cursus ('a running, path') through Old French cours, so the word was not born at sea. Only the phrase "off course" is plausibly nautical in origin. I did not run searches, so this rests on my own knowledge of the etymology.

questions.question: “Colombia is to country as South America is to…”. Which word completes the sentence?
hints: South America is much bigger than Colombia.
Many countries fit inside South America.
Africa, Europe and Asia are one too.
questions.description: A word puzzle with more ground to cover than a family road trip.
questions.fun_fact: South America has 12 independent countries, and Brazil alone covers almost half of its land.

questions.question: One museum room shows a woolly mammoth, a saber-toothed cat and the first humans. What do they have in common?
questions.answer: They all lived in the Cenozoic Era
wrong_answers: They all lived in the Mesozoic Era
They all lived in the Paleozoic Era
They all lived in the Precambrian
hints: None of them shared the planet with a T. rex.
It is the era we are living in right now.
It began just after the big dinosaurs died out.
questions.description: A museum room with more hair than a prehistoric barbershop.
questions.fun_fact: “Cenozoic” comes from Greek and means “new life.”

questions.question: Megalodon left behind almost nothing but fossil teeth like this one, because its skeleton was made of a material that rarely fossilizes. Which one?
hints: Today's sharks have skeletons made of the same material.
It is softer and bendier than bone.
You have it in the tip of your nose and in your ears.
questions.description: A shark so big the tooth fairy would need a truck.
questions.fun_fact: The biggest megalodon teeth are over 15 cm (6 in) long, bigger than a child's hand.

questions.question: The air plant hangs from branches and even power lines, needs no soil, and its leaves are covered in silvery scales. What are those scales for?
questions.answer: To catch water and food from the air
hints: Its roots are used almost only for holding on.
It has to get what other plants take from the soil from somewhere else.
They work like sponges when it rains or when there is fog.
questions.description: The laziest plant in the world: it doesn't even bother to get a pot.
questions.fun_fact: The air plant is a relative of the pineapple: both are bromeliads.

questions.question: Riddle: I live inside a frozen mountain on a Norwegian island near the North Pole, and people call me the “Doomsday Vault”. What do I keep?
questions.answer: Crop seeds from around the world
wrong_answers: Gold bars for the world's reserves
hints: What I keep could help the world start over after a huge disaster.
Almost every country in the world has sent me something to keep safe.
If you opened me, you would find beans, rice, corn and wheat… uncooked and ready to plant.
questions.description: A place so cold and so hidden that not even the bravest delivery driver dares to go there.
questions.fun_fact: The vault is in Svalbard because the cold of the permafrost would keep the seeds frozen even if the power went out.

questions.question: The real flowers of the bougainvillea are tiny and white. So what makes it look so colorful?
wrong_answers: A fungus that dyes its branches
hints: It isn't part of the flower, even though it's attached to it.
Botanists call them “bracts.”
It's the same plant part that does photosynthesis, just in a different color.
questions.description: A plant that dresses up for a party but hides its real face.
questions.fun_fact: The poinsettia, the famous Christmas flower, pulls the same trick: its red “flower” is also made of modified leaves.

questions.question: In biology class, you take apart a lily flower and separate the stigma, the style and the ovary. Which part of the flower are all three pieces of?
hints: It is the female part of the flower.
It usually sits right in the center of the flower.
Pollen lands there, and that is where the seeds form.
questions.description: The part of the flower where everything starts turning into fruit.
questions.fun_fact: The red threads of saffron, one of the most expensive spices in the world, are the stigmas of a flower.

questions.question: Riddle: “I am the manguaré, the great drum of the Bora people; when struck, my voice carries messages for kilometers through the jungle.” What am I made of?
hints: My material comes straight from the jungle, and it's very heavy.
I have no animal skin that vibrates.
A whole tree, emptied out on the inside.
questions.description: The jungle's group chat: no Wi-Fi, but plenty of rhythm.
questions.fun_fact: Manguarés are played in pairs: a “male” one and a “female” one, each with its own sound.

questions.question: According to a famous legend of the South American rainforest, what is Paititi?
questions.answer: A lost city of the Incas
wrong_answers: A sunken galleon full of treasure
hints: It is said to be hidden in the jungle where Peru, Bolivia and Brazil meet.
People say it had streets, palaces and lots of people living there.
It's a “cousin” of the legend of El Dorado.
questions.description: A name that sounds like baby talk, but hides a giant legend.
questions.fun_fact: According to the legend, the Incas hid their treasures there so the Spanish conquerors couldn't find them.

questions.question: What is the main component of the gas that is collected from landfills and burned to make electricity?
hints: Microbes make it when they break down garbage without air.
Cows also let it out when they burp.
It is the main component of the natural gas used in kitchen stoves.
questions.description: Garbage passes gas too, and someone had the bright idea to put it to work.
questions.fun_fact: Landfill biogas is roughly half methane and half carbon dioxide.

questions.question: You want to buy cheap used clothes. Which of these places is NOT a typical place to find them?
hints: Think carefully about what each word means.
One of these places sells new things for sewing.
It's where you buy buttons, thread and zippers.
questions.description: Your favorite jacket had a whole other life before it met you.
questions.fun_fact: The name “flea market” comes from the French “marché aux puces”, because the old clothes sold in Paris markets were said to have fleas.

questions.question: Each green dot in this photo is a complete living thing, smaller than a grain of rice. Which group does it belong to?
hints: They make food from sunlight, like the grass in the park.
Hard to believe, but they are distant relatives of roses and sunflowers.
It's the smallest in the world of all those that can bloom.
questions.description: Blink and you'll miss a whole garden.
questions.fun_fact: Wolffia is the smallest flowering plant in the world: its flowers are so tiny you can barely see them with the naked eye.

questions.question: What do Mount Everest, Aconcagua and Mount Vinson have in common?
questions.answer: Each is its continent's highest peak
wrong_answers: Each is in the Andes mountains
Each is in the Himalaya mountains
hints: They are on different continents.
Mount Vinson is in Antarctica.
Aconcagua holds that same title in the Americas.
questions.description: A to-do list for climbers with way too much vacation time.
questions.fun_fact: Mount Vinson, about 4,892 m (16,050 ft) tall, is so remote in Antarctica that nobody climbed it until 1966.

questions.question: I'm a pine tree in the mountains of California, over 4,800 years old. I'm named after a Bible figure famous for living 969 years. Who is he?
hints: He was the grandfather of someone famous for building an ark.
People say someone is “as old as…” him when they mean very, very old.
His name starts with M.
questions.description: A tree so old its birthday cake would need a whole forest of candles.
questions.fun_fact: The exact location of the Methuselah tree is kept secret to protect it from visitors who might want to take home a souvenir.

questions.question: How many chambers (atria and ventricles) does a frog's heart have in total?
hints: It has fewer chambers than a human heart.
In this, amphibians are halfway between fish and mammals.
It's an odd number: two atria and just one ventricle.
questions.description: An organ that works day and night without a vacation, even if its owner lives in a puddle.
questions.fun_fact: Because its heart mixes the blood a little, a frog gets extra help by also breathing through its moist skin.

questions.question: Complete: the elephant is to its trunk as the giant anteater is to its…
hints: It pokes its snout into ant and termite nests.
It doesn't have a single tooth.
It's long and sticky, and it flicks in and out super fast.
questions.description: An animal whose whole menu is right there in its name.
questions.fun_fact: A giant anteater's tongue is about 60 cm (2 ft) long and can flick in and out about 150 times a minute.

questions.question: Riddle: I'm a mangrove root, but I don't dig down. I poke up out of the mud like a pencil, and the tide covers and uncovers me. What am I for?
questions.answer: Taking in oxygen from the air
hints: I do most of my work when the tide goes out.
There's almost no oxygen in mangrove mud.
I work like a diver's snorkel.
questions.description: A tree standing with its feet in salty mud came up with a clever trick.
questions.fun_fact: These roots are called pneumatophores, from Greek words meaning “air carriers”.

questions.question: In Collodi's book “Pinocchio”, a coachman sells donkeys at the market. What were those donkeys before?
questions.answer: Boys who didn't want to study
hints: The same thing happens to Pinocchio himself.
Before they had long ears, they spent all day playing.
The coachman took them to a place with no school and no teachers.
questions.description: A trip that's pure fun from start to finish, until it ends in a hee-haw.
questions.fun_fact: In the Disney film that place became an island, but in the book it's a land the children reach in a cart pulled by little donkeys.

questions.question: Riddle: I'm the largest continuous sea of sand in the world, I cover the south of the Arabian Peninsula, and my name means “the empty quarter.” Who am I?
hints: Saudi Arabia, Oman, Yemen and the United Arab Emirates share my land.
My dunes can be more than 200 m (650 ft) tall.
My name is in Arabic and starts with “Rub.”
questions.description: A desert named after a room nobody ever wants to clean.
questions.fun_fact: Beneath its sands lies Shaybah, one of Saudi Arabia's great oil fields.

questions.question: The oilbird nests in pitch-dark caves and flies between the rocks without crashing. How does it find its way?
questions.answer: With the echo of its own sounds
wrong_answers: With the heat of the rocks
hints: It's about how they find their way without seeing anything.
They make sounds and listen to what comes back.
It's called echolocation.
questions.description: A place so dark that not even a lamp would help you find the way out.
questions.fun_fact: The oilbird is the only flying bird that feeds on fruit at night, and Alexander von Humboldt studied it in 1799 in the Cueva del Guácharo in Venezuela.

questions.question: Benjamin Franklin, the man with the famous kite in the storm, invented three of these things. Which one did he NOT invent?
hints: One of his inventions came straight from his kite experiment.
The one that isn't his came more than a hundred years later.
That one is mostly credited to Thomas Edison.
questions.description: A man who flew kites in the middle of a storm… and no, don't try this at home.
questions.fun_fact: Franklin never patented his inventions: he wanted everyone to be able to use them for free.

questions.question: What do a cat, an owl and a crocodile have in common?
wrong_answers: They see in black and white
hints: It has to do with how they protect their eyes.
It's a thin film that slides sideways across the eye.
On top of the usual two, they have one more.
questions.description: A cat, an owl and a crocodile walk into a doctor's office… and no, this isn't the start of a joke.
questions.fun_fact: You can sometimes see a cat's third eyelid when it's half asleep or sick: it's a thin white film in the corner of the eye.

questions.question: Daedalus designed it, it was on Crete, and Theseus got out of it by following Ariadne's thread. What was it?
hints: A monster was locked up inside it.
That monster was half man, half bull.
It is full of corridors and dead ends.
questions.description: A job for a king with more secrets than Grandma's junk room.
questions.fun_fact: The English word “clue” comes from “clew,” an old word for a ball of thread, like the one Ariadne gave Theseus.

questions.question: A kitchen knife is to a Swiss Army knife as an AI that can only play chess is to…
hints: The Swiss Army knife isn't bigger: it can do more things.
Scientists haven't managed to actually build it yet.
Its short name is AGI, and it's the opposite of a “narrow” or specialized AI.
questions.description: Machines have their own “when I grow up, I want to be…” too.
questions.fun_fact: Several AI labs, such as OpenAI, openly say that building artificial general intelligence is their main goal.

questions.question: Copilot is made by Microsoft and shows up in Windows, Word and Excel with a colorful icon. Its name comes from the person who sits next to the pilot. What is Copilot?
questions.answer: An assistant that answers your questions
wrong_answers: A checker that underlines your mistakes
A guard that blocks computer viruses
A search tool that finds your files
hints: It has nothing to do with planes, even if the name sounds like it.
You can ask it to sum up a document or help you write an email.
It's a chatbot, from the same family as ChatGPT.
questions.description: Someone has to sit next to the pilot, and it isn't always a person.
questions.fun_fact: Before it came to Windows, the name was used for GitHub Copilot, launched in 2021 to help programmers write code.

questions.question: It started in 2013 as a joke, its symbol is the Shiba Inu dog from the Doge meme, and Elon Musk has posted about it many times. What is it?
hints: Some people buy and sell it.
It doesn't exist as paper bills or metal coins.
It's a relative of Bitcoin.
questions.description: Such doggo. Very internet. Wow.
questions.fun_fact: The dog in the meme was named Kabosu and lived in Japan with her owner, a teacher.

questions.question: The name of the Canary Islands comes from Latin and hides an animal. Which one?
hints: The Romans already knew about these islands in the Atlantic.
In Latin, this animal was called “canis.”
It's the animal that wags its tail when you come home.
questions.description: A name that looks obvious, but has hidden a surprise since Roman times.
questions.fun_fact: It's the other way around from what most people think: the canary bird is named after the islands, not the islands after the bird.

questions.question: What do Hong Kong, Singapore and Jamaica have in common in their history?
hints: That European empire left all three its language as an official language.
That empire had the most powerful navy in the world in the 19th century.
In all three places, people still drive on the left.
questions.description: Three places with beaches, lots of heat and a past that arrived by ship from Europe.
questions.fun_fact: Hong Kong was handed back to China in 1997, after more than 150 years under British rule.

questions.question: In the film “My Neighbor Totoro,” how many Totoros appear?
hints: He is not alone in the forest.
They are not all the same size: the biggest one is the one waiting for the bus in the rain.
It's the same number as the little pigs in the story with the big bad wolf.
questions.description: The giant cuddly toy everyone would love as a pillow on a rainy day.
questions.fun_fact: Totoro appears in the logo of Studio Ghibli, the Japanese studio that made the film in 1988.

questions.question: García Márquez is to “One Hundred Years of Solitude” as Isabel Allende is to…
hints: It is Isabel Allende's first novel, from 1982.
It tells the story of several generations of the Trueba family.
Its title is about a home full of ghosts.
questions.description: A question for people who read long novels with even longer family trees.
questions.fun_fact: “The House of the Spirits” began as a letter Isabel Allende started writing to her grandfather in 1981.

questions.question: In “Love in the Time of Cholera”, Florentino Ariza waits and waits for his love, Fermina Daza. How many years does he wait, according to the novel?
hints: It's a very long time: when they finally get together, they are both old.
The novel says: “… years, nine months and four days.”
It's a number just over 50.
questions.description: The longest wait in literature, worse than the line at the bank on a Monday.
questions.fun_fact: García Márquez based this novel partly on the love story of his own parents.

questions.question: I'm the Minecraft enchanting table: I have a book that floats and opens when you come close. What happens if you surround me with bookshelves?
wrong_answers: You can enchant several items at once
You no longer need lapis lazuli
hints: The bookshelves must be nearby, but with one free block between them and the table.
Look at the numbers next to each enchantment option.
More books around it, more magical wisdom for the table.
questions.description: A piece of furniture that reads more than you do, and it doesn't even have eyes.
questions.fun_fact: With enough bookshelves around it, the Minecraft enchanting table can offer level 30 enchantments.

questions.question: On a day trip, you drink tap water, swim in a river and later row on a mountain lake. What do those three waters have in common?
hints: None of them tastes like the sea.
It's the kind people and animals can drink.
Its name uses the same word as bread just out of the oven.
questions.description: A day out in the country with three different dips and not a single wave.
questions.fun_fact: Almost all the water on Earth is salty: fresh water is only about 3%, and most of it is frozen.

previous.feedback: The question asks what three given things have in common (“What do those three waters have in common?”). That style is retired (reason 7), and it applies to the source too. The translation itself is faithful, and the new hint 3 (fresh bread) works well in English.

questions.question: He's called the father of geometry, wrote a book called “Elements” and lived about 2,300 years ago. Which civilization was Euclid from?
hints: His civilization was famous for its philosophers.
He came from the same culture as Pythagoras and Archimedes.
His civilization also invented the Olympic Games.
questions.description: The man who turned triangles into a bestseller for more than 2,000 years.
questions.fun_fact: Euclid's “Elements” is one of the most-printed books in history and was used in schools for more than 2,000 years.

questions.question: This lump of corroded bronze was pulled from a Greek shipwreck in 1901. What was the Antikythera mechanism used for?
questions.answer: Predicting eclipses and movements in the sky
wrong_answers: Measuring how deep the sea is
hints: It had dozens of gear wheels, like a clock.
It showed the Sun, the Moon and maybe some planets.
It is seen as the oldest known astronomical calculator.
questions.description: Divers looking for sea sponges found a 2,000-year-old bronze puzzle on the seabed.
questions.fun_fact: Nobody built a device with such complex gears again until the astronomical clocks of the Middle Ages, more than a thousand years later.

questions.question: Which of these energy sources is NOT renewable?
hints: Renewable sources never run out: they come back on their own.
The one you want is dug out of a mine, like a rock.
It's used in nuclear power plants, like the one where Homer Simpson works.
questions.description: Some energy comes back by itself every day, and some is gone for good once it runs out.
questions.fun_fact: One uranium fuel pellet, about the size of a fingertip, gives as much energy as a ton of coal.

questions.question: Riddle: I am Brísingamen, the golden necklace of the goddess Freya. Four brothers in Norse myth forged me. What kind of beings were they?
hints: In Norse myths, these beings also made famous weapons for the gods.
They live underground and are the best blacksmiths.
They are small, bearded and work in mines.
questions.description: The shiniest jewel in Asgard, and nobody bought it at the mall.
questions.fun_fact: In the myths, dwarves also forged Mjölnir, Thor's hammer.

questions.question: What is an oath, like the one some people make to their flag?
hints: It is said out loud and with great respect.
Whoever makes it commits to doing something.
It's like saying “I promise”, but in a very serious way.
questions.description: When school asks you to be really serious, at least for a little while.
questions.fun_fact: In many Latin American countries, children make their oath to the flag at a special school ceremony.

questions.question: The ancient Egyptians painted this eye on their boats and wore it around their necks. What did they use it for?
questions.answer: To protect themselves and stay healthy
wrong_answers: To guide their boats along the Nile
To show that they were nobles
To measure the passing of time
hints: Both rich and poor people used it.
The living wore it, and it was also placed on mummies.
According to the myth, the falcon god's eye was healed after a fight.
questions.description: An eye that has been watching for thousands of years and still doesn't need glasses.
questions.fun_fact: The Eye of Horus is still worn today as a pendant on necklaces and shows up in many video games.

questions.question: The “Mona Lisa” is to the Louvre as which painting is to the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam?
hints: It was painted by the same artist the museum is named after.
It shows yellow flowers in a vase.
These flowers turn their heads to follow the sun.
questions.description: A museum for a painter who sold almost nothing while he was alive and is now too famous to fit through the door.
questions.fun_fact: Van Gogh painted several versions of “Sunflowers” to decorate the bedroom of his friend, the painter Paul Gauguin.

questions.question: Turkey is to Christmas dinner in the US as ________ is to Christmas dinner for millions of families in Japan.
hints: You buy it from a famous fast-food chain.
The custom started with an ad campaign in the 1970s.
It comes in buckets, and the brand's founder was a colonel with a white beard.
questions.description: A Christmas tradition that was born in an advertising office.
questions.fun_fact: So many families in Japan order it that they have to reserve their Christmas bucket weeks in advance.

questions.question: Who were the first to come and worship baby Jesus, on the very night he was born?
hints: They were working at night in the fields near Bethlehem.
An angel brought them the news while they watched over their animals.
Their job was looking after sheep.
questions.description: The most exclusive guest list in history, and not a single celebrity on it.
questions.fun_fact: According to the Bible, the Wise Men didn't arrive that night: the Gospel says they found the child in a house.

questions.question: Which ancient people gave Mexico its name and founded their capital where Mexico City stands today?
hints: They ruled central Mexico when the Spanish arrived.
Their capital was called Tenochtitlan and was built on a lake.
They called themselves the “Mexica.”
questions.description: A city so important that it lent its name to the whole country.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico City was built on a lake, so some of its buildings are slowly sinking.

questions.question: Charmander is to Fire type as Lucario is to…
hints: Lucario can sense other creatures' aura, but that's not what decides its type.
Machop and Hitmonchan are this type too.
It's the type of Pokémon that throw punches and kicks.
questions.description: A dog that never barks, but can read everyone's energy.
questions.fun_fact: Lucario actually has two types at once: Fighting and Steel.

questions.question: What links the film “Captain Phillips”, speedboats attacking cargo ships, and warships guarding oil tankers in the Indian Ocean?
hints: It's modern piracy, from this century.
It happens near the entrance to the Red Sea.
These pirates come from the country whose capital is Mogadishu.
questions.description: Pirates with no parrot and no wooden leg, but with very fast boats.
questions.fun_fact: “Captain Phillips” is based on the real hijacking of the cargo ship Maersk Alabama in 2009.

previous.feedback: The question asks what several given things have in common ("What links the film “Captain Phillips”, speedboats… and warships…?"). That is the retired "what do they have in common" style. The source uses the same style ("¿Qué tienen en común…?"), so the source has the same problem.

questions.question: They call me hardtack, and I turn up in lots of pirate stories. Sailors soaked me before biting, and I lasted months in the hold. What am I?
wrong_answers: A sponge cake of egg and sugar
An oat cake made with honey
hints: Sailors sometimes found weevils living inside me.
I was baked several times to dry out every bit of moisture.
I'm made of just flour, water and salt.
questions.description: The pirates' favorite snack, if you don't care about your teeth.
questions.fun_fact: Some pieces of hardtack more than 150 years old are still kept in museums.

questions.question: I'm the Amazon River: in the rainy season I rise several meters and spill into the rainforest. What happens then?
wrong_answers: Pink river dolphins leave for the sea
Monkeys move down to live on the ground
hints: For months, the forest is half underwater.
Down there, visitors with fins start showing up.
Some of them eat the fruit that falls from the branches.
questions.description: A river that leaves home every year without asking permission.
questions.fun_fact: Some Amazon fish eat fruit and drop the seeds far away, so they help plant the rainforest.

questions.question: A giant tree trunk is hollowed out with fire and an ax, and left long and pointed at both ends. What is it used for?
hints: The pointed ends help it cut through something that moves.
In the rainforest, rivers are like roads.
It's going to need some paddles.
questions.description: A tree that got hollowed out and found itself a whole new career.
questions.fun_fact: Some canoes carved from a single tree trunk can carry more than ten people.

questions.question: At a school fair, one ticket buys one cupcake. In the carbon credit market, one credit stands for… what?
questions.answer: One metric ton of CO₂ kept out of the air
wrong_answers: One kilogram of CO₂ kept out of the air
One liter of CO₂ kept out of the air
100 metric tons of CO₂ kept out of the air
hints: It's an amount of greenhouse gas.
It's a fairly big unit, not one you'd use on a kitchen scale.
It's a thousand kilograms of carbon dioxide.
questions.description: Polluting with permission: the grown-up version of “I'll trade you my dessert for your homework.”
questions.fun_fact: Carbon credits became famous with the Kyoto Protocol, adopted in Japan in 1997.

questions.question: Monarch butterflies fly from Canada and the United States to spend the winter in mountain forests. In which country are they?
hints: Spanish is spoken in this country.
The butterflies never cross the equator.
It's the country of mariachis and tacos.
questions.description: Travelers who need no passport, just a pair of colorful wings.
questions.fun_fact: No single monarch butterfly makes the whole round trip: its great-grandchildren finish the journey back north.

questions.question: On which day is the crown-shaped sweet bread with candied fruit and a hidden surprise inside traditionally eaten?
hints: By that day, Christmas and New Year's are already over.
Its crown shape is a clue about who is celebrated that day.
It's the day of Melchior, Caspar and Balthazar.
questions.description: A bread with a prize inside, like cereal boxes used to have.
questions.fun_fact: A tiny baby Jesus figure is hidden inside the bread, and in Mexico whoever finds it must treat everyone to tamales on February 2.

questions.question: iCub is a robot the size of a small child, built at an institute in Genoa. Which Italian scientist co-led its development?
hints: He has worked in Genoa for most of his career.
He became scientific director of the Italian Institute of Technology.
His first name is the Italian form of “George”.
questions.description: A baby that never cries, never sleeps and comes with an instruction manual anyone can read.
questions.fun_fact: Dozens of iCub copies are spread across labs around the world, and they all share their design freely.

questions.question: I'm the name of the horsemen of the steppes of Ukraine and southern Russia, and I come from a Turkic word. What did my name, “Cossack”, first mean?
hints: The same word gave its name to a country in Central Asia.
The name tells how they lived, not where they lived.
The opposite of a serf or a slave.
questions.description: A name that sounds like a Russian dance, but has more galloping in it than squatting.
questions.fun_fact: The word “Cossack” has the same origin as the name of the Kazakhs, the people of Kazakhstan.

questions.question: I'm a warrior of the First Crusade, and people call me a “crusader”. Where does my name come from?
questions.answer: From the cross sewn on their clothes
wrong_answers: From crossing the sea by ship
hints: Before setting out, they made a vow in a religious ceremony.
They wore it on them, where everyone could see it.
It is a Christian symbol.
questions.description: A warrior name so tangled it could have come straight out of a crossword.
questions.fun_fact: The First Crusade set out in 1096, and many of its warriors walked thousands of kilometers to reach Jerusalem.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this shiny round part with a small arm on top sits inside a device. What device is it?
hints: It's hidden inside many computers.
It keeps your photos and files even when you turn the computer off.
The first word of its name is the opposite of “soft”.
questions.description: Something that spins faster than you do when you hunt for the remote under the couch.
questions.fun_fact: The arm of a hard drive floats above the spinning disk at a gap far smaller than the width of a hair.

questions.question: What technology does the super-fast train between Shanghai and its airport use?
hints: It floats a tiny bit above the track.
It works with the same force that sticks things to the fridge door.
It uses very powerful magnets.
questions.description: A train that gets you to the airport before you've finished looking for your passport.
questions.fun_fact: Shanghai's maglev train covers about 30 km (19 miles) in under 8 minutes.

questions.question: Which key nutrient found in meat can you also get from beans, lentils and chickpeas?
hints: Meat and eggs have this nutrient too.
Your body uses it to build and repair itself.
Athletes drink shakes full of it.
questions.description: Never eaten a burger in its life, and still nobody beats it in a race.
questions.fun_fact: Rice and beans eaten together give a more complete protein than either one eaten alone.

questions.question: In “Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban,” how many years did Peter Pettigrew hide as Scabbers, the Weasleys' pet rat?
hints: A normal rat lives about 3 years, and Scabbers lived much longer.
It's the same amount of time Sirius Black spent in Azkaban.
It's more than ten years, but less than 15.
questions.description: The oldest pet in the wizarding world, and not because of a healthy diet.
questions.fun_fact: Lupin learned that Pettigrew was still alive when he saw his name moving on the Marauder's Map.

questions.question: Complete this: “Bowser is to Super Mario Bros. as M. Bison is to…”
hints: It's a one-on-one fighting video game.
Ryu, Ken and Chun-Li are characters in this game.
One of its fighters shouts “Hadouken!”
questions.description: A final boss in a red cape and military cap who won't even let you win at rock, paper, scissors.
questions.fun_fact: In Japan, M. Bison is called Vega, and the name M. Bison belongs to the boxer there.

questions.question: We are the Borg from “Star Trek”: we travel in a cube-shaped ship and always say “Resistance is futile.” What do we want to do to you?
hints: We are half living beings, half machines.
For us, the word “I” doesn't exist: there is only “we.”
We would give you implants so you think exactly like us.
questions.description: Space neighbors who aren't here to borrow sugar, or to say hello.
questions.fun_fact: The Borg Queen first appeared in the 1996 movie “Star Trek: First Contact.”

questions.question: What nickname is given to the city where this monument stands?
hints: The nickname comes from poets of ancient times.
A famous saying claims that all roads lead to this city.
It is the opposite of “temporary.”
questions.description: A city with so much history that even its ruins have ruins.
questions.fun_fact: The Roman poet Tibullus was already calling it that in the 1st century BC.

questions.question: In a village near Burgos, Spain, at Corpus Christi, a man dressed as a devil jumps over people lying on mattresses in the street. Who are they?
hints: The festival is called El Colacho and is several centuries old.
Their families dress them in their best clothes before laying them on the mattresses.
All of them were born during the past year.
questions.description: A festival where the one who jumps highest is also the ugliest guy in town.
questions.fun_fact: By tradition, the devil's leap “cleanses” the children of original sin and protects them from illness.

questions.question: I'm a famous saint of Ireland. Legend says I taught with a three-leaf clover, and on my day, March 17, half the world wears green. Who am I?
hints: I lived more than a thousand years ago.
A huge cathedral in New York is named after me.
In Irish, my name is Pádraig.
questions.description: A saint so green that even his symbol is a plant.
questions.fun_fact: In Chicago, the city's river is dyed green to celebrate Saint Patrick's Day.

questions.question: Every February 2 in the US, Phil the groundhog comes out of his burrow. Depending on whether he sees his shadow, what does he “predict”?
wrong_answers: Whether the corn harvest will be good
Whether the year will bring good luck
How many hurricanes there will be
hints: Phil lives in a town in Pennsylvania called Punxsutawney.
It has to do with the weather in the coming weeks.
If he sees his shadow, he hides back in his burrow… and the cold sticks around.
questions.description: The only celebrity in the world whose job is to climb out of a hole once a year.
questions.fun_fact: The tradition inspired the movie “Groundhog Day” (1993), in which Bill Murray lives the same February 2 over and over again.

questions.question: The Seven Dwarfs are to Snow White as the ___ are to Gru.
hints: They are small and very mischievous.
They are yellow, and many of them wear goggles.
They love bananas.
questions.description: A villain so bad that everyone ends up loving him, especially his little helpers.
questions.fun_fact: The Minions speak a made-up language that mixes words from many languages, including Spanish.

questions.question: At the store you see butterfly-shaped pasta called “farfalle”. If “farfalle” is to “butterflies”, “orecchiette” is to…
hints: It's a part of the body.
You have two of them, one on each side of your head.
You use them to listen to music.
questions.description: A pasta so tiny it fits on the tip of your finger.
questions.fun_fact: In Bari, in southern Italy, women make orecchiette by hand right in the street, pressing each piece of dough with their thumb.

questions.question: You just picked olives in an olive grove in Italy, as people have done since ancient Rome. Where do you take them to make oil?
hints: That's where they get crushed with stones or machines.
The old ones had big stone wheels that turned round and round.
The same kind of place is used to grind wheat.
questions.description: A fruit so oily that people squeeze the oil right out of it.
questions.fun_fact: Some olive trees in Italy are more than a thousand years old and still grow olives.

questions.question: Complete the sentence: shōjin ryōri, the traditional cooking of the monks in Japan's temples, is completely…
hints: It has to do with what the monks choose not to eat.
It uses tofu, vegetables, seaweed and mushrooms.
It has no meat and no fish.
questions.description: A menu so calm it meditates before it's served.
questions.fun_fact: Many Japanese temples still serve shōjin ryōri to visitors, on lacquered trays.

questions.question: I'm fried dough eaten at Christmas. In Mexico I'm flat and crunchy with honey; in Colombia I'm a little cheese ball. What am I?
hints: I'm fried in very hot oil.
In Spain I'm sometimes filled with cream.
My name starts with “Bu”.
questions.description: Dough, hot oil and a little patience: the recipe for happiness in December.
questions.fun_fact: Buñuelos came to the Americas with the Spanish, and each country changed them in its own way.

questions.question: According to the most common story, the first cheeseburger was made in Pasadena, California. In which decade?
hints: It was in the 20th century.
It was the age of jazz and silent films.
It was the same decade that radio became popular.
questions.description: Someone looked at a burger and thought: “It needs a little yellow blanket.”
questions.fun_fact: The cheeseburger is usually credited to Lionel Sternberger, who, the story goes, was only 16 or 17 years old when he made it.

questions.question: This black panther found Mowgli as a baby and took him to live with the wolves. What is its name?
hints: It's not the bear who sings or the tiger who hunts Mowgli.
It's the one who keeps telling Mowgli off and urging him to go back to the humans.
Its name starts with B, just like its bear friend's.
questions.description: The jungle's most stylish babysitter, dressed all in black.
questions.fun_fact: Black panthers are leopards or jaguars with lots of dark pigment: in the right light, you can still see their spots.

questions.question: About how wide can a leaf of the giant Amazon water lily grow?
hints: It's much bigger than the leaf of any plant in your home.
A grown-up could lie down on it, stretched out.
It's about as long as a small car.
questions.description: A plate so big that not even a whole family barbecue could fill it.
questions.fun_fact: The ribs under this leaf inspired the gardener Joseph Paxton when he designed London's Crystal Palace.

questions.question: In southern Vietnam, the Mekong splits into many branches before reaching the sea. There it's called the “River of ___ Dragons.” What number is missing?
hints: The number is hidden in the river's Vietnamese name, Cửu Long.
It's a single-digit number.
It's the number just before 10.
questions.description: A river so stylish it dresses up as a whole bunch of dragons at the end.
questions.fun_fact: The Mekong Delta has floating markets where people buy fruit straight from one boat to another.

questions.question: In the movie WALL·E, what does EVE come to Earth to find?
hints: Finding it would prove that people can live on Earth again.
What she finds fits inside an old boot.
It's something green that grows out of the soil.
questions.description: A visitor from space with more style than a brand-new phone and a worse temper than a Monday morning.
questions.fun_fact: Apple designer Jony Ive helped shape EVE's look so she would seem like a sleek, modern gadget.

questions.question: A robot walks on six legs, moving three at a time while the other three hold it up. Which group of animals is it copying?
hints: Look at the number of legs.
Spiders have eight, so it isn't them.
Ants, beetles and cockroaches belong to this group.
questions.description: A robot that would need three pairs of shoes just to leave the house.
questions.fun_fact: Walking with three legs always on the ground makes a tripod, so the robot never loses its balance, just like a cockroach.

questions.question: In what year did the animated series “PAW Patrol” first air?
hints: It's from this century.
It came out when touchscreen phones were already common everywhere.
It first aired the same year the movie “Frozen” hit theaters.
questions.description: Six puppies and a boy with a tablet handle more emergencies than real firefighters.
questions.fun_fact: Its creator, Keith Chapman, also came up with the series “Bob the Builder.”

questions.question: I'm a secret agent in a hat, living with two inventor stepbrothers who don't know my double life. My kind lives wild in only one country. Which?
hints: I'm Perry, from “Phineas and Ferb.”
My kind has a duck's bill and lays eggs, even though it's a mammal.
It's the land of kangaroos and koalas.
questions.description: Lazy pet by day, secret agent in a hat by night: every cat's dream.
questions.fun_fact: The platypus is one of the very few mammals in the world that lay eggs.

questions.question: I'm a dog who can stretch, grow huge or tiny, and I go on adventures in the Land of Ooo with my human brother Finn. Who am I?
hints: I'm on a Cartoon Network show.
My friend Finn wears a white hat with little ears.
I'm yellow and my show is “Adventure Time”.
questions.description: The perfect dog: stretches like chewing gum and never needs a walk.
questions.fun_fact: “Adventure Time” started as a short cartoon in 2007, years before it became a series.

questions.question: Riddle: I'm a space probe. I left Earth in 1977, flew past Jupiter and Saturn, and now travel beyond the planets. What do I carry in case aliens find me?
questions.answer: A record of sounds and music from Earth
wrong_answers: A flag from every country in the world
Seeds from plants that grow on Earth
A letter written by children of the world
hints: A team led by the astronomer Carl Sagan put it together.
It comes with drawn instructions showing how to use it.
It's golden and shaped like your grandparents' old vinyl LPs.
questions.description: The slowest letter in the universe, sent with no address and no stamp.
questions.fun_fact: The Voyager Golden Record carries greetings in 55 languages and even the song of a humpback whale.

questions.question: What do the trains run on along most lines of the Mexico City Metro?
hints: It isn't future technology: it has been in use for more than seventy years.
The idea came from the Paris Metro, which wanted quieter trains.
It's the same thing a mechanic pumps up when a car gets a flat.
questions.description: A metro that rolls with more style than you walk.
questions.fun_fact: The little pictures for each Mexico City Metro station were made so that anyone could find their way, even people who couldn't read.

questions.question: This is the Big Boy, one of the largest steam locomotives ever built. What was it made for?
hints: A US company built it in the 1940s.
Its huge pulling power mattered more than speed.
It had to pull very heavy trains up the mountains of the western United States.
questions.description: If this were a toy train, you'd need a living room the size of a stadium.
questions.fun_fact: Only 25 Big Boys were ever built, and one of them, No. 4014, ran again in 2019.

questions.question: Which luxury train ran from Paris to Istanbul and is the setting of an Agatha Christie novel with Hercule Poirot?
hints: Its route went from Western Europe toward the east.
Istanbul sits at the gateway to Asia.
Its name means “the express to the East”.
questions.description: A luxury train where nobody gets off until a detective has asked them a few questions.
questions.fun_fact: The Orient Express made its first trip in 1883.

questions.question: I'm a famous character. So I never forget a detail, I keep each fact in a room of my “mind palace” and walk through it in my imagination to find it. Who am I?
hints: I'm a detective.
I live in London, and a doctor friend writes down my adventures.
My address is 221B Baker Street.
questions.description: For anyone who can never remember where they left their keys: someone keeps a whole building inside their head.
questions.fun_fact: The mind palace is the ancient “method of loci”, which legend says the Greek poet Simonides invented about 2,500 years ago.

questions.question: With toothpaste and a cloth, you can make something shiny again after it turns black over time. What is it?
hints: It's something that used to be very shiny.
It gets darker because it reacts with the air.
It's a precious metal, cheaper than gold.
questions.description: A bathroom product with a secret second job in the dining room.
questions.fun_fact: Silver turns black because it reacts with sulfur in the air and forms a layer of silver sulfide.

questions.question: Which insects ooze a yellow liquid from their legs when disturbed and are set loose in vegetable gardens to eat aphids?
hints: These insects are hunters.
Farmers use them as a natural way to control pests.
They are usually red with black spots.
questions.description: A tiny bug that drinks your plants' juice without asking first.
questions.fun_fact: Some ants look after aphids like cows, so they can drink the sweet liquid the aphids give off.

questions.question: We're brothers, we wear masks and prison numbers, and we keep trying to rob Scrooge McDuck's money bin. Who are we?
hints: We show up in the adventures of DuckTales.
Our mom is a thief too.
Our name comes from a breed of dog, the same breed as Snoopy.
questions.description: A very close family, especially when they're planning something they shouldn't.
questions.fun_fact: The Beagle Boys were created by cartoonist Carl Barks and first appeared in a comic book in 1951.

questions.question: He's a billionaire, lives in a mansion in Gotham, and his butler is named Alfred. Where did his fortune come from?
hints: We're talking about the man behind Batman's mask.
He didn't have to earn it all by himself.
His family was already rich and owned a big company before he was born.
questions.description: A butler, a mansion and a secret cave don't come cheap.
questions.fun_fact: Bruce Wayne has appeared on Forbes magazine's lists of the richest fictional characters.

questions.question: M-Pesa, a service for sending money by phone, launched in 2007 in an African country. Which one?
hints: It's a country in East Africa.
It's famous for its safaris and its marathon runners.
Its capital is Nairobi.
questions.description: Sending money by text message before it was cool.
questions.fun_fact: “Pesa” means “money” in Swahili, and the “M” stands for “mobile.”

questions.question: I'm a Caribbean beach where planes land almost right over the swimmers' heads. Which island am I on?
hints: My name is Maho Beach, and I star in lots of viral videos.
My airport is named after a Dutch princess.
My island is split between France and the Netherlands.
questions.description: A place where sunbathing comes with free hair styling by jet engine.
questions.fun_fact: Saint Martin is one of the smallest islands in the world shared by two countries.

questions.question: The white lines airplanes leave in the sky form very high up, where it is extremely cold. What are they made of?
hints: They are close cousins of clouds.
The engine releases hot water vapor that cools down all at once.
It’s the same thing that forms frost in a freezer.
questions.description: Airplanes can draw too, but only in straight lines.
questions.fun_fact: When the air is very humid, these trails can last for hours and turn into real clouds.

questions.question: I'm four gold stripes on a pilot's sleeves. What am I for?
questions.answer: To show the pilot is the captain
wrong_answers: To count the years spent flying
To show how many languages they speak
To show how many engines the plane has
hints: The stripes change with the job in the cockpit.
The co-pilot usually wears three.
They show who is in charge of the plane.
questions.description: A uniform that speaks without saying a single word.
questions.fun_fact: Pilots' stripes come from navy uniforms, where they also show rank.

questions.question: After a run, what does a drink with electrolytes help your body get back?
wrong_answers: The sugar the body uses to sleep
hints: Think about what comes out of your skin when you exercise a lot.
Sweat tastes a little salty.
They are minerals like sodium and potassium.
questions.description: After a race, even the bravest runner stares at the bottle like it's buried treasure.
questions.fun_fact: Sweat tastes salty because it carries sodium, one of the electrolytes a sports drink puts back.

questions.question: I'm a fermented milk from the Caucasus, made with little white grains that look like tiny cauliflower. What am I?
hints: My grains are a mix of bacteria and yeasts.
I taste a little sour and a bit fizzy.
My name starts with K and ends with R.
questions.description: A milk that comes with its own little pets.
questions.fun_fact: Kefir grains grow and multiply, so you can give some away for others to make their own kefir.

questions.question: The male builds a bower of twigs and decorates it with blue objects, even plastic bottle caps, to attract a mate. Where does it live?
hints: It lives in the Southern Hemisphere.
This region is famous for its marsupials.
Koalas and kangaroos live there too.
questions.description: The most obsessive interior decorator in the whole animal kingdom.
questions.fun_fact: Some male bowerbirds steal blue decorations from their neighbors' bowers.

questions.question: Its flat head looks like a dead leaf, it breathes through a tube-shaped nose and it catches fish by sucking them in. Where does this turtle live?
hints: It lives in the warm, slow waters of a tropical rainforest.
It is called the mata mata.
It shares its river with piranhas and pink dolphins.
questions.description: A turtle that dressed up as a dry leaf and forgot to take off the costume.
questions.fun_fact: The mata mata doesn't chew: it snaps its mouth open so fast that the fish gets swallowed along with the water.

questions.question: Euro banknotes went into circulation in 2002. Which of these currencies was NOT replaced by the euro?
hints: It belongs to a country that joined the European Union after 2002.
That country is in the European Union but still has its own currency.
Its capital is Budapest.
questions.description: In 2002, half of Europe emptied its wallets and started over with brand-new money.
questions.fun_fact: Hungary joined the European Union in 2004, but people there still pay in forints.

questions.question: In a New York store, prices are marked with $. If € stands for the euro, $ stands for the…
hints: Its name comes from an old European silver coin, the “thaler”.
Scrooge McDuck has millions of them.
Its most famous banknote is green.
questions.description: An S that got a stripe and suddenly became a millionaire.
questions.fun_fact: The $ sign was used for the peso before the dollar, and today both use it.

questions.question: The Spanish children's song “La farolera” goes: “six and two are eight, and eight sixteen, and eight twenty-four, and eight…”. What number comes next?
hints: The song keeps adding the same number.
Each step adds 8 to the number before.
It's 24 plus 8.
questions.description: A song where someone falls down and, instead of getting up, starts doing math homework.
questions.fun_fact: Before electric light bulbs, there were people whose job was to light the street lamps by hand every night.

questions.question: I'm a dry, hollow gourd with ridges, and you play me by scraping me with a stick. What am I?
hints: I'm a percussion instrument.
People don't shake me or hit me: they scrape me.
You hear me a lot in salsa and cumbia, and my name sounds like “GWEE-roh”.
questions.description: An instrument that loves getting its belly scratched.
questions.fun_fact: A traditional güiro is made from the dried, hollow fruit of a plant in the squash family.

questions.question: You do it with both hands, it makes noise, and the song “If You're Happy and You Know It” asks you to do it. What is it?
hints: The audience does it at the end of a show.
Your hands hit each other.
People say “Give them a big hand!” just before doing it.
questions.description: A song that turns being happy into a workout.
questions.fun_fact: In later verses, the song also asks you to stomp your feet and shout “Hooray!”

questions.question: A cyclist’s legs are to the pedals as an engine’s pistons are to…
hints: Pedals turn an up-and-down push into a spin.
In the engine, this part takes the push from the pistons and turns it into rotation.
It’s a long metal shaft bent into a zigzag of elbows.
questions.description: A cyclist and a gasoline engine have more in common than you’d think.
questions.fun_fact: A bicycle’s pedal arms work like a tiny crankshaft, which is why bike mechanics call that part the “crankset”.

questions.question: This windshield cracked, but it didn’t shatter into pieces. What is it made of?
hints: It isn’t a single piece: it has several layers.
Between two layers of glass there is a sheet of plastic.
Its name is the same word used for sealing a paper ID card in clear plastic.
questions.description: A glass that breaks but flatly refuses to fall apart.
questions.fun_fact: Side windows are usually made of tempered glass, which breaks into lots of small pieces without sharp edges.

questions.question: Three of these luxury car brands were founded in Germany. Which one wasn't?

It's as British as afternoon tea.
questions.description: Four luxury cars walk into a party, and one of them doesn't speak the same language as the others.
questions.fun_fact: The little silver statue on the hood of every Rolls-Royce is called the “Spirit of Ecstasy.”

questions.question: You're in Matsumoto, Japan, in front of one of the country's oldest castles. Which bird gives it its nickname?
hints: The nickname comes from the color of its walls.

questions.description: A Japanese castle with a bird for a nickname, just like athletes who get named after animals.
questions.fun_fact: Matsumoto Castle still has its original wooden main tower from more than 400 years ago, which is very rare in Japan.

questions.question: When the castle was attacked, soldiers gathered in me: open to the sky and surrounded by walls. What am I?
hints: I'm inside the walls, but I have no roof.
Many cities in the Americas, like Lima and Cusco, have a main square, the “Plaza de Armas”, named after the same idea.
Big houses and schools often have one of me too: an open space in the middle of the building.
questions.description: The only place in the castle where nobody complained there was no room for the horse.
questions.fun_fact: The “Plazas de Armas” (“squares of arms”) of many Latin American cities got their name because troops gathered there in colonial times.

questions.question: Look at this detail of a fairy-tale castle in Germany. Which king, nicknamed “the Swan King”, had it built?
hints: He ruled a region in the south of Germany.
He was a huge fan of Wagner's operas.
The capital of his kingdom was Munich.
questions.description: A king who spent more on dreams than on armies.
questions.fun_fact: Neuschwanstein inspired Sleeping Beauty Castle at Disneyland.

questions.question: Darth Vader is to a black helmet as a Star Wars stormtrooper is to…
hints: Think of the Empire's soldiers marching in rows.
Their suit covers them from head to toe and makes them all look the same.
They look like they're made of plastic the color of snow.
questions.description: A thousand identical soldiers and not one can aim: the great mystery of the galaxy.
questions.fun_fact: The name “stormtrooper” was borrowed from German shock troops of World War I.

questions.question: In which decade did Stanisław Lem publish his novel “Solaris”?
hints: It's about scientists on a space station studying a planet covered by a living ocean.
It came out the same year Yuri Gagarin flew into space.
Tarkovsky turned it into a film in 1972, a decade later.
questions.description: A planet that's all ocean and reads your mind too: a terrible vacation spot.
questions.fun_fact: “Solaris” has two famous films: Andrei Tarkovsky's (1972) and Steven Soderbergh's with George Clooney (2002).

questions.question: Joseph Lister introduced it in 1867. It used carbolic acid and keeps wounds from getting infected. What is it called?
hints: It has to do with killing germs.
The alcohol and iodine you put on a cut do exactly this.
Its name means “against rotting.”
questions.description: Before this, surgeons operated in the same stained coat they wore last week.
questions.fun_fact: Listerine mouthwash is named in honor of Joseph Lister.

questions.question: Which German physicist discovered that voltage equals current multiplied by resistance?
hints: He published his law in 1827.
Today the unit of electrical resistance is named after him.
That unit is written with the Greek letter omega.
questions.description: A law that puts up resistance, but only to the current.
questions.fun_fact: When Ohm published his law, many fellow scientists dismissed it, and he lost his job as a teacher.

questions.question: Oppenheimer led the lab that tested the first atomic bomb in the New Mexico desert. In which year?
hints: It happened during the Second World War.
The United States built it in secret as part of the Manhattan Project.
It was in the middle of the 20th century, in the 1940s.
questions.description: A scientist Hollywood gave three hours of film and zero minutes of jokes.
questions.fun_fact: The test was called “Trinity”, and its flash was seen more than 200 km (124 miles) away.

questions.question: In which decade was “A Beautiful Mind”, the movie about mathematician John Nash, released?
hints: The lead actor is Russell Crowe.
It won the Oscar for Best Picture.
It came out the same year as the first Harry Potter movie.
questions.description: A movie where the equations have more suspense than the villains.
questions.fun_fact: John Nash won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1994 for his ideas on game theory.

questions.question: I'm the monster in a 2006 animated film: my door is my mouth, my rug is my tongue, and I swallow balls. What am I?
hints: I don't walk: I never leave my street.
I have windows that look like eyes.
I have a roof, a chimney and a yard that nobody dares to enter.
questions.description: The grumpiest grumpy neighbor in the whole neighborhood.
questions.fun_fact: “Monster House” was produced by Steven Spielberg and Robert Zemeckis and was nominated for the Oscar for Best Animated Feature.

questions.question: Who composed the famous two-note theme from “Jaws” (1975)?
hints: He is American and has worked with Spielberg on almost all of his films.
He composed the music for “Jurassic Park”.
He also wrote the famous march from “Star Wars”.
questions.description: Two notes were enough to make sure nobody ever swam calmly in the sea again.
questions.fun_fact: That music won John Williams the Oscar for Best Original Score.

questions.question: I wrote the novel about a snowy haunted hotel that Stanley Kubrick made into a film in 1980, though I didn't like his version. Who am I?
hints: I'm American and I live in Maine.
I wrote “Carrie” and “Misery”.
I also wrote “It”, the one with Pennywise the clown.
questions.description: A vacation at a mountain hotel: what could possibly go wrong?
questions.fun_fact: Stephen King disliked Kubrick's version so much that in 1997 he made his own TV miniseries of “The Shining”.

questions.question: He wears a costume of colorful diamonds and a black mask, and he was born in Italian comedy theater. Who is he?
hints: He is a playful, very nimble servant.
His costume looks like it's made of colorful patches.
His name starts with “Harle-”.
questions.description: The character who made diamonds fashionable four hundred years ago.
questions.fun_fact: A pattern of colorful diamonds is still called a “harlequin” pattern.

questions.question: I'm the brain trick that makes you see faces in outlets and clouds; my name joins the Greek words for “beside” and “image.” What am I?
hints: Your brain is so well trained to spot faces that it finds them even where there are none.
That's why many people see a rabbit or a face on the Moon.
It starts with “pare-” and has the word “idol” hidden inside.
questions.description: That wall outlet is staring at you with a surprised look, and it's not your fault.
questions.fun_fact: Some people see a famous figure's face in a piece of burnt toast, and one such snack even sold at auction for thousands of dollars.

questions.question: I'm nicknamed “golden blood,” and only a few dozen people in the world have me. What blood type am I?
hints: I'm not one of the eight common types (A, B, AB and O, positive or negative).
My red blood cells lack every antigen of one very well-known system.
That system is the same one that makes blood “positive” or “negative.”
questions.description: Blood so exclusive it has no one to share with.
questions.fun_fact: People with Rh null blood can donate to many people with rare Rh types, but they can only receive blood from another Rh null donor.

questions.question: I sparkle with diamonds, I'm kept in the Tower of London, and I only come out on very special occasions. Who wears me on their head?
hints: I'm golden and round.
I'm put on during a big ceremony.
The person who wears me lives in a palace.
questions.description: A piece of jewelry so important it has its own tower and its own guards.
questions.fun_fact: In 1671, a man named Thomas Blood tried to steal the Crown Jewels and squashed the crown flat to hide it.

questions.question: Hatzegopteryx, a huge flying reptile, probably hunted small dinosaurs on an island in what is now Romania. In which period did it live?
hints: It was a pterosaur, a relative of the pterodactyls, not a dinosaur.
It shared the Earth with Tyrannosaurus rex, which lived on another continent.
It's the period that ended when an asteroid hit the Earth 66 million years ago.
questions.description: A real airplane, but with a beak, wings made of skin and a very bad temper.
questions.fun_fact: Its open wings measured about 10 m (33 ft) across, and standing on the ground it was as tall as a giraffe.

questions.question: In 1888, I split the dinosaurs into two groups by their hips and named the ornithischians. Who am I?
hints: I was a British paleontologist of the 19th century.
I called the other group saurischians, “lizard-hipped.”
I didn't invent the word “dinosaur”; a more famous Briton did.
questions.description: The big question of the Jurassic world: bird hips or lizard hips?
questions.fun_fact: Even though ornithischians are “bird-hipped,” birds actually descend from the other group, the saurischians.

questions.question: In Jurassic World, Blue leads the pack of velociraptors that Owen trains. How many raptors were in that pack?
hints: Owen controls them with a snap of his fingers and a clicker.
Besides Blue, there are Charlie and Delta…
Charlie and Delta have one more sister named after a letter of the radio alphabet, just like them.
questions.description: A gang with real claws and a very brave trainer.
questions.fun_fact: Real velociraptors were about the size of a turkey and had feathers, much smaller than the ones in the movies.

questions.question: Tantalus is to the water he can never drink as Sisyphus is to…
hints: His punishment takes place on a hill.
He always gets close to the top, and then it all starts over.
Albert Camus wrote an essay about him pushing something heavy uphill.
questions.description: Some punishments are worse than going to bed without dessert, and this question proves it.
questions.fun_fact: Albert Camus ended “The Myth of Sisyphus” (1942) by saying we must imagine Sisyphus happy.

questions.question: Adidas is to three stripes as Nike is to…
hints: Look at the sneakers of someone near you.
It looks like the mark a teacher draws when an answer is right.
It's like a comma lying on its side.
questions.description: A Greek goddess who now lives on the feet of half the planet.
questions.fun_fact: Nike is named after the Greek goddess of victory, and its logo is often described as one of the goddess's wings.

questions.question: Versace's famous 1994 black dress, covered in gold safety pins, took its idea from a 1970s street style. Which one?
hints: It was a rebellious style born in London and New York.
Its fans wore colorful mohawks and leather jackets.
The band Sex Pistols was its great symbol.
questions.description: A luxury dress held together by what your grandma keeps in her sewing box.
questions.fun_fact: Actress Elizabeth Hurley became famous overnight after wearing that dress to a movie premiere.

questions.question: The Hermès silk scarf is 90 cm (35 in) on each side, and Grace Kelly once wore one as a sling for a broken arm. Which country is the brand from?
hints: Hermès started in 1837 making harnesses and saddles for horses.
Its main store is on an elegant street in the country's capital.
That capital has a very famous iron tower.
questions.description: A little square of silk that costs more than plenty of coats.
questions.fun_fact: Hermès launched its first silk scarf in 1937, exactly 100 years after the company was founded.

questions.question: In which decade did Madonna wear her famous cone-shaped corset, designed by Jean Paul Gaultier, on tour?
hints: Madonna was already a worldwide star by then.
The tour was called “Blond Ambition”.
It started right at the beginning of that decade, the same year as the World Cup in Italy.
questions.description: A piece of clothing so pointy it almost needs a “Caution” sign.
questions.fun_fact: Gaultier said that as a boy he made a cone corset for his teddy bear, Nana.

questions.question: It's the first test model of an invention, built before mass production to find mistakes. What is it called?
hints: New car models get one before they reach the showrooms.
The Wright brothers built several before they managed to fly.
The word starts with “proto”, which means “first”.
questions.description: The dress rehearsal before an invention steps on stage.
questions.fun_fact: James Dyson says he made 5,127 prototypes before he got his bagless vacuum cleaner right.

questions.question: Pastel fridges with rounded corners, radios with knobs and new record players that copy the 1950s. What style is this?
hints: It looks to the past, not to the future.
It's like your grandparents' clothes, but freshly made.
Its name comes from Latin and means “backwards”.
questions.description: Something new that dresses up as old to look more interesting.
questions.fun_fact: “Retro” comes from the Latin word for “backwards”, as in “retrospective” or “retrograde”.

questions.question: Raymond Loewy, the great industrial designer, created the colors of this US presidential plane. In which country was he born?
hints: He fought in the First World War before he emigrated.
He arrived in New York in 1919.
He was born in Paris.
questions.description: The man who dressed the most important plane in the world in blue-and-white pajamas.
questions.fun_fact: Loewy also redesigned the Shell logo and the Coca-Cola soda fountain dispenser.

questions.question: It comes from the collagen in animal skin and bones, and it makes gummy candies chewy. What is it?
hints: It comes from animals, not plants.

questions.description: An ingredient that went from a pot of boiling bones to a bag of candy, and nobody noticed.
questions.fun_fact: Because of gelatin, many gummy candies aren't vegetarian, so some brands use pectin from fruit instead.

questions.question: I’m a yellow canary who lives in a cage, and I always say “I tawt I taw a puddy tat!”. Which cat chases me?
hints: He is a Looney Tunes character, just like Bugs Bunny.

He sprays spit when he talks and never manages to catch the little bird.
questions.description: A chase that has gone on for decades and still has no happy ending for anyone.
questions.fun_fact: The first cartoon that paired the two, “Tweetie Pie” from 1947, won an Oscar.

questions.question: In the Pixar film “Monsters, Inc.”, which actor voices Sulley, the big furry monster?
hints: He is a big American actor with a deep voice.
Billy Crystal voices his partner Mike.
He also played Fred Flintstone in the 1994 film.
questions.description: Scaring kids is serious work, and somebody has to do the voice.
questions.fun_fact: To make Sulley look real, Pixar had to animate more than 2 million hairs on his body.

questions.question: In which decade did Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson detect the background radiation, the “echo” of the Big Bang?
hints: The discovery later won them the Nobel Prize in Physics.
They used a giant antenna at Bell Labs.
They published it in 1965.
questions.description: Two scientists blamed some pigeons for a noise that came from the beginning of the universe.

questions.question: You're watching X-Men and Magneto looks familiar: the same actor also played Gandalf. What's his name?
