His last name starts with “Mc”.
questions.description: A wizard and a magnetic villain fight over the same white beard.
questions.fun_fact: Ian McKellen was nominated for an Oscar for playing Gandalf in “The Fellowship of the Ring”.

questions.question: The writing on the One Ring appears when the ring is heated in a fire. What language is it written in?
hints: The letters may look Elvish, but the language is not.
Sauron invented it for his servants.
It is the language of the land where Mount Doom stands.
questions.description: The fine print on a contract nobody should ever sign.
questions.fun_fact: When Gandalf read the inscription out loud at the Council of Elrond, everyone present shuddered.

questions.question: I am the lord of horses, swift as the wind, and I carry Gandalf with no saddle or reins. Who am I?
hints: I am one of the Mearas, the noble horses of Rohan.
My coat is silvery white.
My name begins with the dark shape that follows you on a sunny day.
questions.description: A luxury taxi for wizards: no saddle, no reins and no meter running.
questions.fun_fact: The Mearas let only the kings of Rohan ride them… until Shadowfax chose Gandalf.

questions.question: I was a little girl; my dad sold cars and gave my name to the brand with the three-pointed star. What is my name?
hints: The brand is German and makes luxury cars.
My name is Spanish, even though my family was Austrian.
In Spanish, my name means “mercies” or “favors.”
questions.description: Some dads give their daughter a doll; this one gave her a whole car brand.
questions.fun_fact: Emil Jellinek, Mercedes's dad, raced cars in Nice under the nickname “Monsieur Mercedes.”

questions.question: Etsy's founder said the name came from hearing “eh, sì” in an Italian movie. Who directed that movie?
hints: It was a black-and-white Italian movie from the early 1960s about a film director who has run out of ideas.
His movies are full of circuses, clowns and dreamlike parades.
He was born in Rimini, and his last name became an adjective for dreamlike, over-the-top scenes.
questions.description: A shop for handmade things whose name came to someone watching a movie on the couch.

questions.question: Translating brand names: “Volkswagen” is to “people's car” as “Samsung”, in Korean, is to…
hints: The founder wanted something big, many in number and lasting forever.
Look up at the sky at night.
“Sam” means “three” in Korean.
questions.description: Brand names that, once translated, sound like a poem or a government announcement.
questions.fun_fact: Samsung started in 1938 selling dried fish, vegetables and noodles, long before it made phones.

questions.question: In 2017, Apple admitted that an update slowed down some iPhones on purpose. Which ones?
hints: It had nothing to do with where or when they were bought.
Apple said it did this so they wouldn't suddenly shut down.
It's the part that wears out after many charges.
questions.description: Your phone isn't tired: someone pulled the handbrake.
questions.fun_fact: After the scandal, Apple cut the price of battery replacements and had to pay millions of dollars in settlements.

questions.question: At O. J. Simpson's trial, his lawyer said: “If it doesn't fit, you must acquit.” What didn't fit?
hints: It was a piece of clothing found as evidence.
Simpson tried it on in front of the jury.
You wear it on your hand.
questions.description: Fashion can decide a trial too, if the size is wrong.
questions.fun_fact: The 1995 trial was shown on TV, and millions of people followed it like a soap opera.

questions.question: You're watching Miss Universe 2015: they announce Miss Colombia, then correct it. Which country was the real winner from?
hints: Before she won, the winner had already entered her country's beauty pageant twice.

It is in Asia and its capital is Manila.
questions.description: The shortest crown in history: about four minutes on the throne.
questions.fun_fact: Host Steve Harvey read the card wrong and had to apologize live in front of millions of people.

questions.question: An ad ends with “The Power of Dreams,” the slogan of a Japanese brand named after its founder. Who founded it?
hints: The brand makes cars and motorcycles seen all over the world.

The logo on its cars is a big H.
questions.description: A slogan for daydreamers, but with your seatbelt fastened.
questions.fun_fact: After World War II, Soichiro Honda got his start by fitting small engines to bicycles.

questions.question: A fast-food chain that sold tacos and burritos told people to “think outside the bun.” Which country does that food come from?
hints: It is a country in the Americas.

Its capital city shares the country's name.
questions.description: An invitation to drop the burger and fold the tortilla instead.

questions.question: I'm a solid dome: no one can go inside me, and pilgrims walk around me. The first ones held the ashes of a great teacher. Whose?

questions.question: In the middle of the Court of the Lions in the Alhambra, twelve marble lions stand in a circle. What are they there for?

To serve as an altar for offerings

questions.description: Twelve big cats that haven't moved or complained in centuries.

questions.question: Olivia Newton-John, Sandy from “Grease”, sang at Eurovision for the United Kingdom. In which decade?
hints: It was a few years before she filmed “Grease”.

questions.description: Before she put on a leather jacket for the movies, she put on a dress for a song contest.

questions.question: Sandie Shaw won Eurovision 1967 singing “Puppet on a String” barefoot. Which country did she represent?
hints: Sandie Shaw was a pop star of the 1960s, the decade of the miniskirt.

questions.description: A puppet on a string that moved a whole continent, sung by someone who didn't even bother with shoes.
questions.fun_fact: Sandie Shaw was the first British winner of Eurovision, and she often sang barefoot on stage.

questions.question: Columbus thought he had reached Asia, so the Spanish called the Americas “the Indies.” What name set them apart from the Asian ones?
hints: The name has to do with a compass direction.
From Spain, you had to sail toward the sunset to get there.
The ones in Asia were the East Indies.
questions.description: Columbus's GPS was a little out of date: by about half a planet.
questions.fun_fact: Because of that mistake, the native peoples of the Americas were called “Indians,” even though they had never been to India.

questions.question: Which of these islands was NOT settled by Polynesian sailors before Europeans arrived?

Darwin studied finches and giant tortoises there.
questions.description: Sailors who crossed the ocean with no compass, just stars, waves and birds to show them the way.
questions.fun_fact: The Galápagos had no human inhabitants when Spanish sailors found them by accident in 1535.

questions.question: They're in Indonesia, Magellan set out to reach them, and the Dutch controlled them for centuries. What were Europeans after there?
hints: They are the Maluku Islands, also called the Moluccas.
What they wanted was used to give food flavor.
They were known as “the Spice Islands.”
questions.description: Tiny islands that empires fought over like kids fighting over the last piece of cake.
questions.fun_fact: In 16th- and 17th-century Europe, nutmeg cost many, many times more than on the islands, and only the rich could afford it.

questions.question: Its name comes from Greek, in Harry Potter you must bow to it, and one is called Buckbeak. What is the hippogriff a mix of?
hints: It has wings and feathers.
Its back half is made for galloping.
“Hippos” is Greek for horse.
questions.description: An animal built by someone who just couldn't choose between two.
questions.fun_fact: The Italian poet Ariosto made the hippogriff famous in his 1516 poem “Orlando Furioso”.

questions.question: I have fangs, I hate sunlight, and I march in armies for the Dark Lord. Which writer made me famous?
hints: He was a professor at the University of Oxford.
He studied languages and invented whole new ones, like the languages of the elves.
His most famous work is “The Lord of the Rings.”
questions.description: Monsters who have never once been to the dentist.
questions.fun_fact: Since Tolkien, orcs have shown up in countless video games and role-playing games.

questions.question: In the movie “Cleopatra” (1963), Elizabeth Taylor set a costume record. How many times did she change outfits?
hints: It was a Guinness World Record for an actress in a single film.

It's more than 50 but less than 100.
questions.description: A queen of Egypt with more outfits in her closet than years on the throne.
questions.fun_fact: “Cleopatra” cost so much that it nearly bankrupted the studio that made it.

questions.question: The Great Migration of wildebeest makes a full loop every year. How many countries does it pass through?

These countries are Tanzania and its northern neighbor, Kenya.
questions.description: A traffic jam of millions of legs that happens again every single year.

questions.question: About how long is an adult Egyptian cobra?
hints: It's much longer than a pencil or a ruler.

questions.description: The snake that pharaohs wore as decoration on their foreheads.
questions.fun_fact: The cobra on the pharaohs' headdress is called the “uraeus,” and it stood for royal protection.

questions.question: It's reddish, it comes out of a hippo's skin, and it isn't blood. Which human product does it act like?
hints: Hippos spend many hours under the African sun.

You'd put it on at the beach so you don't get burned.
questions.description: The hippo has its own beauty line, and it refuses to sell it.
questions.fun_fact: This “red sweat” also helps keep the hippo's wounds from getting infected.

questions.question: “Kangaroo” is to “jumping forward” as “sifaka” is to “jumping…”
hints: The sifaka is a lemur from Madagascar that lives in the trees.
When it comes down to the ground, it looks like it's dancing.
It moves like a crab, with its arms up in the air.
questions.description: A lemur that dances like nobody's watching.
questions.fun_fact: The name “sifaka” copies the alarm call this lemur makes: “shi-fak!”

questions.question: I'm a tiger: to everyone else, a stuffed toy; to my friend Calvin, a real one. I share my name with an English philosopher. Who am I?
hints: I appear in a newspaper comic strip, not in a movie.
My creator is Bill Watterson.
My name is that of the philosopher who wrote “Leviathan”.
questions.description: A stuffed toy that has read more philosophy than most grown-ups.
questions.fun_fact: Calvin is named after a thinker too: the theologian John Calvin.

questions.question: Saint Augustine is to “Confessions” as Thomas Aquinas is to…
hints: It is a huge work that was never finished.

Its title says it is a “summary” of what is known about God.
questions.description: A book so long that not even its author got to the end of it.
questions.fun_fact: Because he was quiet and heavyset, his classmates nicknamed Thomas Aquinas “the Dumb Ox.”

questions.question: This 1787 painting shows a famous Greek philosopher surrounded by his students. Who is he?
hints: He was Plato's teacher.
He is credited with the saying “I know that I know nothing”.
A way of teaching by asking questions is named after him.
questions.description: A get-together of friends where nobody asked for popcorn.
questions.fun_fact: David painted Plato as an old man at the foot of the bed, even though Plato was actually young at the time.

questions.question: Inside an igloo you can stay warmer than outside. What job does the packed snow of its walls do?
hints: Packed snow is full of tiny trapped air bubbles.
It does the same job as the wool in a good winter coat.
It barely lets your body heat escape to the outside.
questions.description: A house made of ice that, against all odds, is not a refrigerator.
questions.fun_fact: Inside an igloo, with nothing but the warmth of the people in it, the temperature can be tens of degrees higher than outside.

questions.question: Complete: one hertz equals one vibration or oscillation per…
hints: The hertz measures frequency: how often something repeats.
It is the basic unit of time in the International System of Units.
A clock shows it with its fastest hand.
questions.description: A unit with a German last name that buzzes more than a phone on silent.
questions.fun_fact: Human ears hear sounds from about 20 to 20,000 hertz, and dogs can hear much higher frequencies.

questions.question: I'm shaped like a cone: speak into my narrow end and your voice comes out louder and carries far. What am I?
hints: People use me at marches, sports games and fire drills.
Many of me run on batteries and have a trigger.
My name starts with “mega”, which means big.
questions.description: The best friend of every gym teacher on a school field trip.
questions.fun_fact: Before they had batteries, megaphones were just simple cones of cardboard or metal, and they still worked pretty well.

questions.question: The Koch snowflake is built by repeating the same step over and over. What shape does it start from?
hints: At each step, every side grows a little spike in the middle.
After the first step, the shape looks like a six-pointed star.
The starting shape has three equal sides.
questions.description: A snowflake that never melts, but never finishes being drawn either.
questions.fun_fact: The Koch snowflake has an infinitely long edge, yet the area inside it is finite.

questions.question: Pentagon, hexagon, heptagon… keep going and you reach the dodecagon. How many sides does it have?
hints: “Dodeca” comes from Greek.
It has more sides than a decagon, which has 10.
It's the number of eggs in a dozen.
questions.description: A shape with so many corners it almost thinks it's a circle.
questions.fun_fact: The British one-pound coin in use since 2017 is shaped like a dodecagon.

questions.question: These shapes have the same form and the same size, and they match exactly when you put one on top of the other. What are they called?
hints: Looking alike isn't enough: they must also be the same size.
Similar shapes have the same form, but they can be different sizes.
The word starts with “con”.
questions.description: Two shapes so alike that even their mom can't tell them apart.
questions.fun_fact: Fold a sheet of paper in half and cut out a shape through both layers: the two pieces you get are congruent.

questions.question: Which of these photography books is NOT by the Brazilian Sebastião Salgado?
hints: Salgado spent years on huge projects shot around the world, always in black and white.
The odd one out is a famous 1950s book about a road trip.
It was made by the Swiss photographer Robert Frank while traveling across the United States.
questions.description: An economist who swapped numbers for black-and-white photos.
questions.fun_fact: Salgado and his wife Lélia replanted millions of trees on the family farm in Brazil, which had lost its forest.

questions.question: This boot print was photographed in 1969. Where exactly was it made?
hints: It was on the Moon, during Apollo 11.
The Moon’s “seas” are dark plains without a single drop of water.
The landing site was named after that same sea.
questions.description: The most famous footprint in the universe, and it isn’t on any Walk of Fame.
questions.fun_fact: Buzz Aldrin photographed his own footprint to study how moon dust packs down, not for the family photo album.

questions.question: I was the first human to travel to space, and from up there I said: “The Earth is blue.” Who am I?
hints: My trip was in 1961, before anyone had walked on the Moon.
I came from the Soviet Union.
My first name starts with Y, and my spaceship was called Vostok 1.
questions.description: The first tourist who looked out the window and found out home had a whole new paint job.
questions.fun_fact: Gagarin's trip around the Earth lasted only about 108 minutes.

questions.question: Which video game character has the motto “Gotta go fast!”?
hints: He runs so fast he curls up into a little ball.
He collects golden rings.
He is a blue hedgehog.
questions.description: Someone who has never once had to wait for anything to load.
questions.fun_fact: Sonic is blue because that was the color of the logo of Sega, the company that created him.

questions.question: I wore braces on my legs until a friend shouted, “Run!” Later I ran across the United States. Who am I?
hints: My movie came out in 1994.
Tom Hanks plays me.
My mama always said life is like a box of chocolates.
questions.description: The man who turned a bit of playground advice into the longest jog in movie history.
questions.fun_fact: In the movie, Forrest runs for three years, two months, fourteen days and sixteen hours.

questions.question: Cold War spies hid microfilm everywhere. In which century was microfilm invented?
hints: It's older than it looks.
It was invented soon after photography.
Back then, steam trains were running, but the electric light bulb didn't exist yet.
questions.description: The tiniest thing a spy could hide inside a hollow coin.
questions.fun_fact: During the Siege of Paris in 1870, thousands of messages on microfilm were sent tied to carrier pigeons.

questions.question: The CIA is the famous secret service of the United States. What does the “I” in CIA stand for?
hints: The word describes the agency's job: secretly finding out what other countries are planning.
It is also a word used for spying in general.
It is what an IQ test measures.
questions.description: Three letters that always show up in dark sunglasses in the movies.
questions.fun_fact: The CIA was founded in 1947, just as the Cold War was beginning.

questions.question: Who is this singer, still called “the King”?
hints: He lived in Memphis, in the United States, and became famous there.
He lived in a mansion called Graceland.
His first name starts with E, and he is known as “the King of Rock and Roll”.
questions.description: A singer whose hips were censored on television.
questions.fun_fact: Elvis did his military service in West Germany from 1958 to 1960, in the middle of the Cold War.

questions.question: I'm a Hogwarts subject: in my class, students read tea leaves, and a centaur teaches by watching the planets. What am I?
hints: My main teacher lives at the top of a tower full of incense.
That teacher is Sybill Trelawney, who keeps predicting terrible things for Harry.
My goal is to see the future.
questions.description: A class where you can get top marks if you already know what's on the test.
questions.fun_fact: The centaur Firenze teaches this subject in a classroom that looks like a forest, with moss on the floor.

questions.question: I'm an object: if you write on my pages, the ink disappears and a young man named Tom Riddle writes back. What am I?
hints: I appear in “Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets.”
Ginny Weasley found me and wrote her secrets in me.
Harry destroyed me with a basilisk fang.
questions.description: An object that keeps secrets… and talks back.
questions.fun_fact: The letters of “Tom Marvolo Riddle” can be rearranged to spell “I am Lord Voldemort.”

questions.question: Dr. Dre co-founded the headphone brand Beats. In which decade was it founded?
hints: It came after Dr. Dre was already a 1990s rap legend.
The iPod already existed, but the iPhone hadn't come out yet.
It was founded in the middle of the decade when the 21st century began.
questions.description: Headphones so expensive they should come with their own bodyguard.
questions.fun_fact: In 2014, Apple bought Beats for about $3 billion.

questions.question: I'm a street dance named after the “pop” the body makes. What move is my base?
questions.answer: Tensing and releasing muscles in a flash
wrong_answers: Spinning on your head on the floor
hints: When you watch me, the dancer can look like a robot.
The move happens in the arms, legs, neck and chest, like little jolts.
It's suddenly tightening the muscles, as if something tapped you from the inside.
questions.description: A dance where the body seems to have hiccups, but with style.
questions.fun_fact: Popping was born in the 1970s in Fresno, California, with a group called the Electric Boogaloos.

review.feedback: Hint 1 ("When you watch me, the dancer can look like a robot.") keeps the first-person voice of the source riddle ("Soy un baile…"). The English question isn't in the first person, so "me" doesn't refer to anything. Reword it, e.g. "Watching it, the dancer can look like a robot."

questions.question: Eminem's “Lose Yourself” was the first rap song to win an Oscar. In which decade did it come out?
hints: It came out when people still bought music on CDs.
The 21st century had already begun.
It came out just a couple of years after the turn of the millennium.
questions.description: A song that tells you that you only get one shot, so think carefully about your answer.
questions.fun_fact: Eminem didn't go to collect his Oscar: reportedly he was asleep at home.

questions.question: Its bass makes you move, James Brown was its big star, and its drum beats fed hip hop. What genre is it?
hints: It was born in the United States in the 1960s.
DJs in the Bronx looped its drum parts so people could dance.
George Clinton's band Parliament and bassist Bootsy Collins were also huge stars of this style.
questions.description: Music that makes even your grandpa shake his shoulders without noticing.
questions.fun_fact: The drum break in James Brown's “Funky Drummer” is one of the most sampled pieces of music in history.

questions.question: The founder's son created it in 1896, with flowers and the letters LV. Why was the Louis Vuitton pattern invented?
wrong_answers: To hide stains on the leather
To win a contest in Paris
hints: The brand already had a problem that it still has today.
In 1888 the brand had tried a checkered design, but it didn't solve that problem.
Think of the knockoff bags sold on the street.
questions.description: Letters so famous that even people who can't read know them.
questions.fun_fact: Louis Vuitton started out making flat travel trunks, which stacked better than the ones with curved lids.

questions.question: I wear a uniform with blue, yellow and red stripes, a plumed helmet and a spear, and I protect the Pope. Who am I?
hints: I work in the smallest country in the world.
I live in the Vatican, inside Rome.
My name includes a country famous for its chocolate and its watches.
questions.description: The most colorful bodyguards on the planet.
questions.fun_fact: People often say Michelangelo designed their uniform, but that's a myth: today's version dates from 1914.

questions.question: At the wedding at Cana, the wine ran out. According to the Gospel, what did Jesus turn into wine?
hints: It came out of some large stone jars.
Jesus told the servants to fill the jars to the brim.
It has no color and no taste.
questions.description: The trick every waiter wishes they could learn.
questions.fun_fact: According to the Gospel of John, this was Jesus's first miracle, and the new wine turned out better than the first.

questions.question: The prophet Samuel anointed the first king of Israel. Who was he?
hints: He was from the tribe of Benjamin.
He was so tall he stood head and shoulders above everyone.
He was later replaced by the young David.
questions.description: He had to pick a king with no elections, no debates and no polls.
questions.fun_fact: Samuel later anointed David too, while he was still a boy looking after sheep.

questions.question: Palatine, Aventine and Capitoline are three of them, and they give Rome its nickname. What are they?
hints: Rome's nickname comes with the number seven.
Legend says Romulus founded the city on the Palatine.
From the top of each one, you can see the whole city.
questions.description: Rome has more nicknames than Grandma has for you when she can't remember your name.
questions.fun_fact: The word “palace” comes from the Palatine Hill, where the Roman emperors lived.

questions.question: I'm the pilum, the Roman legionary's javelin, and my iron tip bent when it hit something. What was that for?
questions.answer: So it couldn't be thrown back
wrong_answers: So it was lighter to carry
So it could hook walls for climbing
So it wouldn't rust in the rain
hints: Think about what the enemy would do after it landed.
A bent javelin doesn't fly straight.
The enemy couldn't reuse it against the Romans.
questions.description: A weapon designed to break on purpose, like an umbrella on a windy day.
questions.fun_fact: If a pilum stuck in a shield, the shield became so heavy and awkward that many warriors chose to drop it.

questions.question: When graphite was found in England in the 1500s, people thought it was a metal. Which metal, whose name we still use for a pencil's core?
hints: It's a gray, soft and very heavy metal.
That's why people say a pencil tip isn't poisonous: it never had this metal in it.
When your pencil breaks, people say you snapped this metal.
questions.description: A lie so old you've even written with it in your notebook.
questions.fun_fact: Shepherds in Borrowdale used that graphite to mark their sheep long before anyone thought of writing with it.

questions.question: The putty that bounces, stretches and copies pictures from the newspaper was an accident in the search for fake rubber. In which decade?
hints: Its inventor worked in the lab of a big US electric company.
Only a few years passed between its discovery and its sale as a toy.
Rubber was scarce because of the war, and in 1950 it went on sale in plastic eggs.
questions.description: A failed experiment that bounces, stretches and never did its job, but kept millions of people busy.
questions.fun_fact: No engineer found a serious use for it, until a salesman packed it in plastic eggs and turned it into a toy.

questions.question: In Scotland, it's good luck when a tall, dark-haired man arrives at your home with coal, salt and bread. When must he arrive?
questions.answer: Just after midnight on New Year's
wrong_answers: On the morning of Christmas Day
hints: He has to be the first person to enter the home on that date.
Scots call this celebration “Hogmanay.”
It's when everyone counts down and the calendar starts over.
questions.description: A surprise visitor that nobody in Scotland wants to see arriving empty-handed.
questions.fun_fact: People often say the visitor shouldn't be blond, because that reminded people of the Viking invaders of long ago.

questions.question: One tradition says that if you fold a thousand paper figures like this one, you can make a wish. Which country is it from?
hints: It's a country made up of islands.
There, the crane is a symbol of long life and good luck.
Its flag is white with a red circle.
questions.description: A bird that will never fly, but grants wishes if you're patient.
questions.fun_fact: The crane was said to live a thousand years, so people fold a thousand of them, and the whole set is called “senbazuru.”

questions.question: The bride carries it at the wedding, throws it backward at the end, and whoever catches it is next to marry. What is it?
hints: She holds it in her hands as she walks down the aisle.
It smells very nice.
It's made of roses, lilies or other plants.
questions.description: The only throwing sport played in fancy clothes.
questions.fun_fact: It's said that guests once tore little pieces off the bride's dress for good luck, and throwing the bouquet was a way to distract them.

questions.question: Guess: I was born in 1873 for California's miners, I have copper rivets, and on my label two horses try to tear me apart. What am I?
hints: You wear me on your legs.
I'm almost always made of a blue cloth called denim.
I have pockets, a zipper or buttons, and two legs.
questions.description: A piece of clothing so tough that not even the cavalry could beat it.
questions.fun_fact: Levi's has used its two-horse logo since 1886 to show off that not even two horses could tear its jeans apart.

questions.question: Which place is NOT inside the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, according to tradition?
questions.answer: The grotto where Jesus was born
hints: The church remembers the end of Jesus's life, not the beginning.
The church's name already speaks of a tomb.
That place is in another town: Bethlehem.
questions.description: A church so busy that several Christian communities have to take turns looking after it.
questions.fun_fact: For centuries, two Muslim families have kept the keys to the Holy Sepulchre and opened its door every morning.

questions.question: This is Mount Tabor, in Galilee. According to Christian tradition, what happened on its summit?
wrong_answers: The giving of the Ten Commandments
hints: It happened during the life of Jesus, not in the Old Testament.
Moses and Elijah appeared there next to Jesus.
The Gospels say his face shone like the sun and his clothes turned white.
questions.description: A nice round mountain that looks like it came out of a pudding mold.
questions.fun_fact: To drive up to the top of Mount Tabor, you take a road full of hairpin bends.

questions.question: If I don't draw the plans, nobody knows how to build the house. I design houses, buildings and skyscrapers. Who am I?
hints: I work a lot with pencils, rulers and plans on a screen.
My work starts before the first brick is laid.
I went to university to learn how to design buildings.
questions.description: Without this person, buildings would just be piles of bricks with good intentions.
questions.fun_fact: The word “architect” comes from Greek and means something like “chief builder.”

questions.question: Roughly how long ago was the Great Pyramid of Giza built?
hints: It is much older than the time of Jesus.
It is the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.
It was finished around 2560 BC.
questions.description: A building so old that when it was finished, mammoths were still wandering around.
questions.fun_fact: For about 3,800 years, the Great Pyramid was the tallest structure ever built by humans.

questions.question: Juanito, a boy in a Mexican sombrero, was the mascot of a FIFA World Cup. Which year?
hints: It was the first World Cup played in North America.
At that World Cup, Brazil and Pelé won their third title.
It came right at the start of a new decade.
questions.description: A boy in a hat who never played a single match but showed up in every sticker album.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico hosted the World Cup again in 1986, and that time the mascot was Pique, a jalapeño pepper with a mustache.

questions.question: A famous ad says “A Diamond Is Forever.” Which chemical element is this gem made of?
hints: It's the same element found in the graphite of pencils.
It's the basis of the chemistry of all living things.
Its chemical symbol is the letter C.
questions.description: Anything promised “forever” usually comes in a very small box.
questions.fun_fact: Frances Gerety wrote the line for De Beers in 1947, and in 1999 it was named the best advertising slogan of the 20th century.

questions.question: Which of these characters did NOT live in McDonaldland, the fantasy world of McDonald's commercials?
hints: Three of them were Ronald McDonald's friends.
The answer is the mascot of a different burger chain.
She is a red-haired girl with pigtails.
questions.description: A kingdom where hamburgers grow on trees and nobody pays taxes.
questions.fun_fact: In 2023, a purple shake made in honor of Grimace went viral on social media.

questions.question: Listen: this animal is one of the most rescued from illegal wildlife trade in Latin America. What is it?
hints: It's a bird from the rainforest.
It has very bright feathers and a very long tail.
It's a big parrot, sometimes red, blue and yellow.
questions.description: A bird so colorful that smugglers want it, and so do the people who rescue it.
questions.fun_fact: Macaws can live more than 50 years, so a rescued macaw needs care for a very, very long time.

questions.question: Look at this crest and those orange cheeks: which group of birds does this bird belong to?
hints: It is a very common pet bird kept in cages.
It raises and lowers its crest depending on its mood.
It is related to some large white birds from Australia with a big crest.
questions.description: A bird that always looks like it just styled its hair with gel.
questions.fun_fact: The cockatiel is the smallest cockatoo in the world, and many males learn to whistle songs.

questions.question: The Apollo program took humans to the Moon in 1969. Which twin sister of Apollo gives her name to the new Moon program?
hints: She is a hunting goddess with a bow and arrows.
Like her brother, she is a daughter of Zeus.
The Romans called her Diana.
questions.description: Even NASA has trouble choosing names for its kids.
questions.fun_fact: The Apollo program's Saturn V rocket was about 110 meters (360 ft) tall, taller than the Statue of Liberty with its pedestal.

questions.question: Diana was the “Princess of Wales”. Where is Wales?
hints: It is a place in Europe.
It is on a big island, right next to England.
It is part of the same country as London.
questions.description: A title so grand that you need a map just to understand it.
questions.fun_fact: People in Wales speak Welsh, a very old language with words like “cwtch”, which means a hug.

questions.question: You're on the banks of the River Thames and see white swans with no markings. By an old tradition, who owns them?
hints: Their owner wears a crown.
Every year they are counted in an official ceremony.
They used to belong to Elizabeth II; today they belong to her son.
questions.description: Some very fancy ducks with a very important owner.
questions.fun_fact: Every summer there is “Swan Upping”, a ceremony where people in boats count and check the swans on the Thames.

questions.question: I was Ecuador's currency until 2000, and I'm named after the Grand Marshal of Ayacucho. Which currency am I?
hints: My hero fought alongside Simón Bolívar.
One of Bolivia's capitals has the same name.
Colombia has a department with my name, and its capital is Sincelejo.
questions.description: A currency named after a hero, which retired as soon as the dollar showed up.
questions.fun_fact: Since 2000, Ecuador has used the US dollar as its official currency.

questions.question: I'm Japan's lowest-value coin and I weigh exactly 1 gram. What metal am I made of?
hints: It's a very light, silver-colored metal.
Many drink cans are made of it.
It's also used for the shiny foil that wraps food in the kitchen.
questions.description: A coin so light it nearly flies out of your pocket on its own.
questions.fun_fact: This coin is so light that it can float on water, held up by surface tension.

questions.question: This building was built as a Christian church almost 1,500 years ago. What was its city called back then?
hints: The city lies on a famous strait, where two continents meet.
Later another empire renamed it, and today it is the largest city in its country.
Its name comes from a Roman emperor called Constantine.
questions.description: A city so important it ended up with more names than a dog shared by three families.
questions.fun_fact: Hagia Sophia was the largest cathedral in the world for almost a thousand years.

questions.question: This marble sculpture is in the Vatican. Who made it?
hints: He was an Italian artist of the Renaissance.
He carved it when he was only about 24 years old.
He also sculpted the famous David in Florence.
questions.description: A sculpture so perfect that its maker just couldn't resist signing it.
questions.fun_fact: The Pietà is the only work Michelangelo ever signed: his name is carved on the sash across the Virgin Mary's chest.

questions.question: They called me “The Voice” and I sang “New York, New York.” I was born in the US, but my parents came from another country. Which one?
hints: My parents moved to the United States in the early 1900s, like millions of other Europeans.
Many immigrants from that country settled in New York and New Jersey.
It's the country of pizza and pasta.
questions.description: A gentleman so elegant he even sang in a bow tie.
questions.fun_fact: Frank Sinatra was born in Hoboken, a New Jersey city just across the river from New York.

questions.question: Mariachi is to ranchera as cowboy is to…
hints: Its songs are about pickup trucks, horses and broken hearts.
It's sung with guitar, banjo and lots of longing for life out on the land.
Dolly Parton and Johnny Cash are among its biggest stars.
questions.description: Music with boots, a big hat and a whiff of the stable.
questions.fun_fact: Nashville, Tennessee, is so famous for country music that it's nicknamed “Music City.”

questions.question: I moved from Cancún to Buenos Aires, I deliver food on roller skates and I dream of shining at the Jam & Roller rink. Who am I?
hints: I'm the main character of a Disney Channel series.
The series is named after me.
My first name is the Spanish word for Earth's natural satellite.
questions.description: A girl who can't seem to walk anywhere without wheels under her feet.
questions.fun_fact: Luna was played by Mexican actress and singer Karol Sevilla.

questions.question: They call me a “single,” but I'm not looking for a partner. In music, what am I?
questions.answer: A song released on its own
hints: Artists put me out before their album.
I'm used to promote a record.
On old vinyl records, I often had a B-side.
questions.description: In music, this word has nothing to do with dating apps.
questions.fun_fact: Singles used to be sold on small vinyl records that spun at 45 revolutions per minute.

questions.question: At a Broadway concert: “Don't Cry for Me Argentina” is to “Evita” as “Memory” is to…
hints: Both musicals are by Andrew Lloyd Webber.
The song is sung by Grizabella, a faded old star.
Its characters have whiskers and tails.
questions.description: Songs so famous that people sing them in the shower, even if they've never seen the show.
questions.fun_fact: The musical “Cats” grew out of a book of poems about cats by T. S. Eliot.

questions.question: In which decade did “Singin' in the Rain”, starring Debbie Reynolds and Gene Kelly, come out?
hints: The film was already in color.
It was the golden age of Hollywood's big studio musicals.
It came out early in that decade, soon after 1950.
questions.description: It was pouring down, and someone still danced happily in the street: that's how cheerful those days were.
questions.fun_fact: Debbie Reynolds was the mother of Carrie Fisher, who played Princess Leia in Star Wars.

questions.question: I played detective Sam Spade in “The Maltese Falcon” and Philip Marlowe in “The Big Sleep”, both film noir classics. Who am I?
hints: I was an American actor of the 1940s.
I also starred in a famous romance set in a café in Morocco.
There I said “We'll always have Paris,” in “Casablanca.”
questions.description: Hat, trench coat, cigarette and zero smiles: the official uniform of the black-and-white detective.
questions.fun_fact: The name “film noir” came from French critics, inspired by a French series of crime novels with black covers.

questions.question: I'm an Italian professor, and I wrote a mystery novel set in a medieval abbey, with a friar as the detective. Who am I?
hints: My novel was made into a film starring Sean Connery.
Its title mentions a flower.
I wrote “The Name of the Rose.”
questions.description: A professor who decided the best medieval history lesson was a murder mystery full of monks.
questions.fun_fact: The friar detective in “The Name of the Rose” is called William of Baskerville, a nod to Sherlock Holmes.

questions.question: A normal year of 365 days starts on a Thursday. How many Thursdays does that year have?
hints: Think about how many full weeks fit into 365 days.
52 weeks are 364 days, so exactly one day is left over.
That extra day is the same day of the week the year started on.
questions.description: A whole calendar counted with the 7 times table and a little patience.
questions.fun_fact: That's why in every normal year one day of the week comes up 53 times; in leap years, two days do.

questions.question: There's a party in the town square because the city is celebrating its bicentennial. How many years old is it turning?
hints: “Bi” means two, as in “bicycle.”
“Centennial” has to do with a hundred, like “century.”
It's two times a hundred.
questions.description: A birthday cake with so many candles that you need a firefighter to blow them out.
questions.fun_fact: Many countries in Latin America celebrated 200 years of independence between 2009 and 2024.

questions.question: In which decade did Post-it Notes first go on sale in stores?
hints: Your grandparents didn't have them as kids.
They came before smartphones.
They arrived around the time of the first personal computers.
questions.description: A note that sticks, unsticks and sticks again without losing its dignity.
questions.fun_fact: They grew out of a “failed” glue that barely stuck, plus someone who wanted to mark pages without the paper falling out.

questions.question: Where does the name of the Japanese brand Casio come from?
wrong_answers: From the name of a Japanese volcano
From the name of an Italian city
hints: Many brands got their names this way.
It was founded by several brothers.
The brothers' surname was Kashio.
questions.description: A Japanese brand that has been on the wrists and in the backpacks of half the planet.
questions.fun_fact: In 1957, Casio launched one of the world's first compact, fully electric calculators.

questions.question: Look at this huge fossil tooth with saw-like edges. What kind of animal did it come from?
hints: Its owner lost teeth all its life and kept growing new ones.
Its owner had no bones, only cartilage.
It was a giant sea hunter with fins, and its living relatives still hunt in every ocean.
questions.description: This owner would have needed a very big toothbrush, and a whole box of spares.
questions.fun_fact: A shark can go through thousands of teeth in its life: the spare ones move forward in rows, like on a conveyor belt.

questions.question: This gas-filled organ, taken from a fish, helps it float without effort. Which group of fish has it?
hints: It's called the swim bladder.
Sharks don't have one: they stay afloat thanks to a liver full of oil.
It's the group most fish belong to: sardines, tuna and trout.
questions.description: A party balloon that some fish carry inside them all year round.
questions.fun_fact: The swim bladder and our lungs are related organs: they share an evolutionary origin.

questions.question: Look at this eye. Most fish sleep with their eyes open because they have no…
hints: You use them many times a minute without noticing.
They are like little skin curtains for the eye.
They come down every time you blink.
questions.description: An eye that will never wink at you.
questions.fun_fact: Some sharks have a special membrane, called the nictitating membrane, that covers the eye when they bite.

questions.question: This rainbow trout is common in the cold rivers of the Andes, but it isn't native there. Where does it originally come from?
hints: It was brought to South America more than a hundred years ago for fishing and fish farming.
Its original home is rivers that flow into the Pacific Ocean.
It's native to places like California, Canada and Alaska.
questions.description: A tourist so well settled in that nobody asks for her passport anymore.
questions.fun_fact: Some rainbow trout travel out to sea and come back to the river much bigger; these are called steelhead.

questions.question: In an official agility competition under FCI rules, the dog zigzags through the weave poles. How many poles are there?
hints: It's an even number.
It's more than 10.
It's the same as the number of months in a year.
questions.description: A dog that dodges obstacles better than you do at the mall on the first day of a big sale.
questions.fun_fact: Agility was born in England in the late 1970s, inspired by show jumping competitions for horses.

questions.question: Canine parvovirus mostly strikes unvaccinated puppies and can survive for months in the ground. Which body system does it harm most?
hints: The puppy stops eating.
The puppy loses a lot of fluid and becomes dangerously dehydrated.
It's the system of the stomach and intestines.
questions.description: A tiny virus that sends shivers through every dog breeder.
questions.fun_fact: Canine parvovirus appeared in the late 1970s, and within just a couple of years it had spread all over the world.

questions.question: During a long race through the snow, how many calories does a sled dog burn in a day?
hints: Far more than an adult human, who needs about 2,000.
It runs for many hours a day and also has to stay warm.
It's a five-digit number.
questions.description: A furry athlete who eats breakfast like there's no tomorrow.
questions.fun_fact: In races, sled dogs wear fabric booties to protect their paw pads from the ice.

questions.question: I'm the oldest written papyrus from Egypt, and I describe the daily work of the inspector Merer. What was his team carrying?
questions.answer: Limestone blocks for the Great Pyramid
wrong_answers: Granite for the obelisks of Karnak
Cedar from Lebanon for royal ships
Gold from Nubia for the pharaoh's treasury
hints: I was found in 2013 at an ancient port on the Red Sea.
I was written in the time of the pharaoh Khufu.
My team crossed the Nile from the Tura quarries to Giza.
questions.description: The world's oldest work notebook, and nobody checked its spelling.
questions.fun_fact: The Diary of Merer shows that the stone reached Giza by boat along canals of the Nile, not dragged across the whole desert.

questions.question: I'm a giant temple in Nubia, carved into the rock for Ramesses II. In the 1960s, I was cut into blocks and moved up a hill. Why?
questions.answer: A huge dam was going to flood me
wrong_answers: The desert sand was burying me
They wanted to take me to a museum
hints: The problem came from the Nile River.
Something enormous was built at Aswan.
Behind that project, the gigantic Lake Nasser formed.
questions.description: A move so heavy that even calling every cousin you have wouldn't help.
questions.fun_fact: The Abu Simbel temple was cut into more than a thousand blocks and rebuilt about 65 meters (213 feet) higher up.

questions.question: You're singing the Spanish kids' song “I Had Ten Little Puppies”, and one falls in the snow. How many puppies are left?
hints: It's a really easy take-away sum.
At the start there were ten.
It's the number that comes just before ten.
questions.description: A song where puppies vanish faster than candy from a piñata.
questions.fun_fact: The song helps kids practice counting down: in every verse one puppy goes away, until none are left.

questions.question: Two doors, two guards: one always lies, the other never does. You ask one which door the other would say is the exit. What do you do?
hints: It doesn't matter which of the two guards you ask.
The lie passes through the answer exactly once.
The answer always points to the wrong door.
questions.description: Two guards, two doors and one question: harder than picking an ice cream flavor.
questions.fun_fact: This riddle shows up in the film “Labyrinth” (1986), where Sarah faces two guards watching over two doors.

questions.question: It studies what is right and wrong, asks how we should behave, and is a school subject in many places. What is it?
hints: It is a branch of philosophy.
It deals with values like honesty and fairness.
Many doctors and lawyers must follow a professional code named after it.
questions.description: The subject that asks whether it's okay to eat the last slice of cake without telling anyone.
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from the Greek “êthos”, which means “custom” or “character”.

questions.question: This skull, about 430,000 years old, came from the Sima de los Huesos (“Pit of the Bones”) in Spain. Which human lineage did it belong to?
hints: It isn't our species: it's far too old for that.
DNA from these bones links them to humans who later lived in Europe.
They are ancestors of humans with heavy brow ridges who vanished about 40,000 years ago.
questions.description: A pit where the family tree was traced with DNA almost half a million years old.
questions.fun_fact: Remains of at least 28 people turned up in the Sima, and their DNA is among the oldest human DNA ever read.

questions.question: Three of these human groups are named after the place where their fossils were found. Which one is NOT?
hints: Look for the name that describes a skill, not a spot on the map.
The others come from a cave in Siberia, a valley in Germany and an island in Indonesia.
Its Latin name means something like “the one who is skilled with his hands.”
questions.description: Naming your family after your home address: a very prehistoric habit.
questions.fun_fact: Very few Denisovan bones are known: almost everything we know about them came from the DNA in a single finger bone.

questions.question: Colombia's peace deal with which guerrilla group earned Juan Manuel Santos the 2016 Nobel Peace Prize?
hints: It was Colombia's largest and oldest guerrilla group.
The peace talks took place in Havana, Cuba.
Its name begins with “Revolutionary Armed Forces”.
questions.description: A signature with a very special pen that made headlines around the world.
questions.fun_fact: The deal was signed with a pen made from a bullet.

questions.question: It was founded in 1950, helps refugees and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1954 and 1981. In which city is its headquarters?
hints: It is a UN agency called UNHCR.
It is in a country famous for staying neutral.
It is the same city as the International Red Cross, on a big Swiss lake.
questions.description: An organization that won the same prize twice and still has no time to celebrate.
questions.fun_fact: When UNHCR was created in 1950, it was meant to last only three years; today it works in more than 100 countries.

questions.question: Which of these books was NOT written by Albert Camus, winner of the 1957 Nobel Prize in Literature?
hints: The odd book out was written by an author from Prague.
In that book, a man wakes up to find he has turned into an insect.
Its author was Franz Kafka.
questions.description: A writer who wondered about the meaning of life, and played goalkeeper on the side.
questions.fun_fact: As a young man in Algiers, Camus played goalkeeper, and he said soccer taught him what he knew about morals.

questions.question: In what year did the slogan “Yes we can” become famous in a US presidential campaign?
hints: It was in the 21st century.
That year, the first African American president of the United States won the election.
It was the year of Barack Obama's campaign, four years before he was reelected.
questions.description: Three little words that fit on a cap, on a T-shirt and on the lips of millions.
questions.fun_fact: Obama had already used “Yes we can” in 2004, when he ran for senator in Illinois.

questions.question: Which of these did NOT happen while Andrew Johnson was US president?
hints: Johnson became president in April 1865.
The one you're looking for happened before Johnson took office, while the war was still going on.
It was an order signed by the president before him, Abraham Lincoln.
questions.description: The man who inherited the hardest job at the worst possible moment.
questions.fun_fact: Johnson escaped removal from office in the Senate by just one vote.

questions.question: I was US president and later Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, something no one else has done. I got a giant bathtub. Who am I?
hints: I was president from 1909 to 1913.
I was the first president to throw out the first pitch of a baseball season.
My last name has only four letters.
questions.description: A president who found the White House, quite literally, a bit of a tight fit.
questions.fun_fact: A famous photo shows four workmen sitting together inside the bathtub made for Taft.

questions.question: Hellmann's is to mayonnaise as Tabasco is to…
hints: Tabasco comes in a very small bottle.
A few drops are all you need.
It's made from red chili peppers.
questions.description: A question for people who put sauce on everything, even their cereal.
questions.fun_fact: Tabasco sauce has been made since the 1800s on Avery Island, in Louisiana, in the United States.

questions.question: It's a soft white powder that goes on a baby's skin after a bath, and Johnson's has sold it for over 100 years. What is it?
hints: It comes in a bottle with tiny holes in the lid.
It keeps skin dry so it doesn't get sore.
Its name comes from a very soft mineral.
questions.description: The powder that makes babies smell like babies.
questions.fun_fact: Since 2023, Johnson's baby powder has been made with cornstarch instead of the mineral talc.

questions.question: It's a powder you mix with water, and it tastes like orange. In the 1960s, who made the drink Tang famous?
hints: They drank it in a place with no refrigerators and no fresh fruit.
They drank it far, far away from Earth.
It flew on the spacecraft of the Gemini program.
questions.description: A drink that has traveled more miles than your aunt.
questions.fun_fact: NASA didn't invent Tang: it was created in 1957 by William Mitchell, the same chemist who invented Pop Rocks popping candy.

questions.question: If you walk across the Pons Fabricius in Rome, you step on stones laid there about… how many years ago?
hints: It crosses the Tiber River to reach an island in the middle of the river.
It was already standing when Julius Caesar lived in Rome.
It was finished in 62 BC.
questions.description: These stones have seen more feet go by than the front door of a shopping mall.
questions.fun_fact: The Pons Fabricius is the oldest bridge in Rome still in use almost exactly as it was built.

questions.question: An acoustic guitar has a part called the “bridge.” What is it?
questions.answer: The piece on the body where the strings are attached
wrong_answers: The long part with frets where your fingers go
The top end where the tuning pegs are
The round hole in the middle of the body
hints: It is glued to the guitar's wooden top.
It passes the strings' vibration to the body.
It is at the opposite end from the tuning pegs.
questions.description: A bridge nobody ever walks across, yet it gets everyone singing.
questions.fun_fact: On classical guitars the strings are tied at the bridge; on steel-string guitars they are held in place with small pins.

questions.question: A Tibetan bridge crosses a deep gorge between mountains and sways as you walk. What is it mainly made of?
hints: It's a material that can bend.
Kids also use it to jump at recess.
You can tie knots in it.
questions.description: A bridge for the brave that moves more than your uncle on the dance floor.
questions.fun_fact: In the Andes, the Incas wove hanging bridges out of grass; the Q'eswachaka bridge in Peru is rewoven every year.

questions.question: On farms around Bogotá, you see lots of Holstein cows, white with black spots. What are they mainly raised for?
hints: What they give comes every morning, not just once.
It's used to make cheese, yogurt and butter.
Farmers get it when they milk them.
questions.description: A cow dressed up as a Dalmatian, working a double shift on the farm.
questions.fun_fact: A Holstein cow can give more than 30 liters (about 8 gallons) of milk in a single day.

questions.question: It's French, has a white rind, is named after a region near Paris, and legend says it was crowned “king of cheeses” in 1815. Which is it?
hints: It's soft and creamy inside.
Its rind is white and velvety, not blue and not hard.
Its name is short: just four letters.
questions.description: A cheese with a crown, a white cape and the airs of French royalty.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says diplomats at the Congress of Vienna held a cheese contest, and Brie won.

questions.question: Which animal's milk is used to make French Roquefort and Italian Pecorino Romano?
hints: It's a farm animal.
It lives in flocks, often watched over by herding dogs.
Its coat is used to make wool.
questions.description: Two famous cheeses with the same fluffy mom.
questions.fun_fact: Sheep's milk has almost twice as much fat as cow's milk, which is why sheep's milk cheeses are so creamy.

questions.question: The head of a soap molecule is to water as its tail is to…
hints: Soap molecules are called surfactants.
The tail is the part that “hates” water.
That's why soap gets the oily grime off your dishes.
questions.description: A molecule with a split personality: half best friends with water, half best friends with something else.
questions.fun_fact: The soap tails surround the grease and form tiny balls called micelles, which the water carries down the drain.

questions.question: In “pH”, the H stands for hydrogen. What does the p stand for?
hints: The scale goes from 0 to 14.
It tells you the capacity or strength of the hydrogen ions.
It's the same word as in “… energy”: energy stored up and waiting to be used.
questions.description: Two letters that measure how sour everything is, and one of them has a mysterious past.
questions.fun_fact: The pH scale was invented in 1909 by the Danish chemist Søren Sørensen while he worked in a brewery's laboratory.

questions.question: It comes as a bar, makes lots of bubbles, and you wash your hands with it. What is it?
hints: You find it next to the bathroom sink.
It slips out of your hands when it’s wet.
It rhymes with “rope” and “hope.”
questions.description: Your hands’ best friend after playing in the mud.
questions.fun_fact: More than 4,000 years ago, people in ancient Mesopotamia were already making soap by mixing fat with ashes.

questions.question: After the Great Chicago Fire, the city rebuilt and the first skyscrapers were born there. In what year was the fire?
hints: It happened in the 19th century.
It was a few years after the American Civil War.
It happened a few years before Edison's light bulb was invented.
questions.description: A city that burned down and, instead of crying about it, started building upward.
questions.fun_fact: Legend blames Mrs. O'Leary's cow for kicking over a lantern, but it was never proven.

questions.question: If you walk all the way up Chicago's Willis Tower, how many floors do you climb?
hints: It was the tallest building in the world for more than 20 years.
It's more than a hundred.
It's a three-digit number that starts with 1.
questions.description: A leg workout you can do without leaving the couch.
questions.fun_fact: Fazlur Khan designed the tower as a bundle of nine tubes joined together, an idea that saved a huge amount of steel.

questions.question: Benidorm, on the coast of Spain, boasts a world record for its skyscrapers. Which one?
hints: It's not about the height of a single building.
It's a small city with a huge number of towers.
You have to divide buildings by people.
questions.description: A fishing village that one day decided the beach could be stacked too.
questions.fun_fact: Benidorm is nicknamed “the New York of the Mediterranean” for its skyline packed with towers by the sea.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: a singer who “has the X factor,” like in the famous talent show, has…
questions.answer: A special talent that is hard to explain
wrong_answers: A very deep and very loud voice
Lots and lots of social media followers
A last name that starts with X
hints: In math, x stands for something we don't know yet.
It's what makes you unable to stop watching someone on stage.
The judges look for it, but nobody can quite describe it.
questions.description: A letter so mysterious that mathematicians have spent centuries looking for it.
questions.fun_fact: Simon Cowell created “The X Factor” in the United Kingdom in 2004, and Colombia had its own very popular version.

questions.question: I was an unknown Scottish woman, the audience laughed when they saw me, and in 2009 I sang “I Dreamed a Dream” on a “Got Talent” show. Who am I?
hints: It was the British version of the show.
Millions of people watched the video of my audition online.
My first name starts with S.
questions.description: Proof that you should never judge a song by its cover.
questions.fun_fact: Susan Boyle’s audition got more than 100 million views online in just a few days.

questions.question: What does a YouTube channel have to do to get this silver plaque?
wrong_answers: Be on YouTube for one year
hints: You don't earn it with time or with the number of videos.
It has to do with people who press a red button under your videos.
The gold one is for a million; the silver one is for a number with five zeros.
questions.description: A trophy you don't win by running, but by talking to a camera.
questions.fun_fact: After gold comes the Diamond Play Button, given to channels that reach 10 million subscribers.

questions.question: Guess who: I was born in 1996, my name sounds like “I seek you,” and my logo is a green flower. What was I for?
hints: It was a computer program, not a phone app.
When something arrived, it made a famous “uh-oh” sound.
It's like a grandparent of WhatsApp and Messenger.
questions.description: From the days when the internet made strange noises just to connect.
questions.fun_fact: ICQ was created by a small Israeli company called Mirabilis, and AOL bought it in 1998.

questions.question: Its name comes from the Latin for “edge.” In old Catholic tradition it lay at the edge of hell, and today being there means being stuck and undecided. What place is it?
hints: You won't find this place on a map.
People say plans are here when they're on hold and nobody has decided yet.
It has the same name as a dance where you bend backward to pass under a low bar.
questions.description: The perfect place to wait after your parents answer “We'll see.”
questions.fun_fact: The limbo dance from Trinidad and Tobago has nothing to do with it: dancers bend backward to pass under a bar that keeps getting lower.

questions.question: I'm a saying: “Sow the wind, reap the whirlwind.” What do I teach?
questions.answer: Causing trouble brings you worse trouble
wrong_answers: You should plant seeds on windy days
Storms help the harvest grow bigger
Hard work always brings a big harvest
hints: It isn't advice for farmers.
It's about what happens after you behave badly.
What you do comes back to you, only bigger.
questions.description: A farming saying that won't help you grow a single tomato.
questions.fun_fact: This saying comes from the Bible, from the book of the prophet Hosea.

questions.question: Complete the saying: “Money doesn't grow on…”
hints: The missing word is something from nature.
Leaves, fruit and flowers do grow there.
Birds build their nests in their branches.
questions.description: Parents' favorite line when you ask for the most expensive toy in the store.
questions.fun_fact: Many banknotes aren't made from wood-pulp paper but from cotton fibers.

questions.question: What is this piece of clothing, made by winding a long cloth around the head?
hints: It is worn on the head.
It is very common in India and the Middle East.
Aladdin and many characters from Arabian tales wear one.
questions.description: Several meters of cloth that never end up in the closet.
questions.fun_fact: A Sikh turban can take several meters of cloth, and it has to be wound again every day.

questions.question: The hermit crab is named after hermits. What is a hermit?
questions.answer: Someone who lives alone, away from others
wrong_answers: Someone who travels without ever stopping
Someone who fishes out at sea
Someone who builds houses for others
hints: Many did it so they could pray in peace.
They lived in caves, deserts or mountains.
The word comes from an old Greek word meaning “person of the desert.”
questions.description: A sea tenant who moves out every time the house gets too small.
questions.fun_fact: A hermit crab doesn't make its own shell: it uses empty snail shells and moves into a new one when the old one gets too small.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: Judaism, Christianity and Islam are the three ___ religions.
hints: The name comes from a figure that all three see as their great ancestor.
This figure left the city of Ur, in Mesopotamia.
His wife was called Sarah and his son was Isaac.
questions.description: Three religions with the same great-grandpa on the family tree.
questions.fun_fact: According to the Bible, God promised Abraham as many descendants as there are stars in the sky.

questions.question: Lonesome George is to the Galápagos Islands as Jonathan, the giant tortoise born around 1832, is to…
hints: It is a small, remote island in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean.
It is a British territory.
Napoleon spent his last years there in exile.
questions.description: A grandpa who was already old when your great-grandparents were babies.
questions.fun_fact: Jonathan arrived on his island in 1882 and appears in a photo from that time, already a fully grown tortoise.

questions.question: Take a close look at this tail. Which snake does it belong to?
hints: Its rings are made of keratin, just like your fingernails.
When it feels in danger, it shakes it like a maraca.
Its name includes a noisy baby toy.
questions.description: A tail that comes with its own soundtrack.
questions.fun_fact: Every time the snake sheds its skin, a new segment is added to its rattle.

questions.question: This alligator snapping turtle fishes with a pink “worm” on its tongue. Where does it live in the wild?
hints: It lives in freshwater rivers and swamps.
It shares its swamps with alligators and herons.
Its home is in the rivers that flow into the Gulf of Mexico.
questions.description: A turtle that never goes anywhere without its fishing gear, packed right in its mouth.
questions.fun_fact: It is one of the heaviest freshwater turtles in the world: some males weigh over 80 kg (176 lb).

questions.question: Guess who: “I'm Pascal, a chameleon who lives in a tower with my best friend.” Who is she?
hints: She is a Disney princess.
She has never left her tower.
She has very, very long magic hair.
questions.description: A green buddy who can turn any color he likes, except boring.
questions.fun_fact: Pascal never says a single word in the whole film: he tells everything with gestures and color changes.

questions.question: Its bark gives tonic water its bitter taste, and it grows in the forests of the Andes. Which tree is it?
hints: Quinine is taken from its bark.
For centuries it was used against malaria.
It is also called the “quina tree”, and it appears on Peru's coat of arms.
questions.description: A drink so bitter it tastes less like a soda and more like grandma's home remedy.
questions.fun_fact: The quinine in tonic water glows blue under ultraviolet light.

questions.question: Its can is blue, and in the 1980s its slogan was “The Choice of a New Generation.” Which drink is it?
hints: It's a cola drink.
Its logo is a red, white and blue circle.
Its name starts with P.
questions.description: A question for anyone who always orders “whatever cola you have.”
questions.fun_fact: In 1984, Michael Jackson starred in the “New Generation” ads.

questions.question: The stadium of the Beijing 2008 Olympics is wrapped in crisscrossing steel beams. What nickname did it get?
hints: The nickname comes from something in nature.
What it looks like is made of crisscrossed twigs.
It's where baby chicks live before they can fly.
questions.description: A stadium with a much cuter nickname than its tons of steel deserve.
questions.fun_fact: It was the first stadium to host the ceremonies of both a Summer and a Winter Olympics (2008 and 2022).

questions.question: At Eurovision 2012, Russia came second with a group that baked bread right on stage. Who were they?
hints: They wore headscarves and traditional costumes.
They came from a small village in Udmurtia, a republic of Russia.
They were older ladies, many of them with grandchildren.
questions.description: While other acts brought fireworks, this group brought the oven.
questions.fun_fact: The Buranovskiye Babushki wanted to raise money to rebuild their village church.

questions.question: Tolkien is to Middle-earth as George R. R. Martin is to…
hints: It's a continent with seven kingdoms.
People there fight over the Iron Throne.
It's the setting of “Game of Thrones.”
questions.description: Books so thick they double as gym weights.
questions.fun_fact: George R. R. Martin drew on England's Wars of the Roses for his story.

questions.question: In hieroglyphs, what was written inside a “cartouche”, the oval with a line at its base?
hints: It stands for a knotted rope wrapped around something very important.
Champollion compared the ones on the Rosetta Stone with those on an obelisk from Philae to read his first signs.
It shows who the king is.
questions.description: An oval so important that the Egyptians gave it its own safety rope.
questions.fun_fact: It's called a “cartouche” because Napoleon's soldiers thought it looked like the paper gunpowder cartridges for their rifles, which are “cartouches” in French.

questions.question: Inventors tried to build one for centuries, and patent offices usually reject it. What is a “perpetual motion machine”?
questions.answer: A device that would keep moving with no energy supply
wrong_answers: A clock that sets itself by radio signal
A magnet that never loses its strength
A vehicle that runs only on sunlight
hints: “Perpetual” means it never ends.
It would break the law of conservation of energy.
It would run nonstop without anyone ever giving it fuel.
questions.description: Inventors chased it for centuries, with about as much luck as you have finding the TV remote.
questions.fun_fact: The US Patent and Trademark Office can ask anyone who tries to patent a perpetual motion machine to send in a working model.

questions.question: After becoming F1 world champion, Austrian driver Niki Lauda started his own company. What kind of company was it?
hints: His company had nothing to do with racing.
The company carried his own last name, and he liked to take part in person.
He held a license to fly passenger planes himself.
questions.description: A champion who never learned to sit still, not even after he retired.
questions.fun_fact: Lauda won the F1 title three times and sometimes flew the planes of his own airline, Lauda Air, himself.

questions.question: In F1, which green-striped tires are used when the track is wet but not flooded?
hints: In F1, they are made by Pirelli.
The tires for heavy rain have a blue stripe.
Their name says they sit between the dry tires and the rain tires.
questions.description: For those days when the sky can't make up its mind about raining.
questions.fun_fact: Dry-weather slick tires have no grooves, so in the rain they can't clear the water and the car slides.

questions.question: At the 24 Hours of Le Mans, how many drivers usually share each car in the top class?
hints: They take turns to sleep and rest.
One driver alone could never last a whole day.
As many as the musketeers in the famous novel.
questions.description: A whole day of driving, and there isn't even a lunch break.
questions.fun_fact: At Le Mans, the winning cars usually cover between 4,500 and 5,500 km (2,800 to 3,400 miles) in a single day.

questions.question: Eadweard Muybridge took this series of photos in 1878. What did he want to find out?
questions.answer: If a horse lifts all four legs off the ground at once
wrong_answers: How fast a racehorse can really run
How many steps a horse takes each second
If a horse always lands on the same leg first
hints: Look closely at the legs in each frame.
The human eye couldn't catch it at full gallop.
In one of the frames, the horse seems to fly.
questions.description: The first time anyone checked the video replay on a horse.
questions.fun_fact: Muybridge used a row of cameras that fired one after another, and his photos are ancestors of the movies.

questions.question: My notes on every story, written before I died, are printed in “The Tales of Beedle the Bard”. Who am I?
hints: I was a Gryffindor student and later taught Transfiguration.
In my will, I left this book to a Gryffindor student.
I have a long white beard and I love lemon drops.
questions.description: Bedtime stories that come with notes from a very, very wise reader.
questions.fun_fact: J.K. Rowling handwrote seven copies of the book, and one sold at auction for almost 2 million pounds for charity.

questions.question: I'm a soft leather shoe with no heel that wraps around the foot like a glove. I'm called a moccasin. Who invented me?
questions.answer: The Indigenous peoples of North America
hints: My makers walked through forests and prairies to hunt.
My name comes from an Algonquian language.
I come from the native peoples of what is now the United States and Canada.
questions.description: The perfect shoe for anyone who hates tying their laces.
questions.fun_fact: Many traditional moccasins were decorated with dyed porcupine quills and, later, with glass beads.

questions.question: I'm a flower, and in the 17th century one of my bulbs was worth more than a house. Who went crazy for me?
hints: It's seen as one of the first speculative bubbles in history.
That country has won a lot of land back from the sea.
Today that country still exports millions of these flowers from Amsterdam.
questions.description: An investment so pretty you could put it in a vase.
questions.fun_fact: In 1637, tulip bulb prices suddenly crashed, and many buyers were left with flowers that were worth almost nothing.

questions.question: In colonial Spanish America, what was a “macuquina”?
hints: It was a very common part of daily life in the colonies.
It had an irregular shape and was almost never perfectly round.
It was cut from a metal bar and then struck with a stamp.
questions.description: A word that sounds like a tongue twister, but in colonial times everyone knew it.
questions.fun_fact: Because macuquinas, known in English as “cobs”, were irregular, some cheats clipped little bits of silver off the edges to keep the metal.

questions.question: Its name means “handful,” it already existed in ancient times, and in 2002 it was replaced by the euro. Which country used the drachma?
hints: It is a country on the Mediterranean Sea.
Its capital is one of the oldest cities in Europe.
The Olympic Games were born there.
questions.description: A coin so old it has been changing hands for thousands of years.
questions.fun_fact: The Greek 1-euro coin still shows the owl that appeared on the ancient drachmas of Athens.

questions.question: If someone is called “a real Samson,” like the hero from the Bible, what do they have plenty of?
hints: It helps you carry all the grocery bags in without help.
The Samson of the Bible beat a lion with his bare hands.
It's what you train at the gym.
questions.description: A compliment that comes with a hairstyle attached.
questions.fun_fact: According to the story, Samson's secret was never cutting his hair; when Delilah had it cut, he lost his power.
