questions.fun_fact: The kicker can take his time and set the ball on a stand, the famous “tee”, to aim better.

questions.question: Legend says William Webb Ellis invented rugby. “Webb Ellis” is to “rugby” as “James Naismith” is to…
hints: Naismith was a physical education teacher in the United States.
He invented it at a YMCA school in Springfield, Massachusetts, so his students could play indoors in winter.
The ball has to go through a high hoop with a net.
questions.description: Two gentlemen who, so the story goes, got bored of the usual rules.
questions.fun_fact: The Rugby World Cup trophy is called the Webb Ellis Cup, even though historians doubt he really invented the sport.

questions.question: In rugby, the player running with the ball sticks out an arm and pushes an opponent away with an open hand. Why?
questions.answer: To push off a player trying to tackle them
wrong_answers: To ask the opponent for the ball
To say hello to the opponent
To ask the coach for a substitution
hints: They do it while they keep running.
It's an allowed move that only the player with the ball can make.
It's like saying “get out of my way!” with your hand.
questions.description: A sport where the ball is oval and the manners are, let's say, creative.
questions.fun_fact: This move is called a “hand-off”, and it's allowed, but you can never hit with a closed fist.

questions.question: Nazi Germany built it, it was the first human-made object to reach space, and its engineer later helped the US get to the Moon. What was it?
hints: It flew faster than the speed of sound.
It was designed by Wernher von Braun.
Its name is a letter and a number; the letter comes from the German word for “retaliation”.
questions.description: It was sent off to war, but deep down it always dreamed of being an astronaut.
questions.fun_fact: In 1944 a test V-2 climbed to about 175 km (109 miles), far above the edge of space.

questions.question: It was hard as a brick, didn't melt in the heat, and tasted bad on purpose. It was soldiers' chocolate. What was it for?
hints: It was kept in the backpack.
It gave lots of energy.
It was used when there was no other food.
questions.description: The only chocolate in history that nobody wanted to steal.
questions.fun_fact: The US Army asked for it to taste only a little better than a boiled potato, so soldiers wouldn't eat it as a treat.

questions.question: “Hamlet” is to Denmark as “Titus Andronicus” is to…
hints: Titus is a general who comes home victorious from the war against the Goths.
It is a revenge tragedy, one of the first Shakespeare ever wrote.
It is the same city where “Julius Caesar” takes place.
questions.description: Even before he was famous, Shakespeare knew that nothing sells like a good revenge.
questions.fun_fact: “Titus Andronicus” was probably Shakespeare's first tragedy, and in its day it was one of his biggest box-office hits.

questions.question: Which Shakespeare character says “Out, damned spot!” while sleepwalking?
hints: She is one of the most famous villains in theater.
She helped her husband take the throne of Scotland.
Her husband's name is the title of the play.
questions.description: The toughest cleaning job in history: no stain remover can get this one out.
questions.fun_fact: Many actors believe saying “Macbeth” inside a theater brings bad luck, so they call it “the Scottish play”.

questions.question: In “Romeo and Juliet”, which friar was meant to take Friar Laurence's letter to Romeo but couldn't?
hints: He was a Franciscan friar, like Friar Laurence.
He was locked inside a house for fear of a plague.
He shares his first name with the Beatle who wrote “Imagine”.
questions.description: A perfect plan, ruined by the postal service.
questions.fun_fact: Because the letter never arrived, Romeo didn't know that Juliet was only asleep from Friar Laurence's potion.

questions.question: Paola Bracho is rich and spoiled. She has a poor twin sister and pays her to pretend to be Paola at home. What is the telenovela called?
hints: It is a Mexican telenovela made by Televisa in 1998.
Gabriela Spanic played both sisters.
The title describes someone who takes a place or a throne that belongs to someone else.
questions.description: Being a millionaire wasn't enough: she also wanted a backup copy of herself.
questions.fun_fact: Gabriela Spanic played both twins, so in many scenes she had to act opposite herself.

questions.question: “Topacio,” with Grecia Colmenares as a young blind woman, was a remake of “Esmeralda” (1970). In which decade did it premiere?
hints: It is a Venezuelan telenovela made by the network RCTV.
It premiered more than ten years after “Esmeralda.”
It came out in the same decade as the first Super Mario Bros. game.
questions.description: A precious stone that turned into another precious stone, and then back into the first one.
questions.fun_fact: The story came back in Mexico in 1997, called “Esmeralda” again, with Leticia Calderón in the lead role.

questions.question: They have their own small altar, open off the sides of a cathedral, and are often dedicated to a saint. What are they called?
hints: Rich families often paid for one so they had their own corner for prayer.
The same word is used for the prayer room in a school or a hospital.
Michelangelo painted the ceiling of the most famous one in the world, in the Vatican.
questions.description: Cathedrals have more rooms than Grandma's house.
questions.fun_fact: The word “chapel” comes from the cape of Saint Martin, which was kept in a small shrine guarded by priests called chaplains.

questions.question: I was once the minaret of a mosque, and today I'm the bell tower of Seville Cathedral. My name comes from my weather vane. What am I called?
hints: My lower part was built by the Almohads in the 12th century.
I'm a little over 100 m (330 ft) tall, weather vane included.
My name comes from the Spanish word for “to turn”, which is what a weather vane does in the wind.
questions.description: A tower that changed religions without moving an inch.
questions.fun_fact: Instead of stairs, it has 35 ramps inside, built so people could ride to the top on horseback.

questions.question: Inside the Taipei 101 skyscraper hangs a huge steel ball that steadies it in earthquakes and typhoons. About how much does it weigh?
hints: It has to be heavy enough to stop a giant tower from swaying.
But it still fits inside the building, hanging between the top floors.
It weighs about 660 metric tons (about 730 US tons).
questions.description: A skyscraper that swallowed a giant marble so it wouldn't get seasick.
questions.fun_fact: Visitors can go and see the Taipei 101 ball, and it even has its own cartoon mascots, the “Damper Babies”.

questions.question: The earthquake alarm goes off in your city. Which of these things can that system NOT do?
questions.answer: Warn people days before the earthquake
wrong_answers: Warn people seconds before the strong shaking
hints: The alarm works because electrical signals travel faster than the earthquake's waves.
Mexico City has had one of these systems since the 1990s.
Nobody in the world can predict earthquakes ahead of time.
questions.description: An alarm that runs faster than the shaking ground.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico City, the alarm can give almost a minute's warning when the earthquake starts on the Pacific coast.

questions.question: The Marquis of Pombal rebuilt Lisbon after the great earthquake that destroyed it. In what year was that earthquake?
hints: The shaking was felt in other countries of Europe and even in North Africa.
It struck on November 1, All Saints' Day.
It happened about 20 years before the United States declared independence.
questions.description: A minister who turned a city of ruins into a city built to take a shaking.
questions.fun_fact: To test his new wood-framed buildings, Pombal is said to have had troops march around scale models to imitate an earthquake.

questions.question: I wear a skirt with lots of ruffles and polka dots, and I dance with castanets and clapping. Which country am I from?
hints: It is a country in Europe.
People there speak Spanish.
Its capital is Madrid.
questions.description: A dress that twirls more than a spinning top.
questions.fun_fact: The flamenco dress follows fashion: new designs come out every year for the April Fair in Seville.

questions.question: It looks like a light kimono, shows up at summer festivals in anime and is called a yukata. What fabric is it traditionally made of?
hints: It's a cool fabric, perfect for hot weather.
It comes from a plant.
Almost every T-shirt is made of it.
questions.description: Clothes for watching fireworks without melting in the heat.
questions.fun_fact: “Yukata” means something like “bath clothes”: at first, people wore it after taking a bath.

questions.question: Which African cloth, woven in narrow strips of bright colors, do you see in this photo?
hints: It comes from West Africa.
The Ashanti kings of Ghana wore it at their ceremonies.
Its name has five letters and starts with “K”.
questions.description: A cloth so elegant that once only kings were allowed to wear it.
questions.fun_fact: Every color in kente has a meaning: gold, for example, stands for wealth and royalty.

questions.question: Fred from Scooby-Doo wears a neck scarf like this one, called an “ascot.” Where does its name come from?
hints: The name was famous for something else long before it was something to wear.
The British royal family goes there every year, along with lots of very fancy hats.
It's a racecourse near London.
questions.description: A tie that thinks it's far too fancy for an ordinary knot.
questions.fun_fact: Royal Ascot is so fancy that it has official rules about the size of hats.

questions.question: “Scepter” is to “king” as “crosier” is to…
hints: A crosier is a tall staff used in ceremonies.
Its top usually ends in a hook, like a shepherd's crook.
It is carried by a church leader during ceremonies.
questions.description: A walking stick so important that nobody ever really walks with it.
questions.fun_fact: A bishop's crosier copies the shape of a shepherd's crook, which is used to guide sheep.

questions.question: The inventor of this boot with elastic sides made shoes for a queen and said she wore them every day. Which queen?
hints: Thanks to the elastic, you can pull them on with no laces or buckles.
This queen ruled for more than 60 years and gave her name to a whole era.
She was called “the grandmother of Europe” because her grandchildren sat on thrones all over the continent.
questions.description: Boots so comfy that even a queen could put them on without bending down.
questions.fun_fact: Decades later, The Beatles made a version of these boots so popular that it became known as “Beatle boots.”
